_comment: Last research result per problem (key = algorithm_taxonomy.json problem_id). Written by the research-pr job of algorithm-audit-drift.yml; read by the next run's agents as previous_results.json.

analytic-derivatives.note: Unchanged since 2026-11-16. The closed-form score and information cost O(n(K+p)) and O(n(K²+Kp+p²)) per pass, the per-observation lower bound. A 2026-11-19 search on AD overhead (TMB, CppAD, Stan) found only reports that hand-coded gradients are as fast as AD or faster. The commits since then (569f3f2e, which reuses the first exp() pass in the AC NLL, plus doc-only edits to 39ee46bd and 21e0679a) leave nothing new. The one known improvement, count-weighted covariate-pattern compression, is earlier finding #43925959437.1, triaged 'investigate' as v1.1.0-TODO-196. Nothing has changed that idea, so it is not re-reported. The beta-regression hessian rows mapped here belong to beta regression; their 2026-11 doc changes (observed information) do not affect speed.

lbfgs.note: Updated. Earlier finding #43925959437.2 (make Newton the default) was rejected after the Phase-0 bench (run 44048167550): damped Newton was 1.56x slower than the L-BFGS default on cold-start AC+CR fits at n=200, K=4, p=3. No new evidence overturns that. 2025-26 searches turned up only optimization theory (self-concordant damped Newton, arXiv 2507.23558) and nothing that benchmarks this problem. LBFGSpp has no new performance release, and neither the CRAN Optimization task view (2026-09-23) nor new rival releases (GLMcat 1.0.0, 2025; ordinalNet 2.14, 2026-02; brglm2 1.1.1, 2026-10; VGAM 1.1-14, 2025-12) offer a faster small-d solver. Pattern compression (v1.1.0-TODO-196, investigate) would make each L-BFGS evaluation cheaper; it is already being acted on.

log-sum-exp.note: Trivial, O(K) per call. Commit 569f3f2e already halves the libm calls by reusing the first exp() pass. Nothing faster at equal accuracy.

newton-raphson.note: Updated. On the CR path Newton is opt-in (L-BFGS is the default), and Newton was measured slower than L-BFGS at EDI's sizes (Phase-0, ratio 1.56), so the Newton-default idea stays rejected. The question remains open under v1.2.0-TODO-23. GLMcat (JSS 2025, https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v114.i09) uses Fisher scoring, which for these canonical links is the same algorithm as Newton. It publishes no timing comparisons, so it gives no new evidence. Nothing new on Newton-decrement stopping or AN2C-type regularized Newton was found for small-d concave ordinal MLE.

findings.candidate: Sufficient-statistic / covariate-pattern compression. Tabulate the data once per fit into G distinct (x row, y) patterns with integer counts c_g; for treatment-only, G ≤ 2K, a 2×K table. Then evaluate NLL, gradient and Hessian as count-weighted sums over the G patterns. For AC this is the grouped form of the Poisson-log-linear / multinomial equivalence used by brglm2::bracl with frequency weights. For CR, the existing fast_continuation_ratio_regression_weighted_cpp already accepts subject weights and can take the counts directly. The NLL is exactly the ungrouped NLL: identical (x, y) rows are summed with multiplicity, so no multinomial constant appears. The MLE, vcov and neg_loglik are therefore unchanged up to floating-point summation order.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Theoretical: after one O(n) (or O(n log n) for general X) tabulation, the per-evaluation cost goes from O(nK) to O(G·K). Treatment-only means G ≤ 2K, so roughly n/(2K) fewer flops per eval: about 50x at n=500, K=5. A whole fit then costs about one pass over the data instead of ~30–45 L-BFGS evaluations or ~5–8 Newton gradient+Hessian passes. In the randomization kernel, tabulating each permuted w column is O(n).
findings.suggested_action: Prototype: add a compressed-pattern path to AdjacentCategoryLogitNegLogLik/hessian and route CR through the weighted kernel with counts when the number of distinct (x, y) rows is below about n/2. Start with treatment-only fits and compute_adj_cat_logit_distr_parallel_cpp. Gate on equality of b, ssq_b_1, neg_loglik to 1e-10 against the current path. This mirrors the category-tabulation trick the catalog already adopted for JT/ridit (catalog §6 TODO-9, §10 TODO-1).

findings.candidate: Damped Newton-Raphson with step-halving on the analytic Hessian, with L-BFGS as the fallback. It is already implemented (optimization_alg="newton_raphson") and already used in compute_adj_cat_logit_distr_parallel_cpp; this means making it the default (catalogued as v1.0.5 catalog §2 TODO-1/TODO-2). New external evidence: a benchmark of ordinal logistic MLE (Harrell, fharrell.com, 2024-11-28, revised 2025-06-20) with k=10 intercepts, p=5, n=100,000 timed NR at 0.084 s against optim BFGS at 0.391 s, and at k=1000, p=1 NR at 0.0095 s against BFGS at 0.0375 s. Its stated conclusion: NR is the best Hessian-using algorithm for speed and convergence, and BFGS is appealing only with very many intercepts.
findings.claimed_speedup: About 4–5x wall-clock over BFGS on cumulative-logit ordinal fits at d≈15 (Harrell's benchmark, rms lrm.fit, not the AC/CR models or LBFGSpp). The catalog's theoretical estimate is 1–2x fewer gradient-equivalents.
findings.suggested_action: Run the A/B harness for catalog §2 TODO-1/TODO-2 (wall clock and iterations, AC and CR, n in 50–2000, K in 3–7, p in 1–10). Then switch the defaults to newton_raphson with the existing L-BFGS fallback.

atkinson-da-biased-coin.note: The commits since 2026-11-16 (2c727f4c, abd7e49d, 39ee46bd) only change docs and add an ensure_model_matrix_current() guard in draw_ws_raw. The kernel is unchanged: per (b,t) it rebuilds [w,1,X], forms X'X, runs FullPivLU and takes the full inverse (generate_permutations.cpp:80-119, 258-272). It also still keeps an O(n^2 p) step_data of X_prev copies (:237-248). The catalog's Adopt plan (v1.0.5-TODO-5/TODO-3, catalog P6 and §(d)) is the Schur/block-inverse rewrite, at O(p^2) per (b,t) with C_t^-1 stored per t. This run found that the plan can go one step further. covadap's DABCD.R computes the same probability from the w-independent (F'F)^-1 and an incrementally updated imbalance vector b_t. I checked algebraically that its P = 0.5 - c/(1+c^2), with c = 2a-1, equals EDI's (M11/A+1)^2/((M11/A+1)^2+1), where a = u'z_t. Since a = v'C_t^-1 z_t = v'g_t, the w-independent g_t = C_t^-1 z_t can be precomputed once per t. Each (b,t) then costs O(p) instead of O(p^2), and storage drops to O(np). The singular check s = n_T - v'C^-1v > 0 can be tracked in O(1) per step by the recursive-residual RSS recursion (Brown-Durbin-Evans 1975), which needs the same quantity a, recomputed only at the t where indep_cols changes. A new finding was filed. Nothing else turned up. The 2026 arXiv work (2608.05527 SIGA for minimization, 2607.17176, 2611.08378) is about other designs. carat 2.3.0 NEWS has only a single-covariate bug fix. No new Cholesky or rank-Greville results for 2025-2026 appeared. Sherman-Morrison or greedy sequential D-optimal methods are the kernels the catalog already rejected. The per-arrival assign_wt (O(tp^2+p^3) once per arrival) stays Keep, and its LDLT micro is already catalog P5 / TODO 6.

findings.candidate: Use the imbalance-vector form, as covadap::DABCD writes Atkinson's rule: P depends only on a = z_t' C_t^-1 v_b, where C_t = Z'Z over the previous subjects (w-independent) and v_b = sum over treated z_i (running, O(p) update). Precompute g_t = C_t^-1 z_t once per t; it is w-independent and can be zero-padded to the full column set. Then a = v_b'g_t costs O(p) per (b,t), and pi = (a-1)^2/((a-1)^2+a^2), equal to EDI's (M11/A+1)^2/(...) since M11/A = -1/a. Track the invertibility quantity s = n_T - v'C^-1v (the RSS of w on Z) with the recursive-residual recursion s_t = s_{t-1} + (w_{t-1} - a_{t-1})^2/(1+h_{t-1}), where h = z'C^-1z is precomputed. That is O(1) per step and reuses a. Recompute s directly only at the t where indep_cols changes. With this, step_data shrinks to the g_t and h_t vectors, O(np).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. My own flop count: the draw loop drops from B·n·p^2 (adopted Schur plan) to B·n·p, about p-fold (~10× at p = 10). With the adopted plan's once-per-t precompute included, n = 200, p = 10, B = 501 goes from ~1.2e7 to ~3e6 flops (~4×), or ~400× against the current LU kernel. Memory goes from O(n^2 p) (current) or O(np^2) (plan) to O(np).
findings.suggested_action: When implementing v1.0.5-TODO-5/TODO-3, store g_t = C_t^-1 z_t (and h_t) per t rather than C_t^-1, compute a = v'g_t in O(p), and track s via recursive residuals. Before switching, cross-check probabilities against the current LU kernel and against covadap::DABCD on random designs, including binary covariates where s can hit 0.

branch-and-bound-milp.note: No new candidate since 2026-11-16. The three earlier candidates (BLDM+CKK for p = 1, scip low-rank MIQCP, HiGHS backend) are deferred until 2027-05-01 (v1.2.0-TODO-209/210/211). Nothing found this run overturns the deferral reasons, so they are not re-reported. Their speed claims are unchanged; the conclusion is 'unclear' only because the deferral rule forbids re-reporting them. Checked this run: (1) HiGHS v1.16.0 (11 Nov 2026) turns parallel branch and bound on by default and adds deterministic early termination. If HiGHS is adopted, threads must be pinned to 1 / parallel set to 'off' for EDI's determinism rule. It still has no MIQP, and nothing is quantified, so this is not new evidence against the deferral. (2) designmatch 0.5.5 already defaults to HiGHS (an indirect signal, but it predates the last run and is unquantified). (3) scip 1.10.1-1 is unchanged. (4) ompr 1.0.4 is still linear-only. (5) GLPK is still 5.0 (2020). (6) Mallach's compact linearization (arXiv 1808.08806) is the RLT-1 cardinality-equality row already in catalog §12 table (a). (7) The 2025–26 densest-k-subgraph work (arXiv 2511.11451, 2410.07388) consists of continuous penalty relaxations, not exact solvers at n ≤ 30. (8) BiqBin is an SDP branch and bound, which catalog table (a) already rejects as overkill. The commit 3395b6c3 diff touches only the rcond/cov2cor guard and QR pivot handling, not the MILP.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Commit 3395b6c3 adds a cov2cor rcond check (O(p³), scale-invariant) before chol(Sigma). This is a correctness change with negligible cost against the O(np²) whitening; no speed question arises.

dinkelbach.note: New since the last run: Locatelli, Piccialli & Sudoso (arXiv 2610.04755, 3 Oct 2026) use an outer Dinkelbach loop with an SDP-based fix-and-bound inner solver, and beat Dinkelbach+Gurobi on hard instances. It does not apply here: the feasible set is box/binary only (no cardinality equality), the instances have n = 70–160, it is slower than Gurobi on easy instances (0.73 s vs 20 s), and it needs an SDP solver. Accelerated Dinkelbach (arXiv 2510.26257) targets continuous problems. Charnes-Cooper versus Dinkelbach: no binary benchmark found, and the guidance still favours Dinkelbach when few outer iterations are needed. Gains still come from cheaper subproblems (enumeration, seeding: v1.0.5-TODO-1/-13).

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Commit 3395b6c3 keeps the first rank columns of the pivoted Q and un-pivots R when Z0 is rank deficient. This is correctness only; the cost is unchanged and the step runs once per setup.

simulated-annealing.note: The earlier p = 1 BLDM+CKK candidate is deferred until 2027-05-01 (v1.2.0-TODO-209) and is not re-reported; no new CKK/BLDM work was found (arXiv number-partitioning listing to Aug 2026: only Ising-machine and quantum benchmarks). Other checks: (1) no 2026 source compares SA, tabu and PT under an equal-cardinality swap neighbourhood. (2) An IJCAI 2026 PT runtime analysis is theory on a toy quadratic class. (3) Tabu/SA comparisons on cardinality-constrained portfolios show no dominant heuristic. (4) Johnson et al. (1989): KL is competitive on structured instances and geometric cooling is not beaten by other schedules; this matches catalog table (b) (KL row, n-scaled schedule, TODO-4). (5) dwave-samplers 1.8.0 changes only the build. Nothing new beyond what quantum_upgrade.md TODO-5 and catalog TODO-4 already track.

size-based-dispatch.note: Trivial orchestration (O(1) choice plus an O(n²) mirror check); there is no algorithmic alternative. The cutoff should follow whichever exact solver lands (enumeration to n≈30).

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, unchanged.) With p = 1, mahal_dist, D and l1 are all monotone in |Σ_T x̃ − Σ_C x̃|, which is balanced number partitioning (Kallus 2018, eq. 2.8). Use the balanced largest differencing method (BLDM, O(n log n) time, O(n) space) as the start and Mertens' BLDM + complete Karmarkar-Karp to search towards a certified optimum. The algorithm is anytime and deterministic. The anytime guarantee holds for |n_T − n_C| ≤ 1. Other n_T need Mertens' cardinality pruning, and the first solution is then not guaranteed to be feasible.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for EDI. Mertens reports BLDM at O(n log n). CKK node counts grow exponentially below n_c ≈ 30 (25-bit numbers) and fall above it. With 12 or fewer significant digits, problems of arbitrary size are solvable in practice; double-precision covariates push the hard region to larger n. No source compares this with SA or MILP.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype a C++ BLDM+CKK kernel with a node/time cap behind a p == 1 branch in optimal_solve_auto. Validate it against enumeration at n ≤ 24 and against SA at n = 50/100/200. Add a row to catalog §12 tables (a)/(b).

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, updated.) A low-rank convex MIQCP through the CRAN package scip 1.10.1-1 (Apache ≥ 2): minimize θ subject to θ ≥ ||z||², z = Mw (p continuous), Σw = n_T, w binary. This removes the commercial-solver objection recorded in catalog table (a). New this run: ompr 1.0.4 supports only linear objectives, so this has to use scip's own model API (scip_add_quadratic_cons), not the existing ompr path.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified; no source benchmarks this problem.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look: benchmark scip low-rank MIQCP against GLPK Fortet at n = 15/20/25/30 (p = 5), behind requireNamespace('scip'), and against the enumeration prototype.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, unchanged.) Use HiGHS as the MILP backend, either through ROI.plugin.highs (GPL-2 | GPL-3) or by calling the HiGHS C API from EDI's C++ through highs 1.15.1-2. The 1.15.1-2 NEWS confirms that all 177 C API functions are registered with R_RegisterCCallable (LinkingTo: highs). HiGHS still has no MIQP, so it helps only the linearized models.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Earlier evidence suggests results depend on the formulation.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look: benchmark GLPK against HiGHS on milp_solve_quadratic at n = 15/20/25 and on milp_solve_l1 at n = 20–200, with HiGHS threads fixed at 1 for determinism.

bayesian-bootstrap.note: Re-checked what is new since 2026-11-16. The commits in code_changes.diff are 5bdb9dfb, dd255899, 97e466f1, 3dabce47 and abd7e49d. They add guards and warnings and change no algorithm: min_fraction_usable_samples (v1.0.6-TODO-12), restoring the nested active_resampling_operation (v1.0.6-TODO-185), procedure-NA warnings, a stop for general censoring, the BCa jackknife unit gate, the RR symmetric percentile-t CI on log(RR) (reuses the existing studentized replicate stats), and g-comp fit diagnostics. Weight generation is still one vectorized rgamma(B*n_units, 1), which is O(Bn) and negligible next to the B weighted refits. arXiv's 'Bayesian bootstrap' listing shows nothing relevant after 2026-11-16; the newest item, 17 Nov 2026, is on empirical-Bayes density estimation. Everything that avoids the refits is an approximation of the refit distribution, so it would be an estimator change; the previous result already covered these (GMS/GBS, Lopes-Polson-Sokolov, Ribbon arXiv Jun 2026, Constrained WBB UAI 2026, Private Generative Bootstrap Aug 2026). fwb 1.0.0 (CRAN 2026-10-14) speeds up only its vcovFWB, simultaneous-CI and multinomial-weight paths, and its seed-only determinism matches EDI's model. bayesboot 0.2.3, LaplacesDemon 16.1.8 and rsample 1.3.2 are unchanged. Ziggurat exponential generators (rpgm, about 3x on rexp) would change the realized draws and save only on the negligible weight step. Antithetic or QMC Dirichlet weights: no source quantifies a saving in replicates. The BCa acceleration could come from the replicates themselves (Efron 2014 regression, or Efron-Narasimhan bcaboot) or from influence functions instead of the Bayesian jackknife's n refits. The catalog's NEW-jackknife-influence table already rejects the replicate-regression option (needs B >> n) and tracks the influence-function option as audit TODO-7, with no new evidence since. Per-replicate weighted refits stay warm-started. Batching IRLS across weight vectors is still B x O(n p^2), so it is no asymptotic gain.

analytic-derivatives.note: Exact O(np) NLL and gradient, plus O(np^2) observed and expected information in Ferrari–Cribari-Neto closed form, sit at the cost floor for an exact likelihood. Checked for anything since 2026-11-16: betareg is still 3.2-6 (2026-08-26). gkwreg 2.1.18 (2026-08-24) uses TMB automatic differentiation, which at best matches hand-coded derivatives for a fixed-effects model. nabla 0.7.2 (dual-number AD) targets small models and is no faster. Vectorized special-function libraries (fastapprox, FasterMath) give only about 1e-3 relative accuracy and fastapprox has no trigamma, so they fail the accuracy requirement. Commit 21e0679a only fixed the docs: fisher_information is the observed Hessian. The dead all-n mu pass in ZeroOneInflatedBeta is already tracked in catalog §3.

closed-form.note: Trivial. The Smithson–Verkuilen squeeze and the lgamma/lbeta loglik, deviance and AIC sums are single O(n) passes, so nothing can be faster. The XBX, SLTB and ordered-beta alternatives for 0/1 responses (arXiv 2409.07233, 2509.13167) change the estimator; they are not speedups.

lbfgs.note: Unchanged: betareg (BFGS plus Fisher scoring) and BetaRegression.jl (pure Fisher scoring on closed-form expected information, docs fetched) remain covered by v1.0.5 catalog §1 TODO-7 and O12. The ZOIB split is already Adopt/Prototype. No new LBFGSpp release; the latest, v0.4.0, only adds final_approx_hessian accessors. NEW from code review at e16dd7ae: commit 0e29876e now passes warm_start_fisher_info into fast_beta_regression_with_var_cpp, but optimize_fixed_likelihood never uses it. The lbfgs branch (the default) does not pass it on (_helper_functions_core.h:1635-1636), and optimize_likelihood_newton discards it with (void)warm_start_hessian (:1460). LBFGSpp's minimize() cannot take an initial Hessian either (LBFGS.h fetched). The cached exact observed Hessian from the observed fit is therefore thrown away on every warm-started resampling refit. New finding below.

likelihood-factorization.note: Code re-checked at e16dd7ae. The ZOIB Bayesian-bootstrap replicate still calls betareg::betareg (inference_proportion_zero_one_inflated_beta.R:292), and the parametric-bootstrap simulator still calls rbeta(1) in a loop (:838). Both are already triaged: finding #43925959437.1 is investigate (v1.1.0-TODO-197); finding #43925959437.2 is deferred to 2027-05-01 and is not re-reported. Separability is reconfirmed: Ospina & Ferrari (arXiv 1103.2372, DOI 10.1016/j.csda.2011.10.005); Queiroz & Ferrari arXiv 2605.14011 has had no revision since v1 (2026-05-13). gamlss.dist 6.1-11 (2026-09-10) has no change relevant here.

findings.candidate: One vectorized call over the interior indices: rbeta(length(idx), pmax(mu[idx]*phi,1e-4), pmax((1-mu[idx])*phi,1e-4)). R recycles the shape arguments to the result length.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Removes an O(n) interpreted loop of n separate rbeta calls per PB replicate.
findings.suggested_action: Adopt as a low-priority cleanup, gated on an identical() check of y_sim against the loop under a fixed seed.

findings.candidate: When a valid warm_start_hessian is supplied, polish with Newton steps that start from the cached observed information, e.g. step = H_cached^{-1} g, refreshing H after the first accepted step. The same MLE to tolerance is reached, now at a quadratic rate from a nearby start. Alternatively, if L-BFGS is kept, use the cached Hessian's diagonal or inverse as the initial matrix. LBFGSpp would need a small patch for that; it is MIT-licensed. The same plumbing gap applies to every fitter that routes through optimize_fixed_likelihood, not only beta.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for beta regression. The only external number is an IceCube analysis that reports a 3.6x median reduction in likelihood evaluations when L-BFGS-B is warm-started with both parameters and approximate inverse Hessian. That number comes from a search snippet; the fetched arXiv abstract page of 2609.12941 did not show it, so treat it as unverified. With p+1 typically under 10, one Newton step costs O(n p^2) plus n trigamma calls, about one gradient's worth of special-function work.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate. First decide whether to honour or document warm_start_fisher_info in optimize_fixed_likelihood. Then A/B the warm-started beta refits on bootstrap and randomization paths (L-BFGS cold-curvature vs Newton seeded with the cached Hessian), counting function evaluations and wall time at n=100-1000, p=2-10. This could fold into v1.0.5 catalog §1 TODO-7 (Fisher-scoring polish).

findings.candidate: Use the existing fast_beta_regression_weighted_cpp on the interior rows with the bootstrap weights. Because the ZOIB likelihood is separable, this gives the same weighted beta MLE.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the previous run's fetched EDI benchmark: C++ beta regression is 28.4x faster than betareg.fit at N=1000. Not measured on this path.
findings.suggested_action: Already approved as investigate (v1.1.0-TODO-197); nothing new to do. Re-listed only so the conclusion stays consistent.
findings.new_evidence: No change to the idea. Re-checked at e16dd7ae: the betareg call is still present (line 292). Commits 3dabce47 and 3395b6c3 changed only the worker and estimand paths, not the BB fit.

analytic-derivatives.note: The closed-form score Xᵀ(y−μ) and Hessian −XᵀWX, and the probit generalized-residual forms, cost O(np²), which is the cost of one pass over X, so nothing beats them asymptotically. A new search on AD versus analytic derivatives found only the TMB paper (arXiv 1509.00660), a TMB HMM study (arXiv 2302.10564) and a hydrology preprint (arXiv 2602.06429). None shows AD beating a fused hand-written GLM gradient; the hydrology preprint finds analytic far cheaper. The commits since 2026-11-16 add a separate O(n) NLL evaluator (logistic_irls_neg_ll) for step halving and a Newton-decrement check. Both reuse score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign, so the derivative kernels are unchanged.

irls.note: The C++ LDLT IRLS (logit = Newton; probit = Fisher scoring) is still the right algorithm at small p. sklearn 1.9.1 still recommends exact Newton-Cholesky for n_samples >> n_features, and fastglm 0.1.4 is still the latest release, with no binomial speed changes. New in code (commit 5bdb9dfb): fast_logistic_regression_impl now runs a plain pass first. Only when that pass does not converge does it rerun from the same start with monotone step halving (glm2-style, RJ-2011-012), plus a Newton-decrement convergence fallback. This costs nothing on converged fits; non-converged fits pay at most one extra pass, which is rare and a robustness win, so it is not a finding. New finding: the same commit added compute_weighted_estimate_ivwc to IncidKKCondLogitIVWCSource. It is the per-draw Bayesian-bootstrap replicate, a hot loop, and it fits two stats::glm.fit(quasibinomial) models per draw. Every other weighted-bootstrap logistic path (e.g. inference_incidence_logit.R:57) uses the C++ fast_logistic_regression_weighted_cpp kernel. The deferred finding #43925959437.2 (fractional-logit harden=FALSE glm.fit branch) is not re-reported: its revisit date is 2027-05-01 and nothing new overturns it. The same harden=FALSE estimate_only glm.fit pattern also appears in inference_incidence_gcomp_abstract.R:591 and inference_proportion_gcomp.R:1071, both cold opt-in paths covered by the same deferral reasoning. Separation-diagnosis tooling news: divoRce 1.0-2 (CRAN 2026-10-18; Rusch, Sablica, Hornik, arXiv 2610.09951) and detectseparation 0.4.0. These bear on the catalog's separation-strategy item, not on speed.

lu-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it is one p×p LU log-det in the still-uncalled Firth evaluator (evaluate_penalized_neg_loglik_at), so it is not a hot path. The Firth rivals checked this run (brglm2 1.1.1, 2026-10-07, quasi-Fisher scoring; logistf 1.26.1; the fastglm Firth vignette) all use adjusted-score iteration rather than an LU objective. That matters only if the evaluator gets a caller.

findings.candidate: Route that branch to fast_logistic_regression_cpp(X, y, estimate_only = TRUE), as line 257 already does. It solves the same Bernoulli quasi-score equations by C++ IRLS with an LDLT step. Keep glm.fit as a fallback on non-convergence.
findings.claimed_speedup: fastglm CRAN benchmark vignette (2026-11-06; logistic, p=30): glm.fit 2.75 ms vs C++ Cholesky IRLS 0.67 ms at n=1,000 (~4×), and 29.0 vs 4.7 ms at n=10,000. Not measured on EDI.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look (carried over from 2026-11-16; code unchanged). Switch the branch to the C++ kernel and benchmark one bootstrap at EDI's n.

findings.candidate: Call fast_logistic_regression_weighted_cpp(X, y, weights) in both fits, as the other incidence Bayesian-bootstrap paths already do (e.g. inference_incidence_logit.R:57). Take ssq from the inverse of the returned fisher_information (XᵀWX with W = wᵢμᵢ(1−μᵢ)), which equals glm.fit's unscaled chol2inv(R). Optionally warm-start from the observed-data fits cached by shared(). Keep glm.fit only as a fallback when the C++ fit does not converge.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not measured on this path. The fastglm CRAN benchmark vignette (2026-11-06; logistic, p=30) shows glm.fit at 2.75 ms vs a C++ Cholesky IRLS at 0.67 ms for n=1,000 (~4×). EDI's own benchmark report (R/benchmark/benchmark_model_fits.md, 2026-11-08) shows the EDI logistic kernel at 0.14 ms vs glm.fit at 1.17 ms (8.5×). At the small reservoir and pair counts of KK designs, R-level overhead dominates, so the per-fit gap is likely at least this large. The work is 2 fits × B draws.
findings.suggested_action: Swap both glm.fit calls in compute_weighted_estimate_ivwc for fast_logistic_regression_weighted_cpp, keeping glm.fit as a non-convergence fallback. Check agreement with the current replicate on the v1.0.6-TODO-217 test fixture (log-OR 2.66), then time B = 500 Bayesian-bootstrap draws before and after.

findings.candidate: An exact subset dynamic program written in C++ (deterministic, no solver). Let f(S) be the minimum cost of partitioning the set S of unassigned subjects, with a count of how many size-⌈n/B⌉ blocks are still allowed. The lowest-index subject in S always opens the next block; enumerate its s−1 block-mates among S (s ∈ {⌊n/B⌋, ⌈n/B⌉}), add that block's within-pair distance sum, and recurse. Anchoring on the lowest element removes the B! label symmetry the MILP suffers from. States are bitmasks (2^n, about 1M at n=20, 8 MB of doubles). Transitions per state are at most C(n−1, s−1), so the total is well under 3^n, and 3^16 ≈ 4.3e7 already fits in about 2 s per the cited DP write-up. Exact for any D: custom, negative or asymmetric-symmetrised. Above a size cap, keep the MILP as a fallback.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not benchmarked by any source for this problem. The source for the general submask-partition DP solves N=16 (3^16 ≈ 43M transitions) within 2 s. The fixed-block-size version enumerates far fewer transitions: for n=16, s=4, about 16.5k reachable states × ≤455 transitions, versus EDI's measured 79 s for the MILP. Any ratio is my own estimate, not a measurement.
findings.suggested_action: Add a row to catalog §12 options table (c): 'exact subset DP with lowest-element anchoring (C++, no solver), n ≤ ~22'. Prototype it as an arm of the v1.0.5-TODO-5 benchmark against the current MILP at n ∈ {8, 12, 16, 20}, checking objective equality (not block-id equality). If it wins, dispatch method='ompr' to the DP below the cap. This directly fixes the documented hours-long replay cost at n=16.

findings.candidate: When ⌊n/B⌋ = ⌈n/B⌉ = 2, the objective Σ_blocks D_ij is exactly minimum-weight perfect non-bipartite matching. Dispatch to nbpMatching::nonbimatch, which is already an EDI import used by helper_matching.R. It runs the Derigs/Edmonds blossom algorithm, exact and polynomial (O(n³)). blockTools' algorithm='optimal' uses the same approach for n.tr=2.
findings.claimed_speedup: Exponential to O(n³). Not quantified by a source at EDI's sizes. Pair blocking is optimally solvable while blocks larger than two are NP-hard (Karmakar 2022, citing Greevy et al. 2004 and Lu et al. 2011).
findings.suggested_action: In solve_optimal_blocks, add a fast path when n == 2B: call the existing compute_binary_match_structure / nbpMatching::nonbimatch on D and convert the pairs to block ids. Add a test that the objective equals the MILP's at n=8, B=4.

findings.candidate: Use HiGHS as the open-source MILP backend, through ROI.plugin.highs if it accepts binary/integer types, or through the highs package's model API directly. designmatch 0.5.5 (2026-02-20), a CRAN matching/blocking-design package, now uses highs as its default solver. The scip CRAN package (1.10.1-1, 2026-10-04, Apache-2.0) is a second option through its own model-building API.

findings.candidate: For dist ∈ {euclidean, mahal}, the kernels return squared distances, so when n mod B = 0 the objective is (n/B) × equal-size MSSC. Exact cardinality-constrained MSSC methods then apply: Piccialli & Sudoso's SDP branch-and-cut, and Brusco-style repetitive branch-and-bound. Re-reported from the previous run; nothing newer turned up in the 2025–2026 arXiv scan.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified against GLPK. Piccialli & Sudoso say they solve instances '10 times larger than ... state-of-the-art exact methods'.
findings.suggested_action: Keep as a note in catalog table (c), below the subset DP. Do not pursue unless exact blocking at n ≫ 20 becomes a requirement.

findings.candidate: An exact clique-based equipartition MIP (Brixius, 'Optimal Matched Block Design for Multi-Arm Experiments', Airbnb, Feb 2025, revised Jul 2025). Per the search summaries it gives globally optimal matched blocks for the multi-arm case and solves most of the paper's test instances to optimality, plus a heuristic for larger instances. This is the 'label-free clique partitioning' row of catalog table (c), which currently cites only Grötschel & Wakabayashi 1989. Brixius is a recent applied source for the same objective as EDI: within-block distance with blocks of given size. Use it as a second exact-MIP arm in the v1.2.0-TODO-23 reformulation benchmark, alongside the subset DP (finding .1) and the symmetry-broken label model.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified here. I could not extract the PDF text, so solve times and sizes come only from search-engine summaries ('solves to optimality on most test instances'). No comparison to EDI's McCormick model is known.
findings.suggested_action: Add Brixius 2025 as a citation on the 'Label-free clique partitioning' row of catalog §12 table (c). In the v1.2.0-TODO-23 benchmark, include a written-out clique-equipartition model (y_ij, triangle rows, size rows) as an arm next to the DP and the symmetry-broken label model at n ∈ {12, 16, 20, 24}. Compare objective values, not block ids.

bca-interval.note: I checked for anything new since 2026-11-16 and found nothing that changes the conclusion. bcaboot is still 0.2-3 (CRAN, 2021). boot is 1.3-32 (2025-08-29). The SciPy 1.18 docs still describe BCa with batch/vectorized evaluation, with no new acceleration method. A search on BCa acceleration without the jackknife turned up only ABC/empirical-influence material, which is already v1.0.5-TODO-7 or already rejected. Owen (arXiv 2508.10083, 2025) and Zrimšek & Štrumbelj (arXiv 2403.20182v3) are about accuracy (BCa under-coverage), not speed. z0 (bca_midrank_cdf), a and the quantiles cost O(B); the n_units jackknife refits are the only real cost. The 2026-11-18/19 commits only add NA warnings and boundary diagnostics to bca_ci_core; the algorithm is unchanged.

double-bootstrap.note: Code at e16dd7ae: ci_calibrated_bootstrap (inference_all_abstract_non_param_boot.R:2345-2408) still draws fresh n_outer (≤101) outer resamples × 51 inner draws inside the 5-point α-grid loop (lines 2369-2383). So the earlier hoist finding (#43925959437.1, triaged investigate as v1.2.0-TODO-23) still stands unimplemented. It is not re-reported because nothing new changes it. New this run: Nankervis (2005, CSDA 49:461-475, doi 10.1016/j.csda.2004.05.023) gives deterministic stopping rules for the second-level (inner) bootstrap. They stop inner replications once more draws cannot change the resulting interval, which is a different idea from the Lee-Young 1996 SPRT, which is approximate. In EDI the inner loop only feeds a coverage indicator (est inside the inner type-8 percentile CI), so most outer resamples settle after a few inner draws. This is filed as a new finding that composes with the hoist. Other items checked and not changing the conclusion: the studentized cheap bootstrap (arXiv 2606.25968, 2026) and the single-inner-sample / fast double bootstrap (arXiv 2506.04573) both change the interval, and the FDB rejection stands (Chang & Hall). Prepivoted RBC (arXiv 2512.00566) is specific to nonparametric regression. Zrimšek & Štrumbelj 2025 find the double bootstrap the most accurate CI method, which supports keeping it.

percentile-bootstrap-interval.note: Percentile, basic, studentized and symmetric intervals, tail-count p-values and the smoothed percentile all run in O(B) to O(B log B) on precomputed replicates. That is microseconds next to the B refits. The 2026-11-19 commits add the min_fraction_usable_samples gate and the raw-ratio extreme checks, which are robustness changes, not algorithm changes. New 2026 searches found the cheap bootstrap family, including the studentized cheap bootstrap (arXiv 2606.25968), and a bagged cBLB for kernel causal estimators (arXiv 2603.13662). All of them change the estimator (t-quantiles with few resamples, or aggregation over bags), so none is acceptable as a speedup. Resampling-free quantile bootstrap (arXiv 2202.10992) applies only to sample quantiles, not to EDI's refit statistics. rsample 1.3.2 (2026-01-30) has no relevant new interval algorithm.

findings.candidate: Draw the outer×inner set once (101 outer refits, each with 51 inner refits) and store each sorted inner distribution, or equivalently u_b, the inner-CDF position of θ̂. Then score coverage at all 5 grid α from the same set, with common random numbers across the grid. The grid and the nearest-coverage pick stay as they are. This is the half of v1.0.5-TODO-2 that keeps the estimator; going to continuous prepivoted α can follow separately after its A/B test.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a source claim; this is arithmetic on the code. About 26.8k → 101·52 + 501 ≈ 5.8k refits (≈4.6×). MetricGate's documentation describes the same trick ('store the sorted inner distributions up front', so each candidate α becomes a lookup), but gives no timing.
findings.suggested_action: Hoist the outer×inner loop out of the α-grid loop in ci_calibrated_bootstrap. This can be done now, ahead of or as step 1 of v1.0.5-TODO-2, and needs no coverage A/B beyond a regression check.

findings.candidate: Nankervis-style deterministic inner stopping. Draw the inner replicates for outer b in small chunks, in draw-index order with per-draw seeds. After each chunk, bound the final rank of est among the inner draws: c_below ≤ final count below ≤ c_below + remaining, and the final finite n lies between the current finite count and that count plus the remaining draws. Stop once the covered indicator is the same for every reachable final configuration, at every grid α still being scored. Because this only skips draws that cannot change covered[b], α_adj and the CI are bit-identical to the full computation for a given seed. It composes with the earlier hoist finding #43925959437.1: one stored outer×inner set scored at all 5 α. The stopping rule then needs to resolve all 5 indicators, so it stops at the most demanding α. Draws that would make est outside the CI at α/4 still need nearly the full 51.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for CIs by a fetched source. The arXiv 2404.05006 Remark 2.10 says Nankervis's rules avoid second-level computation that does not affect the resulting interval. A search snippet (not fetched) reports up to a 15× cut in replications for double-bootstrap tests. Arithmetic on EDI's code, not a source claim: for the roughly 85-95% of outer resamples where est is central, the indicator at α up to 2α = 0.1 with 51 draws is settled after about 3-5 draws on each side of est, about 8-15 inner draws. Non-covered outer resamples need all 51. That gives about 2.5-3.5× fewer inner refits, on top of the hoist's ≈4.6× (≈5.8k → ≈2.0-2.5k refits incl. the final B = 501).
findings.suggested_action: When implementing v1.2.0-TODO-23 (the grid hoist), generate the inner replicates for each outer resample in index-seeded chunks and stop once covered[b] is settled at all grid α. Verify with a regression test that α_adj and the CI are bit-identical to the full computation for fixed seeds, and profile the refit count on the standard benchmark designs.

cluster-block-resampling.note: No change since 2026-11-16. The commits since then do not touch the draw algorithms in resample_group_rows_internal, bootstrap_m_indices_internal or draw_matching_bootstrap_sample_cpp. They are a comment change in bootstrap_match_indices.cpp, get_n() in place of private$n in design_matching_abstract.R and design_abstract.R draw_bootstrap_indices, and the removed IVWC fallback in inference_mixin_kk_passthrough.R, which is in the estimator, not the indices. The counting-pass bucketing plus O(G) Lemire draws is still optimal. The 2025-2026 searches turned up only statistic-level shortcuts or estimator changes. MacKinnon WP 1465 precomputes per-cluster sums for OLS. fwildclusterboot is still archived on CRAN (archived 2024-05-29). lmeresampler's cases bootstrap (R Journal RJ-2023-015) is semantic only. Balanced group-level resampling is still tracked under audit J.

iid-index-resampling.note: Nothing new since 2026-11-16. No 2025-2026 method beats Lemire's nearly-divisionless draw for one fixed range. dqrng is still 0.4.1 (2024-05-28, AGPL-3). The randompack R binding reached CRAN as 0.1.10 (2026-08-24, BSD-3; the C library on GitHub is MIT). It is a cross-platform reference and offers no new bounded-integer algorithm. Systematic alias sampling (arXiv 2509.24089) is for non-uniform weights, and its systematic draws change the estimator. The only faster options are the two earlier findings: the bitset in sample_group_units (#43925959437.1) and batched ranged integers (#43925959437.2). Both are deferred to 2027-05-01 with no new evidence, so they are not re-reported. The conclusion moved from faster_option_found to no_faster_acceptable_found only to keep it consistent with the empty findings list; the deferred ideas still stand. Side note: sample_int_replace_cpp reseeds MT19937 on every call, an O(624) init per replicate. At n around 100 that is comparable to the draw cost, but it is what gives per-draw seeding and determinism, and it is negligible next to the per-replicate refit.

largest-remainder-allocation.note: Trivial: closed-form Hamilton apportionment, O(G log G) over a few strata, run once per call. Any other rounding rule changes the allocation, which is an estimator change.

sort-and-sweep.note: build_draw's stable_sort runs only when preserve_order is set (PRW subsampling, next to a full refit). A stable counting sort on row keys of at most n is O(N+n) with the identical order. New context found: a January 2025 libc++ PR (#104683) proposed radix-backed std::stable_sort for integers, and Boost list evidence still says counting sort wins for small k. Neither changes the inventory's 'immaterial' verdict.

stratified-resampling.note: stratified_bootstrap_indices_cpp and exchangeable_resampling_draws_cpp with replace = TRUE are optimal (Lemire draws). For replace = FALSE, the bitset / partial Fisher-Yates idea is finding #43925959437.1, deferred to 2027-05-01 with no new evidence, so it is not re-reported. As with iid-index-resampling, the conclusion changed only for consistency with the empty findings list. Nothing new on balanced stratified generation was found in 2025-2026: a Darmstadt 2026 thesis covers oversampling stratified bootstrap (an estimator change), and bootsurv on CRAN covers survey designs. rsample 1.3.2 (2026-01-30) is unchanged.

findings.candidate: (a) The same rejection loop, but mark seen positions in a dense, reusable std::vector<uint8_t> or bitset of length n. The RNG calls happen in the same order, so the output is bit-identical. (b) Rate-based dispatch as in dqrng: partial Fisher-Yates on a reusable scratch copy of the ids when k/n > 0.5 (this is v1.0.5-TODO-2 and changes the stream), the bitset otherwise.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the CRAN dqrng vignette, measured against base R rather than EDI. At m=1e6, n=1e4 (1% rate), bitset rejection takes 103 µs, R's hash variant 658 µs and sample.int 1.94 ms. At a 60% rate, partial Fisher-Yates takes 10.3 ms against 63.7 ms for sample.int. Not quantified at EDI's n of roughly 100-1e4, and negligible end to end next to B refits.
findings.suggested_action: When v1.0.5-TODO-2 is picked up, first swap the unordered_set for a reusable dense marker (bit-identical) and microbenchmark it at k/n in {0.25, 0.5, 0.9} with n up to 1e4. Adopt partial Fisher-Yates for k > n/2 only if it is still materially faster. Add the bitset row to the catalog §7 options table.

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, SPE 2025): several unbiased bounded integers from one 64-bit word, with one multiplication and no division per value in the common case.
findings.claimed_speedup: The paper reports 1.5-2.5x on shuffles with fast 64-bit generators and 2.6-4.7x with ChaCha, on in-cache arrays. It was not benchmarked for repeated draws from one fixed range or with 32-bit MT19937. Not quantified at EDI sizes.
findings.suggested_action: No action unless profiling shows RNG/index time matters. If it does, prototype a batched bounded_rand in RNG.h and bundle it with the v1.0.5-TODO-2/TODO-3 stream-change window.

brt-monte-carlo.note: The per-draw kernel is unchanged. Masked sums at O(n) per draw is the floor for a fresh resample plus a fresh assignment, and parallel draw materialization is already Adopt (catalog §9). I checked the commits since 2026-11-16, which are all on 2026-11-18/19. They add per-draw w_seed replay for lazy draws (rand_bootstrap_lazy_draw_w, which runs RNGkind and set.seed once per draw: O(1) next to the design re-run), a min_fraction_usable_samples check, and na.rm=FALSE handling inside compute_two_sided_brt_pval_with_sequential_mc. None of them changes the algorithm. New searches found nothing for BRT speed from 2025–26. The arXiv API showed no 2026 sequential Monte Carlo testing paper. BootstrapTests 0.1.1 (GPL-3, 2026-11-14) is about which statistic and resampling scheme give valid tests, not speed. simctest is still 2.6.1. Hash-augmented multilevel splitting (arXiv 2607.12853) targets tiny permutation p-values, which matter little at EDI's B≈501. The Fischer–Ramdas betting finding still stands and is re-reported only to attach the DOI fetched this run and the scope change from the 2026-11-19 sequential Monte Carlo commit.

kaplan-meier-product-limit.note: Re-checked FastSurvival 2.0.0 (CRAN, 2026-11-16, MIT). Its presorted rmst_fast/KM path is the same idea as the already-Adopt presort-once step (catalog §5), and it has no resampling routine. weightedsurv 0.1.0 (MIT) adds weighted KM/RMST but no faster algorithm. The multinomial-weight formulation (1412.1735) was already weighed. The CRAN Survival task view names nothing new beyond prodlim's 'fast algorithm', which is the same product-limit sweep.

logrank-sweep.note: FastSurvival survdiff_fast is still a two-pointer merge over presorted data, the same as the planned presort+merge (Adopt). The CRAN Survival task view's permutation log-rank option (clinfun) uses fixed pooled scores, which do not carry over to BRT draws, where the pooled sample changes with each resample. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

ridit-scoring.note: pridit 1.1.1 (2026-05-31) only refits its PCA pipeline per bootstrap draw. pim 2.0.4 and the large-data PIM fitting paper (1808.05868) solve a different, quadratic pseudo-observation problem. The O(n+L) level-slot rebuild (ridit_kernel_level_slots.md TODO-3) is still the only improvement.

sort-and-sweep.note: New: the CAFS preprint (arXiv 2605.25040, May 2026) claims 1.7–3.1× over pdqsort when K≪N, but only on large arrays. Small-n benchmarks still favour std::sort at a few hundred elements. Counting by level for few-level keys is already tracked (TODO 9).

streaming-moments.note: Trivial: one O(n) pass, the cost of reading the input. The shifted one-pass accuracy fix is already Adopt (TODO-4).

value-space-bisection-selection.note: No 2025–26 work on HL or X+Y selection turned up. Monahan, Antille's O(n log n) linearization and the slope-selection-style quasilinear algorithms are already weighed in catalog §6.

findings.candidate: Sequential Monte Carlo testing by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSSB 87(4):1200–1220, 2025). The p-process is anytime-valid, the binomial and binomial-mixture strategies stop early for both rejection and futility, and the updates are closed form at O(1) per draw over the common-random-number prefix (get_brt_distribution_prefix).
findings.claimed_speedup: This is the paper's claim, not a measurement on EDI. On real data under Fisher's sharp null at α=0.05, the binomial strategy used a mean of 85 permutations (median 53), against 160–200 for Besag–Clifford and a fixed T=1000 (arXiv 2401.07365v5 §7.4). There is no comparison with EDI's Clopper–Pearson band.
findings.suggested_action: No new action: this is already v1.2.0-TODO-34 (investigate). Cite the verified DOI 10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf014, and add the na.rm=FALSE and non-finite-prefix contract from the 2026-11-19 commit (5bdb9dfb) to that TODO's scope.
findings.new_evidence: Two things are new since 2026-11-16. (1) The DOI is now fetched and verified (JRSSB 87(4):1200–1220, published 2025-04-04); last run cited it unfetched. (2) Commit 5bdb9dfb (2026-11-19) changed the sequential Monte Carlo loop: non-finite prefixes under na.rm=FALSE now return NA, and the min_fraction check is not applied. Any betting-rule port must keep that contract. The decision itself does not change.

No new literature on analytic CLMM Hessians turned up.

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: Both earlier findings still stand and are re-reported only so their triage decisions follow them; there is no new evidence. (1) The cluster-weighted native GH objective for the weighted Bayesian-bootstrap path is v1.0.6-TODO-40 (investigate). The code is unchanged: helper_ordinal_mixed_fit.R still calls clmm with nAGQ=20 and row weights. The 2026-11-18 commits touched only GEE separation handling, the KKGLMM X accessor and argument asserts. (2) Stringer exact-gradient AGQ: arXiv 2310.01589 is still v2 (2024-11-11) with no journal DOI. Also checked: GLMMadaptive 0.9-9 (2026-11-17; NEWS shows only minor changes, still no ordinal family); mixor 1.0.7 (2026-07-03); tramME 1.0.8 (2025-09, GPL-2); the lme4 GLMM paper arXiv 2607.12184 (Laplace/AGQ description only, no timings); arXiv 2508.15665 (PCA-AGQ for Bayesian inference, not relevant at 1-D).

lbfgs.note: Only the joint Stringer exact-gradient AGQ + L-BFGS finding stands (already proposed as v1.2.0-TODO-11). The LBFGSpp release page still shows v0.4.0 as the latest, so there is nothing new. No 2026 work on L-BFGS for random-intercept GH likelihoods was found.

model-simplification-surrogate.note: The inventory row is still stale. compute_weighted_clmm_estimate (inference_ordinal_KK_clmm_abstract.R:257) and the KKGLMM weighted path (inference_ordinal_KK_combined.R:531) both call weighted_ordinal_random_intercept_fit (clmm with a random intercept), not a fixed-effects surrogate. Retire or rewrite the row. No literature on fixed-effects surrogates for weighted CLMM bootstrap replicates was found.

multistart.note: The 5-start log σ grid plus L-BFGS plus Newton polish is still fine for non-separated data. New since 2026-11-16: Sablica, Hornik & Rusch (arXiv 2610.08100, v2 2026-10-23) give a single linear-programming criterion for whether a finite MLE exists in cumulative-link (and other categorical) models. That allows a cheap existence pre-check before running all starts on separated data or replicates; see finding. No 2025-26 evidence against deterministic σ grids was found.

findings.candidate: A cluster-weighted native GH objective (w_g multiplying each group's log-integral and its gradient), using L-BFGS warm-started from the point estimate (same as the previous run's finding).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The mechanism (FD gradients plus an inner Newton step per clmm objective call, versus one analytic pass) is unchanged from the previous run.
findings.suggested_action: No change: continue v1.0.6-TODO-40. ordinal 2026.7-26 is still current, so clmm's weight semantics are unchanged.

findings.claimed_speedup: The paper reports 2–4× over lme4/GLMMadaptive for Bernoulli GLMMs. Against 20 fixed nodes it has not been quantified, and the gain is probably modest.
findings.suggested_action: No change: cite the paper in v1.2.0-TODO-11 / TODO-153. Still arXiv v2 with no journal DOI.

findings.candidate: Before fitting, run the single linear-programming overlap test of Sablica, Hornik & Rusch (2026) to decide whether a finite MLE of the cumulative-link fixed part exists. When it does not, skip the multistart and polish and mark the fit or replicate non-estimable directly, consistent with EDI's separation warnings.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. On separated inputs it saves the whole multistart plus polish (≈5+ L-BFGS runs and up to 50·2d gradients) for one small LP. On non-separated inputs it adds one LP.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate, at low priority: read the paper's LP formulation and check on a separated KK ordinal dataset whether it flags the cases where the CLMM/GLMM fits diverge. If it does, consider it as a shared pre-check alongside the v1.0.6-TODO-122 separation handling.

bernoulli-coin-flips.note: Trivial: one uniform per subject, pair or cluster, using the R-parity MT stream. There is nothing faster at EDI's sizes. Checked since 2026-11-16: the commits only touch asserts, docs and the KK14 matching threshold, not the draw kernels (generate_permutations_matching_internal and draw_binary_match_assignments_cpp are unchanged). No new 2026 work on bit-packed or SIMD Bernoulli or sign-flip generation turned up. Bit-optimal Bernoulli samplers (about 2 bits per draw, arXiv 1304.1916) save random bits, not wall time, when MT words are this cheap, and bit-packing was already rejected in catalog P1 because it breaks the stream.

fisher-yates-shuffle.note: Checked: the Durstenfeld shuffle on Lemire bounded_rand in RNG.h remains the standard optimum (O(n), one word per position), and block_ra_batch is unchanged (vectorized runif plus a radix order). There is no new evidence on either previously filed constant-factor option, both triaged defer until 2027-05-01, so neither is re-reported. (1) Batched ranged integers: new since the last run is Microsoft STL PR #6119 (open, not merged). Lemire benchmarks a batched std::shuffle there, 5–7× faster at n = 256–65,536, but with mt19937_64 and against MSVC's slow std::shuffle baseline. That is still a 64-bit generator and still a stream change, so the deferral reason stands. (2) A C++ block_ra_batch kernel: the randomizr 2.0.1 NEWS numbers are unchanged, with no newer release. Randomness recycling (Draper & Saad, arXiv 2505.18879 v5 of 2026-05-07, SODA 2026) claims its Fisher-Yates speed advantage only for cryptographic PRNGs. The low-memory permutation work (arXiv 2505.01287) targets memory, not speed. Floyd, MergeShuffle and sparse sampling pay off only for k ≪ n or one huge permutation; EDI has k ≈ n/2 and many small vectors. Minor: DesignFixedFactorial::draw_ws_raw and the binary-match no-covariate fallback still loop sample() in R. That is per-call overhead of microseconds, the rows are Keep, and switching to the C++ iBCRD kernel would change seed-pinned draws, so this is not a finding.

findings.candidate: A small C++ kernel. For each draw column, a partial Fisher–Yates of k = min(n_T, N−n_T) positions per block, using edi_rng::bounded_rand. It keeps the block_ra law (random rounding of N·prob_T, Bernoulli for singleton blocks) and seeds per draw index so results do not depend on thread count. randomizr 2.0.1 made the same kind of move: blocked assignment now runs in one C++ call.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the randomizr 2.0.1 NEWS (CRAN, Apple M4 Pro, R 4.6.0): block_ra went from 8.9 ms to 1.1 ms at N=20,000 with 2,000 blocks, and from 46 ms to 6.5 ms at N=100,000 with 10,000 blocks, when moving from per-block R calls to C++. EDI's baseline is already vectorized, not per-block, so the gain for EDI is smaller and not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Profile block_ra_batch at typical N·r (1e5–1e6) against a design's per-draw statistic time. Write the kernel under v1.0.5-TODO-11 only if draws are a material share; otherwise close v1.0.5-TODO-11 as Keep. Bundle any stream change with v1.0.6 TODO-149(c).

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 55(1), doi 10.1002/spe.3369). It takes two or more unbiased bounded indices from one random word; with 32-bit words, two indices fit while i(i−1) < 2^32, which covers EDI's n.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the arXiv abstract: it 'can more than double the speed of unbiased random shuffling for small to moderately large arrays'. The paper measured this with 64-bit PCG and Lehmer generators, not MT19937 and not specifically at n = 100–10,000.
findings.suggested_action: Record this as an option in the catalog P2 table. Consider it only together with another planned stream change, such as v1.0.6 TODO-149(c), so seeds are refreshed once, and only if profiling shows RNG words are material.

The closed-form score and information cost O((n_d+n_R)p²), the cost of reading the input. Dual-number or tape AD (nabla 0.7.x, TMB) would only add overhead at small p. Caching lgamma(y+1) is still only a constant-factor micro-optimization.

bfgs.note: The only faster option is already-triaged finding #43925959437.2 (decision investigate/proposed, v1.2.0-TODO-22): a weighted C++ cpoisson Newton in place of R optim(BFGS). It is still open: inference_count_KK_cond_poisson.R:2135 still calls stats::optim, and the 2026-11-17/18 commits did not touch it. Nothing new changes that decision. ucminf 1.2.3 (2026-04-02) is a better BFGS but still quasi-Newton in R, and Newton is still the right choice for a small-p concave likelihood. So no new finding is filed. The label moves from faster_option_found to no_faster_acceptable_found only because the existing finding is already being acted on.

clogit-logistic-reduction.note: The reduction itself is an exact identity, and building it costs O(n_d p), which is optimal. The only faster option is already-triaged finding #43925959437.1 (investigate, approved, v1.1.0-TODO-200): replace stats::glm.fit with fast_logistic_regression_weighted_cpp. It is still open: inference_incidence_KK_cond_logit_glmm_abstract.R:601/606 still calls glm.fit. fast_logistic_regression_weighted_cpp already exists and is used at inference_count_KK_cond_poisson.R:2028. New since 11-16: fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11 on CRAN) contains only fixes. bclogit 1.1.1 (2026-09-30) has Stan syntax and robustness fixes, and it changes the estimator. survival 3.8-x has no clogit speed changes. None of these changes the triaged finding, so it is not re-reported.

closed-form.note: Trivial: for 1:1 strata the conditional likelihood is expit((x1-x2)'b), O(n_d p) per evaluation; nothing faster.

newton-raphson.note: The C++ Newton is at small p on a concave canonical-link likelihood, so it converges quadratically. Gradient-regularized Newton (Doikov arXiv 2308.14742) and trust-region Newton give global-rate guarantees that matter at large or ill-conditioned p, not here. glm2-style step-halving is the robustness item already tracked. No code changes to fast_cpoisson_combined_internal since the last research.

findings.candidate: Route the fit through a compiled IRLS/Newton with prior weights and an offset (or fixed index). Option (a): add a case-weights argument to EDI's existing C++ fast_logistic_regression[_with_var]_cpp, which already supports fixed_idx/fixed_values and warm starts. This is the same change as the cpoisson weights item, v1.0.5 TODO-2. Option (b): use the fastglm-style RcppEigen IRLS (pivoted QR default, step-halving, weights+offset) as a reference.
findings.claimed_speedup: fastglm's own vignette claims 2.2x (QR) to 4.1x (Cholesky) over glm.fit for logistic n=1000, p=30, rising to 2.9x/7.2x at n=1e5. These are the source's claims, not measured on EDI. More gain is likely at EDI's small n, where R per-call overhead dominates (not quantified).
findings.suggested_action: Fold into v1.0.5 TODO-2: add a prior-weights argument to fast_logistic_regression[_with_var]_cpp. Then switch fit_clogit_reservoir_logit (full fit, bootstrap and fit_null) to it, with an equivalence test against glm.fit and a microbenchmark at typical KK sizes.

findings.candidate: The C++ Newton kernel fast_cpoisson_combined_with_var_cpp with a row-weights argument and step-halving: the same concave optimum, quadratic convergence and compiled evaluation. This is the existing catalog §10 Adopt item (v1.0.5 TODO-2), still unimplemented. glm2/fastglm-style deviance-decrease step-halving gives the needed robustness.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source for this model. Expected gains: fewer iterations (Newton, about 5 vs BFGS 20-100) and the R-to-C++ move (cf. fastglm's 2-7x for compiled vs R IRLS).
findings.suggested_action: Implement v1.0.5 TODO-2 (weights argument plus halving in fast_cpoisson_combined). Replace the optim call and benchmark the bootstrap loop.

active-set-projection.note: Checked what is new since 2026-11-16. BSW 0.1.2 (CRAN, 2025-10-06, GPL>=3) is a modified Newton method for the log-binomial model under linear inequality constraints that imports quadprog, and aRD 0.1.0 (2025-08-22) is the identity-link analogue using osqp/quadprog. Both are the same QP/projected-Newton family the catalog already lists. The active-set Newton literature (Forsgren–Murray, which deletes several constraints at once with one factorisation per iteration; Rufibach's active-set GLM; the scar shape-constrained IRLS) offers nothing cheaper than EDI's projection, which reuses the iteration's LDLT at O(|A|p²+|A|³), negligible next to O(np²). The CEM/EM alternatives (Marschner 2014, logbin) converge more slowly by design. No commit since the last run touched project_increment_off_active_bounds.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it is one LDLT and one solve per variance call (O(p³) after an O(np²) X'WX), and the IRLS loop reuses that LDLT for the projection and KKT gate. Nothing problem-specific to reuse.

finite-differences.note: Still finite differences at commit 4ce2b712: constrained_binomial_score_cpp_impl (h=1e-6) and constrained_binomial_hessian_cpp_impl (h=1e-4), plus their weighted versions, at fast_log_binomial_regression.cpp:937-1004. Commit bf7a6ae9 (2026-11-17) sped up loglik_from_eta by skipping exp/log1p for y=1 rows. That lowers the constant of each ℓ-evaluation, but the stencil still needs about 2p(p+1) evaluations against one O(np²) pass for the closed form. The closed form already exists in R (edi_log_binomial_kkt_terms, inference_incidence_log_binomial.R:874-891: score X'(1 or −μ/(1−μ)), information X' diag(μ/(1−μ)²·1{y=0}) X). numDeriv/pracma Richardson and complex-step methods cost more and are not needed. Re-reported as the open v1.1.0-TODO-50 item.

irls.note: Changed from faster_option_found: the only earlier IRLS finding (the ECOS/Clarabel exponential-cone solver, #43925959437.1) was a robustness idea, not a speedup, and it is deferred to 2027-05-01. Nothing new overturns that decision. The Clarabel arXiv 2405.12762 benchmark (CBLIB exponential-cone problems) has ECOS at 2.68 and Clarabel at about 1.45 shifted geometric mean time against MOSEK's 1.0, which says nothing about beating Fisher scoring at EDI's n and p. Code change since then: commit abd7e49d added pull_infeasible_start_into_support (v1.0.6-TODO-142), which moves an infeasible cold or warm start to 90% of the way toward an intercept-only feasible point. This resolves the catalog's 'cold start is still infeasible' incidental and matches the literature advice: detectseparation recommends (−1,0,…,0) or the mean-proportion intercept as start values. New software checked: riskdiff 0.3.0 (2026-02-26, MIT) is a wrapper with fallbacks, not a new algorithm. Trust-region Newton (TRON) is aimed at large-n unconstrained logistic regression, not this problem. No faster acceptable method was found.

kkt-boundary-analysis.note: Checked newer boundary-testing work (arXiv 2509.00223 on LRT boundary asymptotics; the arXiv 2206.15178 chi-bar review) and the detectseparation LP finiteness check (lpsolve via ROI). Nothing cheaper than the multiplier solve that reuses the LDLT, at O(|A|p²+|A|³). The earlier robustness side note still stands: run the LP MLE-finiteness check before fitting. One observation, not a speed issue: the R-side edi_log_binomial_kkt_terms uses a near-bound margin of eta ≥ −1e-4, while the C++ kActiveMargin is 1e-6.

findings.candidate: Exponential-cone program: maximise Σ y·η + (1−y)·log(1−exp η) subject to Xβ ≤ 0 for the log link, or the identity-link analogue with log μ and log(1−μ) terms. Solve it with a primal-dual interior-point conic solver: ECOS (GPL-3, R binding ECOSolveR) or Clarabel (Apache-2.0, needs Rust). This form needs no feasible start and returns certified dual multipliers. Use it as a fallback when IRLS fails the KKT gate, or as the main solver.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a speedup at EDI's sizes. Schwendinger, Grün & Hornik 2021 (§4.6, n=500, hard boundary scenarios), as extracted from the open PDF: only ecos, ipopt* and auglag* always reached the optimum, and their timings are 'rather similar' at 10 covariates. ECOS is 'among the quickest' at 100 covariates. Default glm/glm2 IRLS had 99.9% non-convergence at 10 covariates (1.6% with maxit 10,000), against 0% for ECOS. The timings appear only in a figure, so no IRLS-versus-ECOS ratio is quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add 'exponential-cone interior point (ECOS/Clarabel)' to catalog §1 O4. In the v1.0.5 TODO-32 constrained-solver Prototype, A/B test an ECOS fallback for fits that fail kkt_verdict_at_bounds, on boundary-MLE fixtures (e.g. Schwendinger's simulation C designs), measuring converged rate and wall-clock at EDI's n and p.

findings.candidate: Closed-form score X'(w∘∂ℓ/∂η) and observed Hessian X' diag(w∘∂²ℓ/∂η²) X. For the log link these terms are (y−μ)/(1−μ) and −(1−y)μ/(1−μ)²; for the identity link they are y/μ−(1−y)/(1−μ) and −y/μ²−(1−y)/(1−μ)². The log-link form is already coded in R (edi_log_binomial_kkt_terms) and can serve as the cross-check.
findings.claimed_speedup: Theoretical, not measured: O(np²) against about O(2np³) flops per Hessian, and about 2p² fewer exp/log1p calls. The y=1 shortcut in commit bf7a6ae9 trims the constant of each ℓ-evaluation but not the factor-p gap. It also removes the stencil evaluations that can cross the mean-support boundary near a boundary MLE.
findings.suggested_action: Carry out v1.1.0-TODO-50 (analytic score and Hessian for the log and identity links, weighted and unweighted), and keep an FD cross-check test at interior points.
findings.new_evidence: 2026-11-17 commit bf7a6ae9 changed loglik_from_eta (cheaper ℓ-evaluations for y=1 rows) but left the FD stencils in place. As of commit 4ce2b712 (2026-11-18) they are still at lines 937-1004, so the adopted closed form has not landed and the factor-p gap remains.

analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form Poisson score X'(y−μ) and information X'WX are O(np)/O(np²), the cost of reading X. Searched for AD vs analytic benchmarks (TMB/RTMB, Stan, JAX) dated after 2026-11-16. None is for GLMs. Fourment et al. (phylogenetics) found hand-coded gradients faster than AD. Nothing new.

closed-form.note: Trivial: Pearson χ²/(n−p) dispersion × inverse diagonal, O(n + p³). This is the standard quasi-Poisson estimator, and nothing faster exists.

irls.note: The commits since 2026-11-16 (abd7e49d, fe905ca8, 7bf41069) touch only metadata, assert argument checks, separation docs and jackknife warning suppression. fast_poisson_internal is unchanged: canonical-link Newton = IRLS, LDLT, step-halving with cached Δη. fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11) is still the same Marschner step-halving IRLS, and its NEWS page could not be fetched (socket hang up). No 2026 arXiv paper on faster Poisson IRLS was found. ppmlhdfe/fixest's modified IRLS targets high-dimensional fixed effects, which EDI does not have (small dense p). rqlm 4.5-1 is unchanged and concerns finite-sample CIs. geesmv was archived from CRAN on 2026-10-12. Warm-start / one-step refits change the estimator or are already present. Nothing faster at EDI sizes.

lbfgs.note: L-BFGS is an option only; the default is IRLS. At small p, exact-Hessian Newton on a strictly concave likelihood converges quadratically at O(np²+p³) per iteration. L-BFGS converges only linearly, and first-order methods lack global Lipschitz guarantees for the Poisson NLL (arXiv 2206.00207 and 1511.08895 discussions). The latest LBFGSpp release is still v0.4.0. No new benchmark was found.

analytic-derivatives.note: The information matrix is built in closed form and cached through shared(). Then SE = sqrt([I^-1]_jj). Checked for anything new since 2026-11-16. nabla is still 0.7.2 (2026-10-28) and TMB is 1.9.25 (2026-08-22). Fourment et al. (GBE 2023, doi:10.1093/gbe/evad099) find general-purpose AD (JAX, Stan, etc.) much slower than hand-coded gradients. A JAX Hessian also pays a JIT-compile cost that dominates at small p. The TMB JSS paper compares AD only with ADMB. The fused-pass and block-information searches found nothing quantified that beats closed-form derivatives. Commits since the last run touch only docs, a bit-identical crossprod unroll and a softmax exp reuse. Neither changes the information-to-vcov step.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. How this problem uses it: one LDLT plus a solve against e_j for one diagonal entry (compute_diagonal_inverse_entry), and LDLT.solve(I) in covariance_from_information, at p up to about 20. The re-fetched Eigen benchmark puts LLT only 1.3x faster than LDLT at 8x8, which is not worth losing LDLT's semidefinite tolerance. New 2026 selected-inversion work (arXiv 2601.04904, quadratic selected inversion) targets large structured sparse matrices and gains nothing on small dense ones. The R-side qr() rank check before the Eigen LDLT is the double factorization already tracked in v1.1.0-TODO-155. No commits touched these routines.

eigen-pseudo-inverse.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. This is a fallback for singular or boundary information (symmetric_pseudo_inverse, identified_pseudo_inverse_free_information, the stereotype boundary reduction), not a hot path. SAS NLP and CALIS docs again confirm an eigendecomposition Moore-Penrose (G4) inverse as standard practice for fewer than 60 parameters. Nothing new.

lu-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. invert_free_information still runs FullPivLU and then a separate information.inverse() (_helper_functions_core.h:761-767), so it factors twice. That is earlier finding covariance-from-information#43925959437.1. Its proposed triage is defer until 2027-05-01 (v1.2.0-TODO-11), so it is not re-reported: the re-fetched Eigen benchmark gives the same numbers (FullPivLU 1.9x LLT at 8x8) and is no new evidence. No faster option exists beyond that deferred one, and no code change touched this routine.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. chol2inv on an R factor that already exists (summary_glm_lean) is a closed form. The QR rank check in compute_variance_from_information_matrix is the constant-factor double factorization tracked in v1.1.0-TODO-155. The ColPivQR fallback in compute_diagonal_inverse_entry runs only when LDLT fails. The 2026-11-17 commit changed only a comment in helper_robust_regression.R.

findings.candidate: Factor once. Either reuse the FullPivLU (lu.inverse()), or, for SPD information, use LDLT/LLT with a pivot-based definiteness check and then solve(Identity).
findings.claimed_speedup: From Eigen's dense decomposition benchmark (float; the page says to roughly double the times for double). At 8x8: LLT 0.05 ms, LDLT 0.07 ms (1.3x), PartialPivLU 0.08 ms (1.5x), FullPivLU 0.10 ms (1.9x). At 100x100, FullPivLU is 10.6x LLT. FullPivLU plus PartialPivLU is about 2.6x one LDLT on the factorization step at 8x8. Not quantified for a whole fit.
findings.suggested_action: No new work item. Keep this attached to v1.1.0-TODO-155. The minimal fix is lu.inverse(), which reuses the one factorization. Run an A/B on the vcov fixtures before considering LDLT.

breslow-risk-set-cumsum.note: The code is unchanged since 2026-11-16. .breslow_hazard (helper_survival_fits.R) still has 4 callers and still rescans y_o >= t_k once per event. kk_cox_fully_fixed_null_fit (inference_survival_KK_strat_cox.R:7) still calls the O(nD) R function .cox_neg_loglik_breslow_r. The arXiv API listing to 2026-11-02, coxdev 0.4.0, survival NEWS (3.8-12) and the glmnet coxdev notes still show nothing better than sort plus reverse cumsum. That is also what coxdev, coxstream and FastSurvival 2.0.0 ("risk sets in one pass over the pooled sorted data") do. The previous finding is carried over; v1.2.0-TODO-22 is under investigation.

finite-differences.note: The FD helpers .cox_score_breslow_fd_r and .cox_information_breslow_fd_r still have no callers outside the contract list in inference_survival_coxph.R:203-209, and analytic replacements already exist. New this run: pnd 0.1.3 (2026-05-26, parallel FD with step selection) and a 2026 Voigt preprint, where an FD Hessian cost about 22× a log-density evaluation and a fused analytic pass about 1×. Both confirm that analytic beats any FD variant. Neither Richardson nor hyper-dual is relevant to dead code.

lbfgs.note: No new Cox-specific benchmark of L-BFGS against Newton at small p. LBFGSpp is still v0.4.0 (adds final approximate Hessian accessors, no speed change). The general sources still favour Newton at small p (O(np²+p³) per iteration, quadratic convergence). Side note: after commit abd7e49d, the InferenceSurvivalStratCoxPHRegr initialize() doc and signature give optimization_alg = "lbfgs" as the default, while the dispatch policy (globals.R:1157) maps the class to newton_raphson. The owner may want to confirm which one wins. That is a documentation and consistency question, not a speed finding.

linear-scan.note: Trivial: one O(n) pass, nothing faster. Note: the new kk_strat_cox_drop_within_strata_aliased_cols (v1.0.6-TODO-128, commit abd7e49d) runs per call under harden. It does an O(np) within-strata centering via apply(stats::ave) plus a pivoted QR. A single rowsum()-based centering would cut the R overhead, but the cost is of the same order as one Newton iteration, so it is not material.

newton-raphson.note: New since 2026-11-16: FastSurvival 2.0.0 (CRAN, 2026-11-16, MIT). Its coxph_fast is now an exact Newton-Raphson for a treatment-only (optionally stratified) Cox model, with one sorted pass and step-halving like coxph. That is the same algorithm as EDI's C++ kernel, so it brings no speedup. Its earlier 0.1.0 Pike-Halley closed form was an approximation, an estimator change. coxstream 0.1.0 and Cyclops 3.7.1 are unchanged. The survival NEWS has no fitting change through 3.8-12, and the arXiv API listing to 2026-11-02 has no new exact unpenalized fitter (only subsampling, SGD and GPU work for massive n). The two earlier findings (lazy design ladder, coxdev-based weighted Efron kernel) are carried over. New finding from a re-read of cox_newton_raphson: the loop always does one extra full ll/grad/Hessian pass (O(np²)) only to confirm |Δℓ| < tol. The step-1 candidate value already known from compute_cox_neg_ll_only predicts that test. lifelines reports that a Newton-decrement stop "typically shaves off a single step".

sandwich-estimator.note: No new linear-time sandwich method. The Lin-Wei and Wei et al. cluster sandwich is the outer product of cluster score sums, which EDI computes by prefix sums in O(np) plus O(Cp²). The mmbcv bias corrections are an estimator change, not a speedup. coxdev 0.4.0 provides the same O(n)-per-column score pieces.

sort-and-sweep.note: Boost spreadsort and the djbsort 2026 notes still put the radix crossover at about 1000 to 8192 elements for integer keys. The sort runs once per dataset and is cached via XPtr, so it is not a hot path. Keep.

findings.candidate: After accepting a step-1 candidate with |ll - ll_candidate| < tol, stop with converged = TRUE. When estimate_only and no caller needs the Hessian at the final beta, skip the confirming pass. Otherwise, run only the cheap gradient pass for gradient_norm. A Newton-decrement test (g'H⁻¹g/2 < tol, available from the LDLT already computed) also lets the loop stop before evaluating the candidate. The returned beta is bit-identical under the first variant, because the same candidate is accepted.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for EDI. lifelines' changelog (0.15.0) says its Newton-decrement criterion "typically shaves off a single step, resulting in generally faster convergence". For EDI that means saving 1 of k O(np²) passes per estimate-only replicate, roughly 15-40% of the kernel time depending on k, before the R-call overhead.
findings.suggested_action: Count iterations (num_iter) on a KK and stratified Cox randomization run. If most replicates converge in ≤4 iterations, prototype the early stop for estimate_only = TRUE behind a check that fisher_information and gradient_norm are not consumed, and compare beta bit-for-bit on the package_tests CSVs.

findings.candidate: Use one within-stratum reverse cumsum of exp(eta - max eta) after the existing order(). For the null fit, route to the C++ compute_cox_neg_ll_only. coxdev, coxstream and FastSurvival 2.0.0 all form risk sets this way.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The complexity drops from O(nK) to O(n) after the sort.
findings.suggested_action: Carried over; the code is unchanged. It is already under investigation as v1.2.0-TODO-22, so no new action.

findings.candidate: Build the rungs lazily, generating each only when the previous fit is rejected. The order is the same and the same design is accepted, so results are bit-identical.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. It saves up to about 12 × O(np²) per call, multiplied by the replicates.
findings.suggested_action: Carried over; already v1.1.0-TODO-201 (investigate). When profiling, include kk_strat_cox_drop_within_strata_aliased_cols.

findings.candidate: Build the native weighted Efron Newton kernel on coxdev's header-only C++ (LinkingTo, GPL>=3), then run EDI's damped LDLT Newton.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The saving is the R-side coxph overhead per draw.
findings.suggested_action: Carried over; already v1.1.0-TODO-63. No new action.
