analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form score and Hessian cost O(n d^2), about the same as one pass over the data. Generic AD (TMB, Stan math, JAX, nabla) only adds constant overhead on a likelihood this simple, so nothing is faster. The earlier robustness finding (#43925959437.3, tail-accurate celldiff from rms) is deferred until 2027-05-01. There is no new evidence: rms 8.2-1 (2026-11-01) only adds src/Makevars. So it is not re-reported.

bfgs.note: Unchanged since 2026-11-16. weighted_ordinal_bootstrap_surrogate_fit still calls MASS::polr on every draw. MASS 7.3-66 (2026-07-15) is unchanged. The commits since then are docs and argument checks only and do not touch globals.R:177. Re-reported for consistency (finding .1, investigate, v1.1.0-TODO-202). No new evidence.

irls.note: The fastglm_ordinal finding (#43925959437.4) is deferred until 2027-05-01. fastglm NEWS still gives no timings and nothing on fractional weights; 0.1.4 only fixes builds and edge cases. VGAM 1.1-14 (2025-12-04) is unchanged. Without timings or estimator-equivalence evidence, a speedup over vglm is unproven, so it is not re-reported.

lbfgs.note: Unchanged. Damped Newton on the analytic Hessian (already implemented) is the faster option for the concave links: logit, probit and cloglog. This is finding .2, investigate under v1.2.0-TODO-23. The LBFGSpp releases page shows no release after v0.4.0. The doc commits changed only the tol wording. Cauchit stays on L-BFGS with the Newton-decrement gate because its likelihood is nonconcave.

multistart.note: Updated with new evidence: arXiv 2610.08100 (Sablica, Hornik and Rusch, v2 2026-10-23) and divoRce 1.0-2 (CRAN, 2026-10-18). Together they give one linear program that decides before fitting whether a finite MLE exists for cumulative-link models. Concavity (Pratt) plus existence (the LP) plus a gradient/decrement certificate means the converged point is the unique global MLE. The 4 cloglog restarts are then provably redundant. When the LP shows no finite MLE, restarts cannot help either: 'changing the optimizer cannot restore a finite MLE'. This strengthens finding .5 (investigate, v1.1.0-TODO-203).

newton-raphson.note: Newton with step-halving is still the reference. rms 8.2-1 (2026-11-01) is a build fix only. The orm.fit docs still offer Levenberg-Marquardt for robustness with large offsets, not for speed. ordinal is still 2026.7-26. No 2026 arXiv paper proposes a faster CLM fitter: arXiv 2603.01943 uses VGAM, and 2312.16260 v5 concerns feasibility and has no speed claims. arXiv 2207.06562 and cpmBigData target n of about 1e6, far above EDI's sizes.

reparameterization.note: Centering and scaling is a single O(np) pass. The ordered-cutpoint transforms (softplus or squared increments, NumPyro OrderedTransform, Bambi) are the log-increment family that catalog §2 already rejected because they destroy concavity. Nothing new.

solver-fallback-ladder.note: Trivial orchestration; the rungs run only on failure. VGAM 1.1-14, ordinal 2026.7-26 and MASS 7.3-66 are unchanged, and nothing alters the ladder logic. divoRce could run before the ladder to stop retrying when no finite MLE exists, but that only saves time on failure paths.

findings.candidate: Use the exact-width cell differences from rms orm_links.f90 celldiff (reworked in rms 8.2-0, 2026-10-22). Logistic: 2 sinh(dl/2) sqrt(f1 f2). Cloglog: g2 * (-expm1(-t2 * expm1(dl))). Cauchit: atan2(dl, 1 + x1 x2)/pi. Probit: difference the smaller-valued tail (Phi-bar when x2 > 0). The top and bottom categories use the complementary CDF through argument flipping.
findings.claimed_speedup: None. This is a robustness and accuracy improvement at the same cost: O(1) per observation, a few extra transcendental calls.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: add a tail-accurate cell-probability helper per link in ordinal_fixed_link_helpers.h, and test it against high-precision references for extreme eta. This upgrades the catalog §2 incidental note on cancellation, using the rms 8.2-0 rework as evidence.

findings.candidate: fastglm::fastglm_ordinal(nonparallel=) (fastglm >= 0.1.3, CRAN 0.1.4 dated 2026-11-11). It is a compiled C++ PPO maximum-likelihood fit (logit, probit, cloglog) using observed-information Newton steps, with a block factorization when there are many categories.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified: the NEWS and the ordinal vignette give no timings against vglm, clm or polr.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look, as in the previous run: A/B fastglm_ordinal(nonparallel=) against vglm on EDI's PPO fixtures for agreement, improper-fit handling and wall-clock time. Check fractional weights.

findings.candidate: Gate the restarts on a certificate: (a) a gradient-norm or Newton-decrement test with a positive-definite observed information (as in the existing cauchit and cloglog decrement gate), and (b) the overlap linear program of Sablica, Hornik and Rusch (arXiv 2610.08100, Eq. 25; implemented in divoRce), which decides from the design and outcomes alone whether a finite MLE exists. If the MLE exists and the certificate passes, the point is the unique global optimum, so skip the restarts. If no finite MLE exists, restarts cannot help, so flag non-estimability instead.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. From the code structure, the 4 extra fits per call are skipped whenever the certificate passes. The LP needs one solve per dataset and is cheap, but the paper reports no cost.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into v1.1.0-TODO-203: add the decrement/PD certificate gate, and optionally a pre-fit overlap LP (divoRce as a reference implementation), then A/B on the null-refit multistart cases.
findings.new_evidence: arXiv 2610.08100 (v1 2026-10-06, v2 2026-10-23) and divoRce 1.0-2 (CRAN 2026-10-18) give a single-LP necessary and sufficient test for existence of the MLE in cumulative-link models. This completes the certificate: concavity plus existence plus a local stationarity test proves that restarts are redundant.

findings.candidate: Expose observation weights in fast_ordinal_{probit,cloglog}_regression_cpp, which FixedOrdinalRegression already supports, and fit each draw with EDI's C++ Newton, warm-started from the full-data fit.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Earlier finding #43925959437.1 (SYRK Gram) is rejected; nothing new overturns it, so it is not re-reported. Since 2026-11-16 the only new candidate is batmat (LGPL-3.0, batched SIMD potrf/syrk_add_potrf in an interleaved layout, aimed at <100x100). Its README claims wins over MKL/OpenBLAS/BLASFEO but gives no numbers, and it targets the p^3 and SYRK parts, which the owner's TODO-29/118 measurements show are not a win at p<15. The Eigen CHANGELOG (5.0.1 and unreleased) adds LLT::inverse via xPOTRI, log-determinant helpers and LDLT blocking only for n>96, so nothing changes at p<30. The unreleased LDLT pivot-order and NaN-pivot fixes matter for bit-compatibility when RcppEigen (still 0.3.4.0.2, 2024) updates its bundled Eigen. They are not a speedup. EDI's covariance_from_information and compute_diagonal_inverse_entry already check allFinite on the solve, so the old NaN-pivot 'Success' bug is caught. In the new stereotype rows, chol() plus base rcond() (an LU) is two small factorizations per fit; that is a constant factor at P<30.

eigen-pseudo-inverse.note: Checked COD vs eigen and Jacobi vs QR (Demmel-Veselic, accuracy only) and batched divide-and-conquer eigendecomposition (arXiv 2604.27325, GPU/batch, not small CPU). The eigen-pinv runs only as a fallback, or where the null-space loadings are needed (fast_zinb, the new stereotype boundary reduction), so a spectral decomposition is required. SelfAdjointEigenSolver at p<30 costs microseconds. Eigen's changelog has no speed change for it.

gauss-jordan-elimination.note: The LLT replacement is already Adopt (catalog P1 / TODO 1). Searches found no new head-to-head data. Both are O(p^3), and Cholesky has the better constant on SPD matrices.

lu-decomposition.note: The double factorization in invert_free_information stays tracked in v1.1.0-TODO-155. New in Eigen 5.0.x: FullPivLU/PartialPivLU logAbsDeterminant(). It would help the uncalled evaluate_penalized_neg_loglik_at only once EDI's bundled Eigen updates; LLT 2*sum(log diag) remains the better option there. The code diff since the last research touches no LU code.

qr-decomposition.note: New since 2026-11-16: fastQR 1.2.0 (CRAN, 2026-11-18, GPL>=2) adds an unpivoted LAPACK QR (qr_lapack) and DGEMM backends, but no pivoted or rank-revealing QR. It is not a replacement for ColPivHouseholderQR rank detection and does not change the catalog O11 / kk14 tracking. CQRRPT (CholeskyQR with randomized pivoting, arXiv 2311.08316) targets tall matrices but is RNG-dependent and has no gain at p<30. The commits since then (the hardened-QR drop warning, v1.0.6-TODO-138) change messaging, not the factorization.

schur-complement.note: General guidance (Cornell lecture notes, Higham LDLT pivoting) supports one factorization plus solves over an explicit inverse. That is already noted in v1.1.0-TODO-155 and is a constant factor at p<30. Nothing new found.

sherman-morrison.note: The O(n) closed form is optimal. The robustness finding #43925959437.2 is deferred to 2027-05-01. New source: Ma, Boutsikas, Ghadiri & Drineas (arXiv 2504.04554) give SMW error bounds for approximate inverses. It does not address the compound-symmetry cancellation and is not new evidence for that defer, so the finding is not re-reported. lme4 2.1-0 (2026-10-23) still uses general sparse-Cholesky machinery, which is slower for this case.

findings.candidate: Form only one triangle with a symmetric rank-k update: `MtM.setZero(); MtM.selfadjointView<Eigen::Lower>().rankUpdate(M.transpose());` and pass the selfadjoint view to LDLT. This is Eigen's SYRK path; only the meaningful triangle is updated. Inside the OpenMP region, prefer Eigen's rankUpdate over the BLAS-backed symmetric_crossprod (cblas_dsyrk) to avoid nested multithreaded BLAS. Optionally accumulate MtM row by row while M is filled, so the n x p matrix is never stored.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source. Theoretical: about half the flops of the dominant Gram build (n p(p+1)/2 vs n p^2 multiply-adds), so up to ~2x on that term per replicate.
findings.suggested_action: Swap the Gram build for selfadjointView().rankUpdate in compute_rand_bootstrap_ols_parallel_cpp. Benchmark paired ABBA at typical n (100-1000) and p (3-20), and check results match to 1e-12.

findings.candidate: Use the algebraically identical form W_g = SSW_g + (v_e/a_g) * S_g^2/m_g, where SSW_g = sum (r - rbar_g)^2 is computed by a two-pass or Welford pass over the group. Both terms are nonnegative, so there is no cancellation. The cost is the same O(n) (one more pass over a small group, or Welford in the same pass).
findings.claimed_speedup: none (robustness finding, same O(n) cost)
findings.suggested_action: Add a unit test with v_b/v_e = 1e8 and singleton groups that compares W against long-double or MPFR. If it shows error above 1e-8 relative, switch to the centred form in neg_ll_and_grad and the matching Hessian code.

None is faster for EDI's fixed greedy rule.

qr-decomposition.note: Mostly researched in dense-linear-algebra. Looked at here because of how qr_reduce_preserve_cols_cpp uses it: a fresh QR for each candidate column, O(n p^3). That finding is deferred until 2027-05-01 (v1.2.0-TODO-22). What is new: fastQR 1.2.0 (CRAN, 2026-11-18) adds qr_lapack and fixes complete-Q output after column downdates, but adds no new column-insertion method. arXiv 2412.05905 was revised to v3 (2026-03-06) with no new numbers. Eigen master now has RandColPivHouseholderQR (BQRRP, MPL-2.0). It is not deterministic unless setSeed() is called, and its blocked path only starts at min(n,p) >= 192, where a code comment reports n≈128 losing by 1.5x. EDI's p is far below that, so it does not help. Commit abd7e49d changed only the warning logic in fit_with_hardened_qr_column_dropping, not the numerics. drop_linearly_dependent_cols runs the second qr() only when the design is rank-deficient.

streaming-moments.note: Trivial. scale_columns_cpp is two-pass and memory-bound, with no R caller. arXiv 2605.00247 (2026-04-30) finds a Gram/sum-of-squares batch method fastest but subject to cancellation, and Welford more robust. Neither beats EDI's two-pass on accuracy or meaningfully on speed, so nothing faster is acceptable.

Drop the redundant second round. Cache the candidate lists across replicates, since they do not depend on the weights.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. By counting, up to 24 cor() calls per ladder become 1 (6 become 1 for frailty).
findings.suggested_action: No change: continue v1.1.0-TODO-204 (investigate). Re-reported only so the conclusion and the findings stay consistent.

exact-binomial-test.note: The only faster option is the O(log n) minlike boundary search from R's binom.test, which the owner rejected (finding .2): at EDI's discordant-pair counts the O(d) loop costs microseconds. Nothing new overturns that. arXiv up to 2026-11-17 has no new exact binomial, sign or McNemar computation. The exact2x2 McNemar docs confirm the conditional binomial on discordant pairs is the standard method. DiscreteTests 0.5.3 (2026-11-02) and exact2x2 1.7.0 (2025-08-20) are unchanged since the last check. The sign test is closed form. The code changes since the last run are asserts and docs only.

noncentral-hypergeometric-enumeration.note: The p-value-only Fisher path (finding .1) is deferred to 2027-05-01 and nothing new overturns that, so it is not re-reported. New this run: arXiv 2608.08576 (Aug 2026), a cell-separable DP for exact conditional distributions of r×c tables. It targets r×c tables; a 2x2 table already has a 1-D support, so it brings no gain, and exact CMH with K strata is already a convolution. Liao & Rosen 2001 (doi 10.1198/000313001753272547) uses a recursion plus mode concentration. That is the same O(S) order as EDI's log-weight enumeration, and the minlike p needs the full support anyway. corpora::fisher.pval is fast but not the minlike two-sided p, so it would change the estimator. Code changes since the last run (asserts, docs, the infinite-CMLE nonestimable guard) do not affect speed.

findings.candidate: For p-value-only calls: (a) call EDI's existing zhang_exact_fisher_pval_cpp(n11, n10, n01, n00, delta_0), which uses the same minlike rule with relative tolerance 1e-7 in log space; or (b) the version-safe minimal change: pass conf.int = FALSE to fisher.test, which drops both CI uniroots in every supported R version; or (c) once EDI's minimum R includes it, use fisher.test(..., pval.only = TRUE), new in R-devel, which also skips the CMLE.
findings.claimed_speedup: R-devel NEWS (2026-05-27) says pval.only gives 'substantial speed gains in the case of large counts' but gives no number. By construction it removes the ~3 uniroot searches (tens of O(S) pmf passes) per p-value call. Not measured.

Route the single-stratum pval_exact_fisher through zhang_exact_fisher_pval_cpp, or at least pass conf.int = FALSE, keeping the full fisher.test for the CI and estimate. Gate it with an equality test against fisher.test(...)$p.value. Revisit pval.only when EDI's minimum R (currently >= 3.5.0) includes it.

findings.candidate: R's .binom_test_two_sided_pval_minlike: find the opposite-side boundary (a linear scan on one side of the mode, or a binary search for n >= 1234, contributed by Ravi Varadhan), then p = pbinom(yL) + pbinom(yR-1, upper). That is O(log n) dbinom calls plus two pbinom calls.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the source; by construction it goes from O(n) to O(log n) dbinom evaluations for large n, or about 2x fewer below n = 1234.
findings.suggested_action: Low priority. When zhang_exact_speedups.cpp is next touched, port R's boundary search plus the pbinom tails; otherwise Keep.

exhaustive-enumeration.note: The code is unchanged since 2026-11-16, checked by reading fast_jonckheere_terpstra.cpp. recurse_jt_distribution still runs a composition DFS that is exponential in K, behind the 1e6-allocation DP guard that refuses exact inference beyond that size. The previous finding (tail-only level DP with reachable-range pruning, triaged investigate as v1.1.0-TODO-50) still stands. It is re-reported only to keep this conclusion consistent with a finding; its triage decision should not change. Checked since the last run: (1) the van de Wiel (2001) split-up algorithm, DOI 10.1007/s180-001-8328-6, which splits the probability generating function into two halves and combines them only for the tail; it is coin's non-integer-score exact algorithm. (2) The SAS NPAR1WAY documentation, which confirms the network algorithm retires a node whole when its shortest and longest paths fall on one side of the observed statistic; this is the same rule as the finding. (3) Cheung-Klotz (1997), whose only stated capacity is about 100 per group on a PC. (4) EDISON-WMW (2016), a hash DP over (k, rank sum) that takes 12 min at m=n=500 with ties, so it is slower than a level-count DP on K levels. (5) Sills arXiv 2409.05741, the generating-function view with no speed claim. (6) Releases: coin 1.4-6 (2026-09-30), clinfun 1.1.6 (2026-08-29), exactRankTests 0.8-37 (2026-05-04), kSamples 1.2-12, PMCMRplus 1.9.12, NSM3 1.20, and udist.go (last change 2025-04, cosmetic). None adds a faster exact tied method. No 2025-2026 paper found beats the level DP.

findings.candidate: Same as finding 43925959437.1, now in investigation. Replace the enumeration with a level DP over (level k, treated_so_far), each state holding the distribution of partial 2U. Compute only the two tail masses: retire a node in closed form when its reachable 2U interval [partial+min_rest, partial+max_rest] lies on one side of obs. This is the Cheung-Klotz twoUmin/twoUmax bound, and the same rule as the Mehta-Patel network algorithm's shortest/longest-path retirement used by SAS NPAR1WAY for two-sample linear rank statistics. Replace the 1e6-allocation guard with a DP-cell budget. A related design is the van de Wiel (2001) split-up algorithm: compute the PGFs of the low and high halves of the levels and combine only the pairs that reach the tail. It is a reference variant if the band-pruned DP proves memory-bound, but no source shows it beats a level DP for 2xK tied data.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source for this problem. Catalog theory: 2.8e12 leaves become about 4e8 cell updates at K=11, n=200. van de Wiel (2001) says only that split-up is 'faster than existing procedures in many cases'. Cheung-Klotz claims only that n of about 100 per group is feasible on a PC.
findings.suggested_action: No new action. Keep this under v1.1.0-TODO-50 (catalog §6 TODO-1). When implementing, add the split-up variant and the SAS network-algorithm node-retire rule as design references. Use coin's exact(algorithm='shift') with 2×midrank integer scores, and udist.go, as test oracles.
findings.new_evidence: Nothing new changes the investigate decision. Re-reported only so the method's faster_option_found conclusion has a finding. Added corroborating references fetched 2026-11-18: van de Wiel 2001 split-up algorithm (DOI 10.1007/s180-001-8328-6), and the SAS NPAR1WAY documentation of shortest/longest-path node retirement.

asymptotic-series-recurrence.note: The only commit since 2026-11-16 (39ee46bd) changes roxygen text in fast_math_utils.cpp: it says the upward shift uses no reflection and that x<=0 falls back to R's digamma. The kernels are unchanged. Searched again: Boost and Cephes digamma use recurrence plus a [1,2] rational and the asymptotic series. No source compares them with EDI's shift-to-8 asymptotic series for speed, and the arXiv listing for Sep–Nov 2026 has only analytic digamma results. Digamma and trigamma stay off the O(n) hot path (cached per distinct y). Nothing faster.

closed-form.note: Trivial closed form: O(1) lgamma differences. R NEWS still shows only the 4.5.1 dnbinom/bd0 accuracy fixes, which match the existing near-Poisson accuracy item, not speed.

continued-fraction-lentz.note: Nothing faster beyond earlier finding gamma-family-functions#43925959437.1 (exact DLMF finite sums for integer and half-integer df). That finding is deferred until 2027-05-01. It still holds but is not re-reported, because there is no new evidence. The rsx preprint (arXiv 2606.06434) turned up again but was already cited. Nakayama (2000, JSIAM) reports that modifying factors speed up convergence of the Γ(a,x) continued fraction, but the finite sums make the continued fraction unnecessary at EDI's df anyway. Gil–Segura–Temme (arXiv 1306.1754) is already known and matters only for large a≈x. No new 2026 algorithm papers.

lanczos-stirling.note: No correctly rounded binary64 lgamma from CORE-MATH yet. LLVM libc 2026 patches are half and single precision only. SLEEF 3.9.0 (May 2026) has no published lgamma timing. Intel oneMKL v?Lgamma is proprietary. Rfast's vectorized Lgamma wraps standard code. Lanczos g=7 with 9 terms plus Stirling to x^-13 is already minimal O(1). Nothing faster.

power-series.note: This is the x<a+1 branch of fast_gammaq. The same deferred finding #43925959437.1 covers it (not re-reported, no new evidence). The 2026 Horner/Estrin SIMD work (arXiv 2603.14926) is about generic polynomials. The series here is data-dependent and short, so Estrin gives no gain. Nothing new.

findings.candidate: Add a fast path for integer or half-integer a = df/2 using the exact finite sums: DLMF 8.4.10, Q(n+1,x)=e^{-x}Σ_{k≤n}x^k/k!, and DLMF 8.4.14, Q(n+½,z²)=erfc(z)+e^{-z²}/√π·Σ_{k=1}^{n} z^{2k−1}/(½)_k. df=1 becomes fast_erfc(√(T/2)) and df=2 becomes exp(−T/2). Keep the series/CF path for non-integer a and for a≥30, as Boost does.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Boost.Math says these sums are 'more stable and more efficient than the continued fraction alternative' for a<30 but gives no timing; its accuracy table reports 0 eps on integer/half-integer cases against Rmath's 138 eps max. For df=1 the change swaps an iterative loop plus lgamma/log/exp for one rational erfc. End-to-end gain is likely negligible because each p-value follows a model refit; the main benefit is accuracy.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look, low priority (unchanged from last run). Add the df=1 → fast_erfc(√(T/2)) and df=2 → exp(−T/2) special cases, then the general integer/half-integer finite sums for a<30. Validate against R::pchisq(lower=FALSE) for df ∈ {1..60} and T ∈ [1e-8, 1e3]. Can be folded into the row-O accuracy TODO.

golub-welsch.note: code_changes.diff is empty: no commits since 2026-11-16. _glmm_engine.h:32 still runs a dense SelfAdjointEigenSolver on the n×n Jacobi matrix and takes log(sqrt(pi)·v0²) as log-weights; the 5 copies are unchanged. The earlier finding gauss-hermite-nodes#43925959437.1 is under investigate (v1.4.0-TODO-11i) and still stands. It proposes a shared cached rule built from eigenvalues only, one Newton polish and recurrence log-weights. Nothing new since 2026-11-16 changes it. Checked: lme4 NEWS (2.0-6 symmetrisation; the undated 2.1-0 entry adds normalising constants to nAGQ>1 log-likelihoods, which does not touch node computation); FastGaussQuadrature.jl v1.1.0 (no gausshermite change); statmod 1.5.2 (2026-05-17); pracma 2.4.6 (tridiagonal eigen); gaussquad and fastGHQuad (unchanged since 2022). On arXiv, the newest GH-node papers are still 2509.16716 (Gil–Segura–Temme) and 2603.17448 (modified Halley), both already weighed. 2609.26840 (Pinkse, positive-weight multidimensional rules) and 2604.02041 (Hermite transforms via Golub–Welsch) do not bear on 1-D double-precision rules at n = 7–60. One route not cited before: Laudadio–Mastronardi–Van Dooren (Numer. Algorithms 2022, doi:10.1007/s11075-022-01297-9) take symmetric-weight rules from the SVD of an n/2 bidiagonal matrix. It gives nodes with high relative accuracy in O(n²), plus an algorithm for weights with high relative accuracy. It is a second accurate-weights option for the same investigate item, not a separate speedup. O(n) asymptotic methods still do not pay off at EDI sizes.

findings.candidate: Unchanged from the earlier finding: one shared, cached rule. Nodes come from eigenvalues only (computeFromTridiagonal), polished with one Newton step. Log-weights come from the normalised Hermite recurrence, 1/(H_{n-1}·H_n'), and the rule is symmetrised. New alternative for the accurate-weight step: the Laudadio–Mastronardi–Van Dooren SVD of the n/2 bidiagonal matrix, O(n²), which gives nodes and weights with high relative accuracy.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The rule is built once per fit, so the speed gain is small. Eigen documents about 4n³/3 flops for eigenvalues only against about 9n³ with eigenvectors. The main gain is relative accuracy of the tail log-weights.
findings.suggested_action: Keep the work under v1.4.0-TODO-11i (part D). For the log-weight check at n = 60 and 100, the LMV22 bidiagonal-SVD weights can serve as a second reference next to mpmath or GSTe.
findings.new_evidence: No code or library change since 2026-11-16. Found this run (the paper is from 2022 but was not cited before): Laudadio–Mastronardi–Van Dooren, Numer. Algorithms 92:767–793 (2022), give an O(n²) route to high-relative-accuracy nodes and weights for symmetric rules. It is an alternative implementation for the same investigate item and does not change its decision.

irls.note: Checked what is new since 2026-11-16. CRAN versions are unchanged: geepack 1.3.13, multgee 1.9.0 (r-universe shows 1.9.1 with no NEWS entry), fastFGEE 0.2.2, geeM 0.10.1, glmtoolbox 0.1.12. New since the last run: the geer package (CRAN 0.1.0, 2026-06-23, Rcpp/RcppArmadillo) and Touloumis arXiv 2606.16043 / 2606.16058. Both concern bias-reduced and penalized GEE (estimator changes aimed at small-sample bias). geer's solver is ordinary scoring with step-halving, tolerance 1e-6 and a glm start, so it is no faster than EDI's warm-started closed-form 2x2 C++ kernel. solow-gee (Rust, BSD-3) is plain Fisher scoring with no benchmarks. The search for accelerated or quasi-Newton GEE found only one-step and stochastic GEE2 work aimed at large clusters (estimator changes, no gain at m <= 2). The two new commits add a logit-separation check (an O(n) X·beta pass after the fit), a full-fit separation probe that runs once per object (never per jackknife replicate), and an ordinal cold-start retry that runs only when a warm-started ordLORgee fails. None changes the per-fit cost. The earlier finding gee-fit#43925959437.1 (cache the multgee LOR structure) is deferred to 2027-05-01 and superseded by v1.2.0-TODO-2. There is no new evidence (multgee unchanged on CRAN), so it is not re-reported, and this method's conclusion moves from faster_option_found to no_faster_acceptable_found.

method-of-moments.note: Closed-form O(n) pass over pair Pearson products, still with phi scaling (fast_gee.cpp:126-130); nothing can be faster. findings.candidate: Cache the estimated LOR structure, keyed on (y, pairing m), and pass it back as LORstr='fixed' with LORterm (built with multgee::matrixLOR). According to the multgee reference manual, the structure comes from responses aggregated across clusters into marginalized tables, so covariates do not enter it. It is therefore unchanged across ladder rungs, and across permutation draws whenever y and m are fixed.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. It removes one association-model fit per ordLORgee call; what share of the call that is remains unknown.
findings.suggested_action: Profile one ordLORgee call at typical KK sizes to split the time between LOR estimation and Fisher scoring. If LOR estimation is a material share, prototype the cache and A/B it against current fits for coefficients identical within tolerance.

The real alternative for concave fits remains Newton, which is already catalogued.

newton-raphson.note: The code is unchanged: FullPivLU at _helper_functions_core.h:1490, no descent-direction check, and warm_start_hessian is still (void)-ignored at :1460. The previous finding (#43925959437.1, triage investigate → v1.2.0-TODO-23) still stands. New since 2026-11-16, all modest: arXiv 2604.27406 (2026-04-30) gives a regularized Newton variant whose exact-Hessian version the abstract claims is faster than Mishchenko's regularized Newton on convex benchmarks (no sizes or numbers). arXiv 2605.00581 (2026-05-01) applies the same sqrt(||g||) regularization to Newton boosting and reports convergence where vanilla Newton diverges. RcppTrust 0.2.1 (2026-10-31) is a thread-safe C++ port of trust (GPL-2), useful only as a test reference. No new evidence of a wall-clock win on well-behaved concave fits; the benefit remains robustness.

findings.candidate: A gradient-regularized Newton step: solve (H + λ_k I) s = −g with λ_k ∝ sqrt(‖g_k‖) (Mishchenko / AN2C rule), plus a [−λ_min(H)]_+ shift when LLT/LDLT reports indefiniteness. Factor with LLT/LDLT instead of FullPivLU. Keep step-halving and the L-BFGS fallback as the safety net.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified at EDI's sizes. arXiv 2604.27406's abstract claims its exact-Hessian regularized Newton is faster than Mishchenko's (2023) on convex benchmarks, with no numbers given. arXiv 2302.10065 and 2505.04807 report only that the method is 'competitive'. The expected gain is robustness: fewer halving cascades and L-BFGS hand-offs.
findings.suggested_action: No change to the existing plan (v1.2.0-TODO-23). When prototyping, also consider 2604.27406's adaptive λ rule as a second variant. Measure halving cascades, L-BFGS hand-offs and wall-clock on NB, beta and stereotype.
findings.new_evidence: 2026-04-30 arXiv 2604.27406 claims (abstract only) an exact-Hessian regularized Newton faster than Mishchenko's rule. 2026-05-01 arXiv 2605.00581 reports the sqrt(||g||) rule converging where vanilla Newton diverges. Neither changes the decision; they add a candidate λ schedule to test.

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: Both earlier findings stand; the kernels are unchanged (fast_poisson_glmm.cpp:200/259 still compute exp(eta+b_k) over all n per node, and :283 still does one weighted_crossprod per node). New for this problem: Charvat 2023 (Am. Stat. 77(1):41-50, doi 10.1080/00031305.2022.2110939) gives closed-form Lambert-W cluster modes (LAGHQ). Its abstract names the normal random-intercept Poisson model as an application. Last run used it only for survival frailty. For the Poisson GLMM with cluster totals S_g and Lambda_g, the mode b = sigma^2 S_g - W0(sigma^2 Lambda_g e^{sigma^2 S_g}) is exact, so AGQ needs no nested Newton solve. It then becomes cheap for this kernel too, where 60 non-adaptive nodes are needed today. lme4's 2026 GLMM paper (arXiv 2607.12184) and GLMMadaptive 0.9-9 (2026-11-17) bring no new algorithm.

irls.note: The IRLS row is the weighted stacked logistic glm.fit refit for incidence leaves (no random effect), already O(n p^2) per iteration and warm-startable. Searches for PIRLS vs Fisher scoring on small clusters found accuracy arguments (PQL bias at cluster size 2), not speed alternatives. Nothing faster found.

laplace-approximation-tmb.note: Re-checked on CRAN: glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 (2026-09-29), TMB 1.9.25 (2026-08-22) and RTMB 2.0 (2026-09-17) are unchanged since the last run. New glmmFEL 1.0.6 (2026-09-18, GPL-3; fully exponential Laplace EM) is an accuracy refinement with no speed claim. The lme4 2026 paper restates Laplace as cheap and AGQ as more expensive. Laplace remains less accurate at cluster size 2, and EDI's own GH kernels remain the faster route for the bootstrap paths (existing Prototype).

lbfgs.note: Only through the AGQ finding: with LAGHQ the Poisson mode and its derivatives are closed form, so the exact AQ gradient keeps L-BFGS (or Newton, per Charvat's closed-form Hessian). LBFGSpp is still v0.4.0, with no line-search or performance change.

log-sum-exp.note: Trivial: O(K) per group, max-shift fused with the weights; nothing faster.

louis-identity.note: The cluster-total Louis beta-beta block for the Poisson GLMM (finding .1, v1.1.0-TODO-205) still stands; the code is unchanged. Today's search found nothing faster than the analytic Louis identity for GHQ observed information (lme4 derivatives paper 2011.10414 uses the same identity; R-VGAL is Monte Carlo). Under LAGHQ the same per-group totals feed both the mode and the Louis terms.

soft-barrier-penalty.note: Trivial, O(1). blme/glmmFEL-style priors change the estimator, not the speed.

findings.candidate: Lambert-W adaptive GH (LAGHQ, Charvat 2023) applied to the Poisson random intercept. With per-group totals S_g = sum w*y and Lambda_g = sum w*e^eta (the cluster-total form of finding .1), the integrand mode solves S_g - Lambda_g e^b - b/sigma^2 = 0. Its exact solution is b_g = sigma^2 S_g - W0(sigma^2 Lambda_g exp(sigma^2 S_g)), with curvature Lambda_g e^{b_g} + 1/sigma^2. AGQ with a handful of nodes therefore costs O(G*K') plus one W0 per group, with no nested Newton solve. The mode's derivatives are closed form, which gives an exact gradient for L-BFGS and a Hessian for Newton. Evaluate W0 in log space (or via its asymptotic form) for large arguments to avoid overflow; Boost lambert_w0 (BSL-1.0) or lamW (BSD-2) supply it.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Charvat's abstract claims only that the closed-form derivatives make Newton-type maximization 'convenient and efficient'. Derivation: 60 nodes become roughly 5-11 adaptive nodes on O(G) totals, so per-evaluation work after the O(n p) eta pass drops about 5-10x relative to the cluster-total non-adaptive kernel. Must be measured.
findings.suggested_action: Add to v1.2.0-TODO-11 / performance TODO-153 as the Poisson-GLMM AGQ route, built on v1.1.0-TODO-205 (cluster totals). Prototype after TODO-205 lands, then A/B LAGHQ with K'=7-11 against 60-node GH and glmer(nAGQ=25) on the R8 grid.
findings.new_evidence: New for this problem (2026-11-18): Charvat 2023 LAGHQ was found last run only for survival frailty. weighted-gram-accumulation.note: What changed: commit 6a3651ee (2026-11-17, compiled-code audit) rewrote score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign (_helper_functions_core.h:601-648) to handle two off-diagonal columns per pass over i, giving two independent add chains. The result stays bit-identical. The loops are still scalar, though: there is no SIMD reduction hint, no Eigen dot, and x_j and w are still re-streamed for each column pair. So this commit partly addresses the latency half of finding #43925959437.1 (now investigate under v1.2.0-TODO-12), but not the SIMD half. New this run: the LLVM vectorizer docs (fetched today) say clang vectorizes FP reductions only with the -fassociative-math -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math subset, which EDI does not use. On clang, EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION expands to `clang loop vectorize(assume_safety)` (edi_simd.h:21). The 2020 llvm-dev thread says that pragma relaxes memory-dependence checks, not FP reassociation, so on clang builds (macOS) the 'minimal' option (a) of the earlier finding would probably not vectorize. Explicit multi-accumulator code, Eigen's packet dot (which weighted_crossprod's col-major branch already uses) or an xsimd/tabmat-style tile kernel are portable; the omp-simd hint works only under GCC with -fopenmp(-simd). Unchanged: symmetric_crossprod (DSYRK) is still the best X'X at p ≲ 50. OpenBLAS's latest release is still 0.3.34 (level-3 race fix; no SYRK speedups). RcppEigen on CRAN is still 0.3.4.0.2. fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11) changes nothing here. tabmat 4.3.0/4.3.1 (Oct/Nov) disabled fast math and fixed bugs, with no dense-sandwich speed change. The numpy sandwich-product proposal (2025-08) restates that X'diag(w)X is the GLM bottleneck and points to tabmat, without numbers. Rejected: RXTX (arXiv 2505.09814) saves about 5% of multiplications via recursive 4×4 blocking for XX^T. It is unweighted, changes rounding and gains nothing at p ≤ 20. Recursive GPU SYRK (arXiv 2601.08082) and batmat's batched interleaved small-matrix syrk/gemm_diag are both off-shape for EDI's single-fit tall-skinny Gram. The √w∘X + DSYRK / rankUpdate option stays Keep-tracked (TODO-155); I found no new benchmark at EDI's sizes. An idea not filed as a finding: for weighted-bootstrap refits sharing one X, the Grams of B replicates could be computed as one GEMM, Z'W, with Z = row-wise x_i⊗x_i (upper triangle) and W = n×B weights. That would need replicates run in lockstep, so it is noted for the owner only.

findings.candidate: Same idea as #43925959437.1, refined. (a) Replace the inner reductions with code that vectorizes on both compilers: form u = w∘x_j once per j (as the col-major weighted_crossprod already does, at :321-328) and use Eigen's u.dot(x_k) / u.dot(x_k0), u.dot(x_k1), whose packet reduction is explicit SIMD, or write explicit fixed multi-lane accumulators in a fixed combine order. Do not rely on EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION: under clang it expands to vectorize(assume_safety), which per the LLVM docs does not permit reassociating FP reductions without the -fassociative-math subset. (b) Fuller: a tabmat-style register-blocked tile kernel (xsimd FMA accumulators, lower triangle only, k-blocks summed in fixed serial order), with X'r fused as an extra column.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source at EDI's sizes. The basis is mechanism: SIMD width (2–8 doubles) plus fewer loads per FMA. The 2-chain unroll already in the code removes part of the latency bound only.
findings.suggested_action: Under v1.2.0-TODO-12: note that 6a3651ee already took the bit-identical 2-accumulator step. In the planned microbenchmark (n ∈ {100, 500, 2000}, p ∈ {2, 5, 10, 20}), compare the Eigen-dot / explicit-lane version against the current kernel on both GCC and clang. Do not count on EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION for clang builds; check with -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize / -fopt-info-vec-missed.
findings.new_evidence: 2026-11-17 commit 6a3651ee changed the kernel: two scalar accumulators, still no SIMD, so the finding partly stands. 2026-11-18 fetch of the LLVM vectorizer docs: clang needs the reassociation flag subset to vectorize FP reductions, so option (a)'s EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION route, which maps to vectorize(assume_safety) on clang, would not vectorize there. That narrows the recommended fix to Eigen dot, explicit lanes or xsimd.

best-improvement-swap.note: Since the 2026-11-16 run, the three commits (39ee46bd, 7bf41069, 25100e2f) only changed roxygen and comments in design_fixed_greedy.R and design_fixed_greedy_d_optimal.R. The search code is unchanged. The best-improvement rule still defines the design's allocation distribution, so first-improvement, KL, tabu and other pivoting rules are design changes. GreedyExperimentalDesign is still at 1.6.1 (CRAN, 2026-04-30). Its ChangeLog lists only the GPU full-greedy loop with an O(p) incremental update and no pruning; EDI already has the O(p) update. The newer allocation papers I checked propose different designs, not a faster exact best-swap search: BRAIN (arXiv 2312.17230), fastrerandomize (JAX acceptance-rejection, arXiv 2501.07642), PSRSRR (2602.07613), Langevin rerandomization (2604.07524) and nonlinear GSW (ICML 2026). Under SETH, exact bichromatic Max-IP needs n^{2-o(1)} time in moderate dimension (Chen, Theory of Computing 2020), so no exact subquadratic scan exists for the general per-pair delta. The exact speedups already tracked still stand: G = M'M for O(1) per pair, and Mahalanobis routed through the pruned D engine. Still open, from reading the code rather than the literature: DOptimalPruneObjective::prune_threshold uses 2·max_P, the global maximum of |P| (optimal_design_search.cpp:52, :148). A per-treated-row max over current controls would be a tighter bound that is still valid and returns the same optimum. I have no literature source for it, so it is not filed as a finding.

fisher-yates-shuffle.note: Changed from faster_option_found. The only candidate, batched ranged random integers (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, arXiv 2408.06213), is finding #43925959437.1, which triage rejected: about 1× end to end, and it would change every seed-pinned stream. I found no new evidence, so I have not re-reported it. edi_rng::fisher_yates_shuffle (RNG.h:343) already uses Lemire's nearly-divisionless bounded draw on 32-bit RRng words. A search for 2026 shuffle work turned up nothing newer than MergeShuffle and the batched method. It is O(n) once per draw and negligible next to the swap search.

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire): several unbiased bounded indices from one random word, so fewer RNG calls per shuffle. Alternatively, a partial shuffle of only min(n_T, n−n_T) positions.
findings.claimed_speedup: The paper reports 1.4–2.6× on whole shuffles with 64-bit PCG/Lehmer generators. It was not measured with MT19937 or 32-bit words. In this problem the shuffle is a negligible share of the per-draw cost, since the swap search dominates, so the end-to-end gain is not quantified and is likely near 1×.
findings.suggested_action: Keep it as a recorded option in catalog P2. Adopt it only together with another planned RNG-stream change, so seeds are refreshed once. Do not prioritise it for this problem.

sort-and-sweep.note: These are one-time O(n log n) layout and level-coding steps, dominated by the fits that follow. New 2026 sort papers target large arrays of 10^3 to 3·10^7 keys with AVX2: CAFS (arXiv 2605.25040), a frequency sort for low-cardinality keys, and F5, an in-place MSD radix sort (ICDE 2026). Neither applies to a stable sort of an index permutation with a custom comparator, which is what the GLMM data constructors do. A counting sort on dense group ids remains immaterial, as the catalog records. value-space-bisection-selection.note: Unchanged. The arXiv API listing of 'Hodges-Lehmann', sorted by date, shows nothing algorithmic since 2025: the 2026 items are causal trees and U-processes. X+Y selection searches returned only Kaplan et al. 1802.07041 and Minkowski-sum selection 0809.1171. DescTools is still 0.99.60 (2025-03-28) and robslopes still 1.1.4 (2025-12-19). Hmisc pMedian (5.2-0 to 5.3-1) is newly seen. It is a Fortran 2018 port of Monahan's randomized HLQEST and one-sample only. Monahan-style selection is already in the catalog §6 options table (line 1037), which notes the randomized pivot would break RNG streams; pMedian draws 1000 uniforms, which confirms it. Nothing overturns that decision. The levers remain wilcox_hl_kernel_hoisting.md TODO-3 (tie-safe early stop) and TODO-4 (warm bracket).

walsh-average-enumeration.note: Unchanged. The stats::wilcox.test(conf.int) paths cost little at EDI sizes, and the two-sample point estimate already uses the C++ kernel. Hmisc pMedian and DescTools::HodgesLehmann give exact one-sample HL with ties, which is useful as a test reference: a 2026 r-devel post and the DescTools docs repeat that wilcox.test's pseudomedian is wrong under ties. Neither offers a weighted or two-sample HL that would be faster than EDI's kernel. The SE scale issue (F7/I2) is a correctness matter, not speed.

findings.candidate: Exact closed forms from per-group centered moments. For pairwise differences: var = N/(N−1)·(var_pop(T)+var_pop(C)) with N=n_T·n_C. For Walsh averages: sum = (m+1)S/2 and sum of squares = ((m+2)Q+S²)/4 over centered d. Two-pass centering also removes the sum/sum² cancellation.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source. Algebraically O(n_T·n_C)→O(n_T+n_C) and O(m²)→O(m).
findings.suggested_action: No new decision. Keep the deferral (revisit 2027-05-01), and do it together with the HL SE scale fix when inference_all_KK_wilcox_ivwc.R / fast_wilcox_hl.cpp is next touched.

jackknife.note: [delete-one jackknife: approximate_jackknife_distribution_beta_hat_T_private / build_jackknife_deletion_draws] The commits since 2026-11-16 (abd7e49d, fe905ca8, 6afa9ece) add gates and do not touch the algorithm. A full-data separation check (v1.0.6-TODO-122) now runs before the refits, which saves all n refits when the fit is separated. A minimum of 5 deletion units (v1.0.6-TODO-135) and a BCa gate run after the replicates are built; below 5 units that wastes at most 4 refits, which is negligible. The refit loop at inference_all_abstract_non_param_boot.R:2047-2091 still runs n_units R6 refits for every class, least-squares ones included. So finding #43925959437.1 (exact least-squares downdate, investigate, v1.1.0-TODO-207, still open) still stands and is re-reported. New this run is supporting evidence only: Belotti & Peracchi 2020 (DOI 10.1177/1536867X20976312), whose Stata jackknife2 uses the leave-one-out formula for linear estimators, and clusterIV 0.2.0 (CRAN 2026-10-01, MIT), which uses exact Woodbury block leave-cluster-out updates. The linearized/one-step jackknife (#43925959437.2) is deferred to 2027-05-01 and is not re-reported. Rubinstein & Hopkins (arXiv 2512.12572, v2 May 2026) gives Newton-step leave-k-out error bounds of about k·d/n² for logistic regression without global strong convexity. That firms up the accuracy side, but it is still an estimator change and the per-unit hooks are still missing, so it does not overturn the deferral. The V-fold jackknife (arXiv 2607.22493) is an estimator change already noted. Zhao et al. 2026 (arXiv 2609.13736) run 2n exact GLM refits and call speeding them up an open question, so they offer nothing faster. bcaboot's regression acceleration is already rejected in the catalog (line 1676). | [Quenouille–Tukey bias/variance: compute_jackknife_summary] Closed-form moments, O(n_units) once the replicates exist; nothing faster can exist. | [weighted delete-one jackknife, Bayesian BCa: approximate_bayesian_jackknife_distribution_beta_hat_T] The new commits only change gating and warnings. The exact WLS downdate in the re-reported finding covers it, and the serial vapply is a parallelisation item, not an algorithm change.

findings.candidate: Linearized delete-one-unit/cluster jackknife (CV3L): from the full fit, form per-unit score s_g and information J_g contributions and their totals. The replicate shift is b^(g) = (J − J_g)⁻¹(s − s_g), so G k×k solves replace G nonlinear refits (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb, Econometric Reviews 2025, Eq. 17–18). This is the exact-downdate analogue of the catalog's one-step Newton row, but it builds no per-replicate objects at all. Offer it as an opt-in option for â (v1.0.6-TODO-7 area) and jackknife SE, with the exact refit staying the default.
findings.claimed_speedup: About 40× cheaper than exact CV3 in the paper's empirical (tuition-fee) example (arXiv 2406.00650v2, Section 7.2); not otherwise quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add a CV3L row to the catalog's NEW-jackknife-influence table, citing DOI 10.1080/07474938.2025.2515161. If v1.0.6-TODO-7 adds per-unit score and information hooks, prototype the linearized jackknife on the same hooks as an opt-in option, A/B against the exact jackknife.

findings.candidate: Exact closed-form delete-one-unit/cluster replicates for least-squares estimators: β^(g) = (X'X − X_g'X_g)⁻¹(X'y − X_g'y_g). Form the per-unit cross-products once in O(n·k²), then do G k×k solves (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb 2023, Eq. 15). WLS uses the same identity with weights; a mean difference reduces to O(n) arm-sum updates. Keep the refit loop for nonlinear fits.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified against naive re-estimation. MNW 2023 (arXiv 2301.04527, Section 4) reports about 12–26× over the score method for CV3 at N = 2^20. Belotti & Peracchi 2020 claim a 'substantial reduction in computing time' from the leave-one-out formula without giving numbers. Against EDI, the saving is the whole refit loop: n_units R6 fits become O(n·k² + G·k³).
findings.suggested_action: Already approved as v1.1.0-TODO-207 (investigate); nothing changes the plan. Add Belotti & Peracchi 2020 (Stata jackknife2) and clusterIV (exact Woodbury block leave-cluster-out updates, MIT) as prior art and references to the TODO.
findings.new_evidence: Supporting sources only, no change to the idea: Belotti & Peracchi, Stata Journal 20(4) 2020, DOI 10.1177/1536867X20976312, a production jackknife for linear estimators built on the leave-one-out formula; and CRAN clusterIV 0.2.0 (2026-10-01), a leave-cluster-out jackknife via exact Woodbury block updates. At commit 4ce2b712 the refit loop is unchanged and v1.1.0-TODO-207 is still open.

greenwood-variance.note: Re-checked at 4ce2b712. The C++ get_restricted_mean_se_for_group_at_tau (sort plus suffix sums, O(n log n)) stays Keep. The R weighted_restricted_mean_se_diff (inference_survival_rmst.R:436-448) still builds n_j and d_j with vapply over unique times, O(n·D) per arm per Bayesian-bootstrap replicate. The commits since the last run only changed which tau it reads (rmst_horizon()); the algorithm is unchanged. The previous finding #43925959437.1 (investigate, v1.2.0-TODO-22) stands. New literature since 2026-11-16 changes nothing here: Zhang–Shao–Ye arXiv 2511.01110 on IPTW-KM variance is an estimator change for estimated propensity weights, not a speedup. The method is marked trivial in the taxonomy, but the R weighted version is not single-pass, which is why the finding exists.

kaplan-meier-product-limit.note: Re-checked at 4ce2b712. weighted_km_median (km_diff.R:628-650) still recomputes sum(row_weights[i:n]) at each distinct time. weighted_survival_stat_for_group (rmst.R:364-395) still calls survival::survfit(weights=) per arm per Bayesian-bootstrap replicate. The C++ km_stat_inline, rmst_from_km and get_survival_stat_for_group* sweeps remain optimal for one evaluation (Keep). km_median_arm_bounds runs once per fit and is memoised (Keep). New refinement from re-reading the code: y, dead and w are fixed across Bayesian-bootstrap draws and only row_weights change. A shared weighted sweep can therefore compute each arm's sort order and tie groups once per object, cutting each replicate to an O(n) weighted pass instead of O(n log n). No new faster KM algorithm turned up. survival 3.8-12 NEWS has no speed or weights changes, and FastSurvival 2.0.0 has no case weights. The Rust survival crate 2.1.0 (MIT) has weighted survfitkm and RMST, usable only as a cross-check.

mover-interval.note: Closed form from two intervals, O(1); nothing faster can exist. Problem-level searches found nothing new on MOVER for median differences. Tang (arXiv 2110.12636) and McGrath et al. arXiv 2503.03065v2 concern interval quality, not speed.

findings.candidate: Sort each arm once per object (y and dead are fixed across Bayesian-bootstrap draws), store the tie-group boundaries, and per replicate compute d_j by summing weights within each group and n_j as a reverse cumulative sum. Then apply the same cumprod / reverse-cumsum A / Σ A² d/(n(n−d)) formula, ideally inside the shared weighted C++ sweep from finding 2.
findings.claimed_speedup: Complexity O(n·D) → O(n) per arm per replicate after a one-time O(n log n) sort. Not quantified by any source. FastSurvival's ~30× unweighted single-pass C++ vs survRM2 at n=500 is a different baseline (source claim from the previous run).
findings.suggested_action: Already being acted on under v1.2.0-TODO-22 (investigate). Add to that item: reuse one per-object presort across Bayesian-bootstrap draws.
findings.new_evidence: Not a new speed claim. Re-verified unimplemented at 4ce2b712, 2026-11-18. New: y, dead and w are fixed across Bayesian-bootstrap draws, so the per-replicate cost can be O(n) rather than O(n log n), a small scope refinement for v1.2.0-TODO-22.

findings.candidate: One weighted C++ KM sweep, a weights argument on km_stat_inline / rmst_from_km, with the survfit quantile midpoint convention and RMST by step areas. It is shared by the weighted median, weighted RMST and weighted RMST SE. Each arm's sort order and tie groups are computed once per object and reused across draws, since only the weights vary.
findings.claimed_speedup: weighted_km_median O(n·D) → O(n) per replicate (after a one-time sort), not quantified. Replacing per-replicate survfit: FastSurvival's speed vignette (previous run) reports about 30× for single-pass C++ KM/RMST over survfit at n=500, unweighted, presorted. alternating-irls-theta.note: New this run, a correctness defect that also costs iterations. The one-step θ Newton update in univariate_negbin_tstat (kk21_weights.cpp:570) and multivariate_negbin_tstat (:1045) is θ_new = θ − score/info. Here `info` is the same positive observed information as MASS::theta.ml's info(), which is minus d(score)/dθ. MASS updates t0 + score/info, so EDI's step points away from the MLE. With the [0.01, 1000] clamp, θ is pushed to a bound, where |Δθ| = 0 ends the loop, instead of to the NB2 MLE. Sign checked by hand: d/dθ of the per-observation score is ψ'(y+θ) − ψ'(θ) + 1/θ − 2/(θ+μ) + (y+θ)/(θ+μ)², which is −info. The R reference in test-kk21-negbin-fast-digamma.R copies the same sign, so it cannot catch this. The path is reached only with count_use_speedup = FALSE (default TRUE). The deferred frequency-table finding (#43925959437.1, revisit 2027-05-01) has no new evidence and is not re-reported. fastglm 0.1.4's fastglm_nb is still the same β/θ alternation, with step-halving safeguards.

forward-stepwise-selection.note: The known faster option is score entry from one reduced fit for the beta/NB/ordinal stepwise paths that still refit every candidate. The arXiv API ("forward selection" AND "score test") returned 0 results. The QR-updating paper arXiv 2412.05905 is still at v3 (Mar 2026). statmod is still 1.5.2 (2026-05-17), and leaps is 3.2 (2024). SAS PROC LOGISTIC score entry for cumulative logit is still the ordinal reference. The FWL/Gram-Schmidt continuous path and the logistic score path are already optimal.

The warm-start / incremental-QR IWLS literature (biglm-style, arXiv 2307.07342) targets data that does not fit in memory, not 2-parameter refits.

This is the existing low-priority warm-start Prototype. No new SIS or marginal-screening computation papers (arXiv July–Nov 2026: only Ball-codifference screening).

findings.candidate: Compute the θ score and information sums over the distinct-y frequency table, so D ≪ n special-function calls. This is Anscombe's (1950) trick, used by glmGamPoi's overdispersion MLE, and the same pattern is already in fast_zinb.cpp and fast_hurdle_negbin.cpp.

findings.suggested_action: Profile univariate_negbin_tstat on a KK21 count fixture. Only if the θ-step special functions are a visible share, reuse the distinct-y helper from fast_zinb.cpp.

Fix the R reference in test-kk21-negbin-fast-digamma.R, which copies the wrong sign, and test against MASS::glm.nb / theta.ml.

bisection.note: Unchanged in code. The commits since 2026-11-16 only change how pval_invert_ci_cpp / eval_lrt wrap results (SEXP→RObject in lrt_ci_newton.cpp), tighten assertions, edit docs and drop the capabilities metadata, so pval_invert_ci_cpp is still pure bisection after the bracket. The earlier Chandrupatla/ITP/modAB finding (#43925959437.1, proposed investigate under v1.1.0-TODO-17w) still stands. New dated evidence for modAB: (1) the SciML interval root-finding benchmark (generated 2026-10-21) ranks ModAB first among the bracketing solvers (Bisection, Brent, Falsi, ITP, Ridder, Alefeld) and lists the fastest timings for it on all three functions quoted; (2) NonlinearSolve.jl now recommends ModAB as the default scalar bracketing solver; (3) CERN ROOT ships a C++ ModABRootFinder under LGPL-2.1+; (4) the paper's DOI is 10.3390/a19050332, published 2026-04-24. Row 14 (log-binomial gradient CI) now has algorithm = bisection, but its verdict still says 'Keep (already Brent)' with Brent refs, which is inconsistent. A related 2026 paper, arXiv 2605.03060 (sign-flip score GLM CIs), also inverts with bisection and reports no speed comparison. Gaussian refit rows: the closed form is still pending (v1.1.0-TODO-50), with no new candidate.

brent-root.note: The only row still tagged brent-root is invert_ci_to_find_two_sided_pval_for_treatment_effect, which runs uniroot in α over a CI family for the log-rank test. Its verdict already records the closed form 2Φ(−|z|) for the Wald CI, so a better bracketing solver would gain nothing there. The log-binomial row the previous finding #43925959437.2 targeted was relabelled to bisection on 2026-11-17 (the verdict text still needs fixing; see the bisection note). That row is now covered by the bisection finding, so I have not re-reported #2. I found no new Brent-specific evidence. The SciML 2026 benchmark puts Brent behind ModAB and ITP.

safeguarded-newton-root.note: No code change in lrt_ci_nr_cpp beyond the RObject wrapping. Searches for 2025–2026 Venzon–Moolgavkar or signed-root Newton work found only the 2021 RVM paper (doi 10.1007/s11222-021-10012-y, arXiv 2004.00231) and Bhat::plkhci (also VM). The arXiv API search for profile-likelihood CI algorithms turned up nothing newer. Newton at ~4–8 refits/bound is already below what any bracketing method needs. The signed-root Newton prototype (v1.0.5 audit TODO 4) remains the improvement to make.

warm-start-continuation.note: I found no new deterministic warm-start scheme for CI-inversion refits. aquakin's continuation sweep, glmnet warm starts and the gam crate's REML continuation are all path-dependent chaining, which catalog row 5 rejects. arXiv 2608.06274 (NestyNet II, 2026 preprint) studies tangent-linear warm refits but is not about CI inversion, and it reports that warm and cold refits differ, which supports keeping warm starts off for *_ci keys. The deterministic tangent predictor (v1.0.5 TODO-5) remains the option to build. std_mod_cache.R changed only in docs.

analytic-derivatives.note: New row (KK GLMM block_diag_information). get_gaussian_lmm_fisher_cpp returns the analytic observed Hessian (lmm_analytic_hessian; h_rel is unused), and the R code zeroes the beta x variance cross blocks. Its comment calls the result the expected information. The beta-beta block (sum X'PX) is the same expected or observed. Because the cross blocks are zeroed, the Schur-complement efficient information for beta_T depends only on that beta block, so the variance block, its O(n) terms and the per-call O(n log n) regrouping of the data are wasted work at every delta of the score-CI inversion. This is a constant-factor saving only (see finding). Searches on analytic derivatives versus AD (TMB, Stan, CppAD) found no evidence that AD beats hand-coded closed forms at these sizes.

closed-form.note: Trivial. LR = 2(nll0-nll1) and the Terrell gradient statistic are O(1) closed forms plus one chi-square tail. The only p^3 step is the score test's Schur complement (constant factor, v1.1.0-TODO-155). The commits since 2026-11-16 only change metadata, argument checks and docs.

irls.note: New row: kk_cpoisson_glm_fallback_spec. Its fit_null(delta, start) ignores `start` and calls stats::glm.fit cold at every delta, while the other refit sites are warm-started (the previous note's claim of warm starts does not hold for this row). Passing start = start[-j] keeps the unique concave MLE and cuts IRLS iterations during CI inversion. When the only free nuisance parameter is the Poisson intercept, the null refit has the closed form log(sum y / sum exp(delta*z_j)). See finding. The quasipoisson and robust-Poisson rows are unchanged: C++ IRLS, warm-started. fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11) was already checked.

multistart.note: The cloglog finding (#43925959437.1) is already being acted on as v1.1.0-TODO-208 (investigate), and none of the commits since touch fit_null, so it is not re-reported. New row: the KK GLMM null refit runs joint L-BFGS over (beta, log sigma_e, log sigma_b) and, when warm-started, a second full-fit start, because log sigma_b stalls near the sigma_b = 0 boundary. A profiled 1-D bounded search over lambda = sigma_b^2/sigma_e^2 >= 0 (the lme4 / MixedModels.jl approach) removes both the boundary trap and the second start (see finding). The stereotype multistart stays (nonconcave). The only new 2026 multistart literature found (arXiv 2602.13450 'Inference from random restarts'; BLOC 2603.29169) does not offer a cheaper certified alternative.

newton-raphson.note: The constrained C++ Newton refits (fixed_idx, warm starts) on concave Poisson/GLM likelihoods are already optimal. A new search turned up only Fischer & Lewis 2021 RVM (arXiv 2004.00231), which targets the CI endpoint search, not the per-delta refit, and was already noted. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

parametric-bootstrap.note: The new 2026 item, Michael, arXiv 2606.14837 (June 2026), is an analytic Bartlett adjustment specific to Gaussian random-effects meta-analysis, so for EDI it would be an estimator change, like Hanada & Sugimoto. Rocke's (1989) B ~ 100 mean-of-LR factor is what EDI already does. pbkrtest is still 0.5.5 (2025-07-18), unchanged. Analytic Bartlett-type corrections for the score and gradient tests (Vargas, Ferrari & Lemonte; mdscore 0.1-4) are GLM-specific closed forms, not the same estimator as the MC factor. The catalog option of one factor per CI (v1.0.5 TODO-3) still covers the space.

ridge-regularization.note: At most 8 small solves once per score test. A search on regularized or singular score-test information found only continuity-based alternatives (Ekvall & Bottai 2022, doi 10.1214/22-AOS2177) and supremum tests for singular information (Amengual, Bei & Sentana). These are robustness and estimator changes, not speedups. Note that for the KK GLMM, the block-diagonal fix (v1.0.6-TODO-167) has removed most ridge fallbacks there.

schur-complement.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it runs once per test, not per replicate. The only gain is one LDLT solve in place of the full inverse (constant factor, v1.1.0-TODO-155). For the KK GLMM the block-diagonal information makes the variance block irrelevant (see the analytic-derivatives finding).

findings.candidate: Run one constrained Newton refit with a convergence certificate (max |gradient| below tolerance and a positive-definite Hessian, as ordinal::clm's regularized Newton with step-halving uses), and run the second start only when the certificate fails. This is justified because the basic cumulative-link log-likelihood (cloglog included) is concave with a unique global optimum (Pratt 1981; Burridge 1981), and fixing beta_T restricts it to an affine subspace, which keeps it concave.
findings.claimed_speedup: not quantified by the source; about 2x fewer cloglog null refits by construction when the first start converges
findings.suggested_action: Resolve the cloglog 'Investigate' verdict: make the second start conditional on the first refit failing a gradient-norm certificate, then A/B the LR p-values and CIs on the existing cloglog fixtures.

findings.candidate: A profiled null refit. With beta_T = delta moved into an offset, profile beta (GLS) and sigma_e^2 (closed form) out and search a single bounded parameter lambda = sigma_b^2/sigma_e^2 in [0, lambda_max] with Brent or a safeguarded 1-D Newton. This is the lme4 / MixedModels.jl profiled-deviance construction, with theta >= 0 handled exactly at the boundary. KK groups come in only two sizes (pairs and singletons), so the GLS weight c_g = v_b/a_g takes only two values. The normal equations are therefore A_pairs - c2(lambda) B_pairs + (1 - c1(lambda)) A_single-type sums, built once in O(n p^2), and each profile evaluation costs O(p^3), independent of n. The existing fast_gaussian_lmm_gls_cpp is the building block. One deterministic 1-D search replaces both L-BFGS starts and the 1e-4 switching rule.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the sources. By construction it removes the second start (2x fewer refits during CI inversion) and replaces up to 300 O(n p) L-BFGS iterations with about 20-40 O(p^3) profile evaluations after one O(n p^2) pass. The catalog (row NEW-lmm-closed-form) judged the full-fit version 'speed roughly neutral at p <~ 10'. The gain here comes mainly from dropping the second start and the boundary crawl.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype a profiled constrained refit for fast_gaussian_lmm (offset delta*w, lambda grid plus Brent on [0, lambda_max], GLS via the existing fast_gaussian_lmm_gls_cpp normal equations precomputed per group size). Use it in the KK GLMM fit_null in place of the two-start L-BFGS, then A/B the LR, score and gradient p-values and CIs against the current output on the KK fixtures, including boundary (sigma_b ~ 0) cases.

findings.candidate: Pass start = start[-j] (the nuisance coefficients of the previous null fit, which extract_start already returns) to glm.fit as a warm start. When Z[,-j] is intercept-only in the Poisson reservoir-only fallback, return the closed form log(sum y / sum exp(delta*Z[,j])) without running IRLS.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the sources. A warm start from a nearby delta typically saves a few IRLS iterations per refit. The closed form removes IRLS entirely in the intercept-only case.
findings.suggested_action: Small change: thread `start` through fit_with_fixed into glm.fit(start = ...) with a cold-start retry on non-convergence, and add the intercept-only Poisson closed form. Check that p-values match the current output to within 1e-8 on the existing KK conditional-Poisson fallback tests.

findings.candidate: Once the cross blocks are zero, the efficient information for beta_T (a Schur complement over all other parameters) equals the Schur complement within the beta block alone, sum_g X_g' P_g X_g. A score-test-only path can compute just that p x p block, reuse the sorted LMMData, and compute it once per fit rather than once per accessor.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Constant factor: it skips the variance-block and cross-block O(n) terms and repeated O(n log n) regrouping per delta. Small at p <~ 10.
findings.suggested_action: Low priority. Fold this into the profiled-refit prototype: return a cached beta-block information from the null fit and fix the comment ('observed Hessian with cross blocks zeroed; beta block equals expected').

closed-form.note: Trivial: closed form, O(1) per element (logit, inv_logit, sample_mode, ordinal link cdf/pdf/pdf'); nothing faster. Since 2026-11-16 the only commit (6a3651ee) changed score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign, not any link code. Re-checked Eigen MR !1732 (vectorized double erfc): it reports 64-84% less time on batched arrays but no change at size 1, and its max relative error is 7 ulp, against EDI's full-precision Cephes erfc. RcppEigen on CRAN is still 0.3.4.0.2 (2024-08-24). The per-observation probit path therefore gains nothing and would lose accuracy. The robustness note on the cloglog z<-37 clamp from the previous run still stands.

power-series.note: The fast_log1pexp / log1pexp_array_fast code is unchanged. Re-fetched fdlibm e_log.c: it uses the same s=f/(2+f) reduction with a 7-term Remez polynomial, error ≤2^-58.45. New this run, from my own arithmetic (not a source): the 10-term atanh truncation leaves remainder 2·Σ_{k≥10} s^{2k+1}/(2k+1). At x=0, z=1 and s=1/3, so the first omitted term is 2·3^-21/21 ≈ 9.1e-12 and the total ≈1.0e-11 absolute. That breaks the '<5e-12' bound in the code comment (_helper_functions_core.h:886) and the inventory row, which the deferral relied on. It matches catalog P11's '~1e-11'. A minimax refit would reach near-ulp accuracy with fewer FMAs. The speed gain is marginal because exp dominates. No new arXiv work on faster log1p kernels (searched math.NA and the correctly-rounded libm literature: RLibm, CORE-MATH).

rational-approximation.note: fast_atan uses Cephes range reduction plus a 5/5 rational; probit uses Cephes erfc. Neither has a faster acceptable alternative. SLEEF's latest release, 3.9.0 (March 2025), has no erfc/atan performance changes; 3.8 only fixed overflow bounds in log1p/exp. Eigen's vectorized double erfc (7 ulp) helps only batched calls and is less accurate. CORE-MATH and RLibm aim at correct rounding at libm-competitive speed, so a scalar call is no faster than Cephes.

stable-branch-evaluation.note:
plogis_safe/array, log1pexp_safe/array and fast_log1p_arr (Kahan/Goldberg) cost one exp plus one log or divide per element, which is minimal for an exact result. New since 2026-11-16:
- LogExpFunctions.jl v1.0.4–1.0.6 are accuracy fixes (logexpm1, log1pmx, log2mexp), not speed changes.
- arXiv 2610.31642 (Oct 2026) fixes softmax/cross-entropy via softplus, not per-element softplus.
- Rmpfr 1.1-3 (2026-09-06) keeps the log1mexp note.
The accuracy fix for log_one_minus_exp_neg_hp (use log(-expm1(-λ)) for λ<ln2) remains open. It costs the same and is not a speed issue.

findings.candidate: A minimax (Remez/fpminimax) polynomial in s² on [0,1/9], following the fdlibm e_log.c construction (s=f/(2+f), 7 coefficients Lg1..Lg7, error ≤2^-58.45), using the same Horner evaluation scheme.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. It saves about 3 FMAs per element (7 terms instead of 10) and improves accuracy from ~1e-11 to near-ulp. exp dominates the cost, so the speed gain is marginal.
findings.suggested_action: At minimum, correct the '<5e-12' bound in the _helper_functions_core.h:886 comment and the inventory rows to ~1.0e-11, matching catalog P11, and fill P11's [cite needed] (catalog line 1479) with fdlibm e_log.c. Optionally refit the coefficients as a minimax polynomial.
findings.new_evidence: 2026-11-18 analysis (own arithmetic, not a source): the truncation remainder 2·Σ_{k≥10} s^{2k+1}/(2k+1) at s=1/3 (x=0) is ≈9.1e-12 + 9.2e-13 + … ≈ 1.0e-11. The defer reason said the series 'already meets its claimed <5e-12 abs error'; it does not. Catalog P11 (line 1477) already says ~1e-11, so the code comment and inventory disagree with the catalog.

logrank-sweep.note: Unchanged since 2026-11-16. A single evaluation is already optimal: one O(n log n) sort plus a fused O(n) C++ sweep. FastSurvival 2.0.0 NEWS lists no log-rank speed or algorithm change and no permutation support. At commit 4ce2b712, inference_survival_log_rank.R and inference_survival_gehan_wilcox.R still have no compute_fast_randomization_distr, so every randomization draw re-sorts and re-sweeps. The commits since then add only docs, assert tightening and the ictest arm-sign fix. Finding logrank-family-tests#43925959437.1 (v1.1.0-TODO-209, investigate) still stands; re-reported unchanged.

martingale-residuals.note: Trivial: a closed form from the null fit, O(n) after the sort. The coxph(~1) to C++ swap is already recorded as implementation-only (Keep). The new commits leave weighted_*_mean_difference untouched.

sort-and-sweep.note: Unchanged. The 2026 sorting sources found (CppCon 2026 radix abstract, djbsort 2026 speed docs, arXiv 2605.16667 DialSort) cover int keys or large N, so there is still no evidence of a win for (time, dead, w) records at n around 1000, and the catalog already rejected radix sort. The gain that matters is hoisting the per-draw sort out of the randomization loop at delta=0, which is part of finding #43925959437.1.

turnbull-em.note: Unchanged. The code still calls interval::ictest per observed statistic and per draw, with no icFIT or initfit reuse. The new commit only re-orients the sign. The ictest docs (fetched again) still describe icFIT as 'for increased computation speed' and recommend initfit as the safe reuse path. There are no new releases of icenReg (2.0.16, 2024) or npsurv (0.5-0, 2020), and arXiv shows no new faster NPMLE algorithm. Finding #43925959437.2 (proposed investigate, v1.2.0-TODO-22) stands; re-reported.

findings.candidate: At delta=0, sort the pooled data once and compute label-invariant pooled null martingale residual scores (Nelson-Aalen for log-rank, pooled-KM weighted for Peto-Prentice). Each draw's statistic is then a linear rank statistic: an O(n) dot product, or one W'm product over all draws. This is the coin logrank_test formulation. At delta != 0, fall back to the existing path.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Theoretical: O(r n log n + r overhead) becomes O(n log n + r n).
findings.suggested_action: Already tracked as v1.1.0-TODO-209 (investigate). Nothing new; implement as planned.

findings.candidate: (1) Solve the pooled NPMLE once (it is label-invariant at delta=0). Reuse it via ictest(initfit=) or icFIT=, or wlr_trafo scores, and evaluate each draw as a linear statistic. (2) Speed up the single solve with EMICM (icenReg::ic_np, initfit='initEMICM'), npsurv CNM/HCNM, or SQUAREM.
findings.claimed_speedup: (1) About r times fewer NPMLE solves (theoretical). (2) Du & Varadhan report SQUAREM needing about 15-17x fewer EM evaluations than plain EM, competitive with EM-ICM. Anderson-Bergman's paper claims its EMICM implementation is significantly faster. No source benchmarks at EDI's sizes.
findings.suggested_action: Already tracked: v1.2.0-TODO-22 (pooled-fit reuse) and v1.1.0-TODO-50 (NPMLE A/B). Nothing new.

closed-form.note: Closed-form O(n) mean/var moments (compute_reservoir_and_match_statistics); reading the data is the lower bound. Rechecked 2026-11-16: no new code commits, nothing new.

inverse-variance-weighting.note: IVW of pair and reservoir estimates is an O(1) combination after O(n) or O(np^2) fits; nothing faster. New 2025 work (von Davier arXiv 2503.22080) refines the Satterthwaite effective df for weighted variance sums. That is an inference/accuracy change, not a speedup, so no finding. No code commits since the last run.

linear-scan.note: The pair/reservoir split, gather and summary passes (compute_zhang_match_data_cpp, compute_matching_lin_*_cpp, compute_bootstrap_matching_stats_cpp) are single O(np) or O(n) passes, which equals the cost of reading the data. The X part is already cached per m_vec. No new algorithm in the 2025-2026 matched-pair literature changes this.

pairs-of-pairs-variance.note: Per-replicate BRS λ² is O(n), the lower bound. New since the last run: graph-Laplacian variance estimators (arXiv 2608.10177, Aug 2026), with the complete-graph (Imai 2008) estimator as minimax-optimal. Using it would avoid the one-off O(m^3) blossom pairing (row G, not this problem's entries), but it is an estimator change, not a speedup. Also new: Bai et al. arXiv 2503.10851 (paired-strata design-based estimator) and Chen & Li arXiv 2602.18383. Neither offers a faster way to get the same estimate.

streaming-moments.note: One-pass Σx/Σx² in kk_compound_distr_parallel.cpp is O(Bn). The accuracy fix (shifted one-pass, Chan-Golub-LeVeque) is already Adopt in catalog §7 P7 / TODO-4, and Welford was already rejected as slower in SIMD loops. Searches turned up only blogs reconfirming this, plus pairwise/blocked summation (FABsum), which brings no speed gain. kk_bootstrap_reservoir_stats.cpp is dead code.

random-forest-imputation.note: [full re-imputation per arrival] The previous finding #43925959437.1 (stored missRanger forests, predict each arrival, refit every k arrivals) still stands and is re-reported because of a code change. Commit a32ab62c (2026-11-17, v1.0.6-TODO-44) removed y from the imputation: missRanger and missForest now see private$Ximp only. It also seeds the imputation with the design seed inside a .Random.seed save/restore. Before this, a stored forest included a y column, which a new arrival does not have yet. Now predict(imp, newdata = x_new) applies directly, and every refit is deterministic. Versions checked on CRAN: missRanger 2.6.1 is still current (NEWS re-read; no speed changes since 2.6.0's keep_forests/predict). missForestPredict 1.0.1 is unchanged, and its paper is now published in PLOS One (2025-11-07, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0334125). The paper benchmarks runtime only against miceRanger, not missRanger. That is not new evidence against the defer of #43925959437.2 (revisit 2027-07-01), so it is not re-reported. Mondrian online forests (arXiv 1406.2673) still have no imputation use. | [random-forest chained imputation (missRanger / missForest), fixed designs] No faster same-estimator option found. Versions: missForest 1.6.1 (2025-10-26, ranger backend), mixgb 2.2.3 (2026-01-17), and misspi 0.1.1 (2026-01-25), a new LightGBM-based missForest variant licensed GPL-2 only. mixgb and misspi are boosting, so they are a different estimator. The CRAN MissingData view (2026-10-12) still names missRanger as the fast missForest. mForest (arXiv 1701.05305), which imputes variables in blocks, is also a different estimator. No missRanger-versus-rival timing benchmark was found.

findings.candidate: missForestPredict (Albu et al.; CRAN 1.0.1, GPL ≥ 2, ranger backend). missForest(..., save_models = TRUE, initialization = 'custom', x_init = previous completed X) warm-starts each periodic refit from the last imputation, which should cut chained iterations to convergence. missForestPredict(obj, newdata) imputes a single arrival with the saved per-iteration models. Re-imputing the training set reproduces the original imputation exactly, which gives a deterministic, auditable path.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The paper claims only 'competitive results … within short computation times'. The iteration savings from a warm start are an inference; the mice literature reports that most of the cost is burn-in iterations.
findings.suggested_action: Note missForestPredict (DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2407.03379) in catalog §12(e) as the alternative offering warm starts and exact training replay. Benchmark iterations to convergence, warm versus cold, at n ≈ 100–500 inside the v1.0.5-TODO-9 prototype.

findings.candidate: The same idea as #43925959437.1. Call missRanger(Ximp, keep_forests = TRUE, data_only = FALSE) every k arrivals, with the same seed. In between, impute each new row with predict(imp, newdata = x_new, iter = 4). Refit whenever columns or factor levels change. missRanger ≥ 2.6.0 is already imported.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the sources. Structurally, about k times fewer forest fits, with only a predict per arrival in between. The missForestPredict PLOS One paper reports that imputing new rows from saved models is 'comparable to linear imputation' in runtime (its Table 9).
findings.suggested_action: Keep in v1.2.0-TODO-23. Note in the prototype that v1.0.6-TODO-44 (no y; seeded) removes the missing-y obstacle for predict on new arrivals.
findings.new_evidence: Commit a32ab62c (2026-11-17): the imputation no longer includes y and is seeded with the design seed. Stored forests are now fit on X only, so predict() on a new arrival, whose y is not yet observed, applies directly and reproducibly. Previously the forests were fit with a y column that new rows lack.
