boundary-reduced-refit.note: No commit since 2026-11-16 touches fit_zinb_zi_boundary_fallback or fit_zip_reduced_fallback. The three new commits change a jackknife unit, a spelling, and score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign. Each fallback is one extra L-BFGS fit that runs only on the boundary path. This run's ZINB θ→∞ search, the glmmTMB troubleshooting results (flag the boundary and suggest the reduced Poisson/no-zi model), the VGAM zinegbinomial notes (switch to zipoisson when k is large), the JSS count-regression paper, and the CRAN pages of glmmTMB (1.1.15.2, 2026-09-29) and pscl (1.5.9, 2024) turned up nothing beyond what EDI already does automatically. The only way to remove these fits is still the α=1/θ reparametrization in catalog §3 TODO 4, which is a robustness change, not a speedup.

convergence-certification.note: No code change to newton_stalled_at_optimum (re-read at _helper_functions_core.h:1439), ordinal_newton_decrement_ok, the Poisson-limit certificates or the gradient threshold. The certificates are cheap and run only on rare paths: one Hessian plus a values-only eigensolve on line-search-failure exits, one LDLT only when covariates are badly scaled, 2–3 objective evaluations for the boundary certificates, and O(1)/O(np) for the rest. Re-searched the Newton decrement (self-concordant bound), the Dennis–Schnabel relative gradient, nlminb rel.tol and the L-BFGS ‖g‖<ε·max(1,‖x‖) rule. The CRAN Optimization view (2026-09-23) still adds only optimflex's AND-combined criteria, and the recent arXiv listing has nothing on certification. No cheaper test keeps the same acceptance set.

separation-detection.note:
bootstrap_estimates_extreme is an O(B) scan plus one quantile. Its file changed only in normalize_jackknife_unit, not in this function. New or confirmed since the last run:
- Correia–Guimarães–Zylkin arXiv 1903.01633 v10 (2026-05-06), now published (doi 10.1080/07474938.2026.2673989). It verifies MLE existence for GLMs with high-dimensional fixed effects; its ReLU/simplex routines live in the Stata ppmlhdfe.
- Sablica–Hornik–Rusch arXiv 2610.08100 v2 (2026-10-23): a single-LP overlap check, with no cost claims.
- detectseparation 0.4.0 (unchanged).
- Eck–Geyer, doi 10.1214/21-EJS1815.
All of these are exact per-fit existence checks. Each costs at least a fit or an LP per replicate, which is more than the heuristic, so none is a speedup. They remain possible robustness upgrades on the observed fit only.

Per the Eigen benchmark re-fetched this run, LLT and LDLT are already the fastest dense least-squares paths (6.8 ms vs 36 ms for ColPivQR at 10000x8). Commits since 2026-11-16 changed only comments and the score/Fisher export helpers in fast_gaussian_lmm.cpp, not make_start.

closed-form.note: Trivial: the iteration-0 information Xᵀdiag(w)X and the NB observed Hessian are single-pass O(np²) closed forms; nothing faster exists. The constant-factor notes (weighted_crossprod reuse, Incidental 13) are already recorded. The 2026-11-17 commit unrolled score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign bit-identically, which only helps.

irls.note: Used only for the GEE independence-GLM starting β. This run re-checked GEE practice: geeasy (init.beta defaults to NULL, i.e. a GLM fit), geeM (intercept from InvLink(mean y)) and a 2026 penalized-GEE preprint (arXiv 2606.16058) all start from an independence fit, as EDI does. A cheaper start would not reduce total work: canonical-link IRLS converges quadratically in about 5–8 iterations. The savvyGLM / shrinkage-GLM paper's optimized start (CVXR) costs more and is aimed at fragile links.

method-of-moments.note: The Pearson θ start (NB and truncated NB) and the marginal-cumulative-proportion thresholds are O(np) / O(nK) closed forms, run once per fit. MASS theta.mm is the same Pearson moment estimator. I found no new 2026 work on truncation-corrected θ starts or on threshold initialization for cumulative-link models (the arXiv searches found only MCMC and neural-collapse papers). Nothing faster.

multistart.note: Nothing new beyond the already-triaged finding mle-starting-values#43925959437.2 (single QR for both hurdle-NB start columns, deferred until 2027-05-01 as v1.2.0-TODO-233). The ZINBGT preprint (arXiv 2604.09319) uses data-dependent deterministic starts, the same idea as EDI's grid. Stochastic global methods (MLSL, GenSA, DEoptim, per the CRAN Optimization task view) still break determinism and cost more.

bisection.note: New finding: for the Zhang exact combined CI (zhang_bisect_ci_boundary / zhang_ci_exact_combined), both component p-values are minlike exact p-values in exponential families of δ. Their included support sets change only at closed-form breakpoints (exactci vignette; Klaschka & Reiczigel 2021). So the endpoints and an empty acceptance set can be found exactly by a breakpoint sweep, instead of bisection, which can stop at an inner crossing of a non-unimodal p. Earlier findings still stand and are not re-reported because nothing changes them: .1 reservoir shift-equivariance (investigate, v1.0.6-TODO-41), .3/.4 Glazer–Stark (investigate). Re-checked: arXiv 2405.05238 is still v3 (Feb 2025) with no journal ref, and permutest is still 1.0.0. Deferred before their 2027-05-01 revisit date: .2 Zhu–Liu/Xu quadratic jump points (Xu 2512.14024 still v1) and .5 ITP. The SciML 2026 ModAB improvements (BracketingNonlinearSolve docs) are the same idea family as ITP: they are not new evidence against the 'each eval is microseconds' reason. STB (2508.17591 v2, 30 Oct 2026) is unchanged: it covers fresh-noise p only. Code since 2026-11-16: the SMC prefix logic was reworked (v1.0.6-TODO-166; a short prefix now draws the next batch instead of returning). Commit 3395b6c3 removed warm-start chaining across permutations for determinism under num_cores (v1.0.6-TODO-61). That raises the per-replicate refit cost inside every p(δ) evaluation for iterative models, but the cost sits in the replicate loop, not in the root search, and is accepted for determinism.

breakpoint-inversion.note: Checked CIPerm (still 0.2.3, 2022, MIT), Xu 2512.14024 (still v1, no code) and the jstatsoft/R Journal searches: no new one-pass inversion. EDI's sorted-breakpoint sweep for affine statistics is already the Nguyen/CIPerm method, and the O(B²) probe count is negligible at B ≤ low thousands. Extending breakpoints to minlike exact p's is filed under bisection/brent-root.

brent-root.note: Changed since the last review: zhang_ci_inside_point now falls back, when the 3 candidates and stats::optimize are all rejected, to a 2001-point grid plus 5 local optimize refinements (zhang_ci_inside_point_grid, v1.0.6-TODO-216, commit 5bdb9dfb). Each evaluation rebuilds both minlike p's, with about 3S lgamma calls for the reservoir. The grid exists because optimize stops at local maxima of a non-unimodal minlike product. The breakpoint sweep in the finding decides exactly, with about k+S evaluations, whether the acceptance set is empty and where its maximum is. Chandrupatla/TOMS748 versus Brent (lmi evaluation counts) is unchanged: nothing helps on jumps.

exponential-bracketing.note: Wald-seeded doubling, ≤7 expansions. uniroot extendInt docs show the same idea, with no fewer evaluations. Commit 21e0679a only documents the radius floor of 1. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

findings.candidate: The response shift −δ·w_perm is a linear function of the design (w_perm is its trt column). Quantile-regression shift equivariance, β̂(y+Xγ, X) = β̂(y, X)+γ, therefore gives T_b(δ) = T_b(0) − δ and T_obs(δ) = T_obs(0) − δ exactly. Draw the permutations once (CRN), fit B rq models once, and p_R(δ) = mean(|T_b(0)−δ| ≥ |T_obs(0)−δ|) becomes a closed-form step function with breakpoints (T_b(0)+T_obs(0))/2. This reuses closed_form_ci_from_affine_null_draws with c_b = 1. The same algebra also shows a validity issue. As δ→+∞, p_R → Pr(T_b ≤ T_obs), and as δ→−∞, p_R → Pr(T_b ≥ T_obs); one of these is ≳ 0.5, so p_R never falls below α on that side. When m = 0 (Bernoulli; all subjects in the reservoir) the combined p equals p_R, so bisection ends at the bracket edge. The standard test would subtract δ·w_obs before permuting, and that form is not affine.
findings.claimed_speedup: Derived from the code, not measured. The reservoir component falls from about (number of bisection steps, 10–50) × nsim_rand rq fits per bound to nsim_rand fits in total, roughly 20–100× on that component. The matched-pairs component (sign flips with intercept rq) is unchanged.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate first as a possible validity bug (the reservoir p-value does not vanish for large |δ|; check the m=0 Bernoulli path with a unit test). Then either fix the null adjustment to the observed w, or, if the current form is intended, replace the per-δ refits with the one-shot affine breakpoint inversion.

findings.candidate: Exact jump-point inversion for studentized statistics. Each draw's pivot equation t(z_π, Y+δθ) = t_obs reduces to a quadratic in δ with explicit roots (Zhu & Liu 2024; Xu 2025 generalizes this to rational statistics). Sort the ≤ 2B roots and sweep ±1/B steps to get the exact p-curve.
findings.claimed_speedup: Zhu & Liu (Biometrics rejoinder) report about 23 s per two-sided interval versus about 4 h for grid inversion (n=100, 10^4 MC draws), about 0.3 s at n=8 exhaustively, and about 146 s at n=10,000. Xu claims an order of magnitude over grid search without timings. Neither compares against bisection, so versus EDI the gain is about (10–20 evaluations × B refits) → B coefficient extractions.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look (updated): when checking whether the studentized BRT pivots are rational in δ, use Zhu & Liu's explicit quadratic roots as the template. If they are, prototype quadratic breakpoints in closed_form_ci_from_affine_null_draws.

findings.candidate: Keep the fixed-sample (CRN) bisection, made conservative as in Glazer & Stark: p = (1+#)/(1+N), with the endpoint taken on the rejecting side. This argues against prioritizing Robbins–Monro.
findings.claimed_speedup: Glazer & Stark (lizard data, n=30, N=6000): 0.33 s versus 0.47 s for Garthwaite (about 1.4×), and conservative rather than approximate. Not measured for non-affine refit statistics.
findings.suggested_action: Re-check the premise of garthwaite_buckland_ci_search.md (v1.2.0-TODO-21) against Glazer & Stark 2025. Narrow it to refit-heavy, non-affine statistics or downgrade it.

findings.candidate: Glazer–Stark fixed-sample inversion: one sign-flip/permutation matrix per CI search, with the conservative p. Their Theorem 1 gives coverage ≥ 1−α, and bisection then runs on a deterministic function (catalog TODO-6a).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for quantile regression. The number of evaluations stays about the same, but steps spent resolving MC noise are removed and the search can stop once the bracket holds a single jump.
findings.suggested_action: Use Glazer & Stark as the reference when prototyping catalog TODO-6a, together with the reservoir-equivariance finding above.

findings.candidate: ITP with n0=0 (Oliveira & Takahashi 2021). It never needs more evaluations than bisection and converges superlinearly when the crossing lies inside a smooth piece.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this problem. Expected about 20 → 8–10 evaluations per bound when the crossing is smooth, and never worse. Each evaluation costs only O(d+S), so the gain is small.
findings.suggested_action: Correct the 'step function' rationale in the inventory. Optionally record ITP (n0=0) in the options table; low priority.

findings.candidate: An exact breakpoint sweep for minlike exact p-values. Both components are exponential families in δ: d+ ~ Bin(k, expit δ), and the reservoir n11 ~ noncentral hypergeometric with log-OR δ. So log f(x;δ) − log f(x_obs;δ) = (log c_x − log c_obs) + (x − x_obs)·δ is affine in δ. The set of support points summed in each minlike p therefore changes only at the closed-form points δ_x = (log c_obs − log c_x)/(x − x_obs), shifted by the log1p(1e-7) tie tolerance EDI uses. There are at most k + S such points. This is the structure the exactci vignette uses for the Poisson minlike CI, and Klaschka & Reiczigel (2021) give fast algorithms at these discontinuity points. Between consecutive points of the merged, sorted list, each component's p is a smooth sum of pmfs over a fixed index set, and the δ-free log c_x are precomputed once. Evaluating the combined p at each breakpoint and its one-sided limits gives three things exactly: (a) whether the acceptance set is empty, which replaces the optimize and 2001-grid fallback; (b) the outermost accepted pieces, i.e. Fay's matching interval, the smallest interval containing all non-rejected δ; (c) each endpoint, from one bracketed root solve inside a single smooth piece, where Brent or ITP is superlinear.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source; derived from the code. On the empty-set or hard path, about 2001 + 5×~25 evaluations, each with about 3S lgamma calls, become about (k+S) breakpoint evaluations with no lgamma. That is roughly 5–20× at k, S of a few hundred. On the normal path (3 candidates + about 2×(doubling + 20–40 bisection steps)) the cost is similar or modestly lower; the gain there is exact endpoints and no missed outer crossing, not speed. Absolute times are milliseconds either way.
findings.suggested_action: Re-open the catalog row 'enumerate jump points' (Exact-discrete CI inversion table) in light of v1.0.6-TODO-216. Prototype a δ-free precompute plus a merged-breakpoint sweep for the combined minlike p, replacing zhang_ci_inside_point_grid and the inside-point bisection. Check it against the current output on fixtures where the set is an interval, and against exact2x2/exactci on single-component cases (m=0; reservoir empty). Record whether the CI should be the matching interval when the set is non-convex.

New since 2026-11-16: fastglm's NB stability vignette, which compares only against MASS and gives no timings. fastglm NEWS lists nothing after 0.1.4 (2026-11-11). Neither changes the dead-code reason, so I did not re-report the finding. The commits since the last run only touch docs and examples.

analytic-derivatives.note: These are closed-form O(np)/O(np^2) passes, with lgamma/digamma cached per distinct y. Searches for AD (TMB) against hand-coded NB gradients found no benchmark where AD wins. The arXiv listing since 2026-11 has nothing new on NB score or information formulas beyond 2407.05824. The finite-sum / log1p form for large theta is an accuracy point (catalog item 16, minor), not a speedup.

lbfgs.note: No source since 2026-11-16 compares joint L-BFGS on (beta, log theta) head-to-head with Newton or with IRLS/theta alternation at EDI sizes. The fastglm vignettes compare against glm.nb only. LBFGSpp v0.4.0 adds final approximate-Hessian accessors only. statsmodels' NegativeBinomialP defaults to BFGS on the joint vector. Fisher-scoring/alternation (v1.0.5-TODO-5) and the alpha=1/theta L-BFGS-B parametrization (catalog P3) remain Prototype. The 1000x-faster moment estimator (arXiv 2508.04111) is an estimator change, already rejected under catalog O6.

newton-raphson.note: Joint Newton (FullPivLU, step-halving) on (beta, log theta) is the optional path. Searches on trust-region, damped and boundary-constrained Newton for NB, and on maxLik maxNR, found no new NB-specific method or benchmark. The MM algorithm for high-dimensional sparse NB (J. Syst. Sci. Complex. 2024) targets penalized high-dimensional fits; MM converges linearly, so it is not a win at p<=10. The paper was paywalled and not read.

truncated-series-summation.note: Dead code with no R caller. Yu, Dousti Mousavi & Yang (arXiv 2306.04798, Statistical Papers 2024) is still the reference; it is a reordering of the same sum that needs one trigamma call. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

findings.candidate: Route the fallback through EDI's own C++ NB2 MLE (fast_neg_bin_cpp, no new dependency), or through fastglm::fastglm_nb (fastglm 0.1.4, GPL (>= 2)). fastglm_nb runs the same IRLS/theta alternation in C++ with an inner Brent search for theta and a moment-based start.

blossom-matching.note: Commits since 2026-11-16 (21e0679a, 2c727f4c, fe905ca8, 39ee46bd, 35484055) only change roxygen docs and comments in inference_continuous_KK_bai_abstract.R and helper_matching.R; the nonbimatch calls are untouched. Re-checked: nbpMatching is still 1.5.6 (2024-09-25, GPL >= 2) on CRAN. designmatch is still 0.5.5 (2026-02-20) and uses MIP solvers, which are not faster for exact pair matching. Blossom VI (arXiv 2604.20351, v2 21 Jul 2026) still lists no released code and targets graphs of up to ~10M edges; at EDI's n (tens to hundreds; m = n/2 pair averages in compute_halves) there is no gain on a dense complete graph. van Rantwijk's mwmatching (MIT, Python plus header-only C++) is O(nm log n), which equals O(n^3 log n) on complete graphs, so it is no faster than the dense O(n^3) blossom. The Euclidean exact algorithms (Varadarajan, O(n^{3/2} log^5 n)) are planar or low-dimensional and impractical, and they do not cover Mahalanobis-whitened p-dimensional inputs at small n. Hougardy-Tammemaa 2026 is approximate (an O(n^0.206) ratio), which would be a design change. Auction methods found are bipartite only. The p=1 sort-and-pair path is O(n log n) and optimal. compute_halves is cached, so it is off the hot path. Keep.

nonparametric-bootstrap.note: Previous conclusion stands. For the same bootstrap distribution, nothing beats i.i.d. resampling plus B refits warm-started at the full-data MLE. Balanced resampling is still the tracked prototype (P3 / audit J); searches found no new peer-reviewed balanced or antithetic results. Importance (tilting) resampling is already in P3. BLB has a new adaptive variant (arXiv 2608.16892), but it still targets massive data. Linear and one-step bootstraps (arXiv 1712.01435, 1504.02382) are the k-step family, which was rejected and has no new evidence. Multinomial-weight vectorization (Chaibub Neto) only helps moment statistics, and the KK compound kernel is already O(n) per replicate in C++. Code changes since 2026-11-16 are not algorithmic: robustness and NA-reason fixes, the min_fraction_usable_samples gate, the nested resampling-operation restore, and the compound_beta_hat refactor (same arithmetic). The I7/I9 implementation issues are unchanged. New since the last run: fwb 1.0.0 (CRAN, 2026-10-14) now ships a 'cheap' CI type (Lam 2022), and Lam & Wang (JMLR 27(93), 2026) carry the cheap bootstrap into SGD. The Studentized Cheap Bootstrap preprint is still v1 with no journal reference. The cheap-bootstrap finding (investigate, v1.4.0-TODO-20) is re-reported with this as new evidence.

rejection-sampling.note: Unchanged. The g-comp rejection of unusable resamples is a statistical choice, and the mean-diff loop is unreachable (I10). The new rerandomization samplers (Metropolis-Hastings + SIR, arXiv 2602.07613; Langevin-gradient LGR, arXiv 2604.07524; FastRerandomize v3, 2026-01) target covariate-balance assignment draws, not degenerate-bootstrap rejection. The separation literature (van Smeden 2016; Firth + bootstrap) concerns robustness and bias, not speed.

ridit-scoring.note: Unchanged. The O(n+L) level-slot rebuild is already tracked (ridit_kernel_level_slots.md TODO-3). The new CRAN package pridit 1.1.1 (2026) is PCA-based ridit scoring with a plain bootstrap loop, so it offers no faster algorithm. Ridit and ridittools also offer none.

value-space-bisection-selection.note: Unchanged. No 2025-26 work on HL / X+Y selection turned up. Monahan Alg. 616 (DescTools) is still the reference, and the plain HL bootstrap kernel is dead code. The IVWC variance loops are tracked as TODO 5.

findings.candidate: k-step bootstrap (Davidson & MacKinnon 1999; Andrews 2002, Econometrica 70(1):119–162): a fixed k Newton / line-search Newton steps from θ̂ per replicate. It is higher-order equivalent to the standard bootstrap for t-CIs and Wald tests under the iid and block bootstraps.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Andrews calls it 'a very attractive alternative computationally'. With EDI's warm start, the gain is only the iterations beyond k plus convergence checks: likely ≈1–3x for Newton/IRLS families and more for L-BFGS families. This is an estimate, not measured.
findings.suggested_action: First measure how many iterations warm-started bootstrap refits actually take on representative fixtures. Only if that is well above 3 for some family, prototype an opt-in k-step mode for studentized/t-based bootstrap CIs; otherwise record 'no gain at EDI's warm-start setup' in the catalog §9 J options table.

findings.candidate: Opt-in cheap bootstrap CI (Lam 2022): psi_hat +/- t_{B,1-a/2} * S, with S^2 = (1/B) * sum (psi*_b - psi_hat)^2, at B of about 5-10. The studentized cheap bootstrap (He, Lam & Yan, arXiv 2606.25968) is its companion for the (theta*, se*) path.
findings.claimed_speedup: About 50-100x fewer refits (501 -> 5-10), by arithmetic, not measured. No new benchmark at EDI sizes.
findings.suggested_action: Under v1.4.0-TODO-20, use fwb 1.0.0's 'cheap' CI (GPL >= 2) as a reference implementation and test oracle for EDI's opt-in cheap-bootstrap CI type, and add the JMLR 2026 paper to the citations. No change to the triage decision.
findings.new_evidence: fwb 1.0.0 (CRAN, published 2026-10-14) adds a 'cheap' CI type (Lam 2022) that works from 1 replicate, a GPL-compatible reference implementation; the previous run cited fwb only for seeding. Lam & Wang, 'Cheap Bootstrap for Fast Uncertainty Quantification of SGD', JMLR 27(93) 2026, is a peer-reviewed extension of the cheap bootstrap. The studentized preprint is still v1 (no revision, no journal reference) as of 2026-11-19.

erfc-normal-cdf.note:
The previous finding still stands (triage: investigate, v1.1.0-TODO-50). The code is unchanged since 2026-11-16 (code_changes.diff only edits roxygen comments): pnorm_fast and fast_log_pnorm, and through it fast_log_pnorm_vec_cpp, are still clamped at |x|>=8. Status checks this run:
- Stan Math PR #3406, the erfcx-based std_normal_lcdf, is still open and unmerged. Its latest numbers (2026-10-22) are 1.2-1.4x over Stan's old code on [-30,30], with erfcx/lcdf error within about 2.7*2^-52 against mpmath.
- The R NEWS through R 4.6.2 still has only the R 4.5.0 item 'pnorm(x) underflows more gracefully'.
- New alternative erfcx kernel: Zaghloul 2024 (Numerical Algorithms, doi 10.1007/s11075-023-01608-8). It uses Chebyshev subinterval polynomials plus Taylor series and Laplace continued fractions, and per the search snippet claims a 1.3-20x efficiency gain over built-in functions. I could not fetch it (paywalled), so it is not verified.
- A March 2026 log erfc tail-bounds preprint (Misawa, preprints.org 202603.0686) returned 403, so it is not verified either. It is asymptotic bounds, no faster than erfcx.

rational-approximation.note:
What I checked since 2026-11-16:
- R NEWS through R 4.6.2: no qnorm change, so AS241 parity with R still holds.
- No 2026 arXiv paper on double-precision normal quantiles turned up. Shaw-Luu-Brickman (arXiv 0901.0638) is GPU-oriented and old.
- No new Boost.Math 1.90 erfc or quantile change found in the search results.
- SLEEF 3.9 erfc (1.5 ULP, BSL-1.0) is unchanged, and still has no benchmark at EDI's scalar call sites.
- Marsaglia's JSS 2004 Phi (abs error < 8e-16) is not faster than Cephes.
Cephes erfc, Acklam (warm starts only) and AS241 remain appropriate.

findings.candidate:
Build the negative-x branch on erfcx, as SciPy xsf log_ndtr and Stan Math PR #3406 do:
- log Phi(x) = log(0.5*erfcx(-x/sqrt2)) - x^2/2;
- Mills ratio phi/Phi = sqrt(2/pi)/erfcx(-x/sqrt2).
The erfcx kernel can be Cody rationals (Stan PR) or the Johnson Faddeeva Chebyshev tables (xsf, MIT). A possible third kernel is Zaghloul's 2024 Chebyshev-subinterval erfcx.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not measured against EDI. Stan PR #3406 (comment of 2026-10-22) reports std_normal_lcdf 1.2-1.4x faster than Stan's previous code on z in [-30,30]; the baseline is Stan's code, not EDI's Cephes erfc. Zaghloul 2024 claims 1.3-20x over built-in erfcx, according to a search snippet; I did not verify this because the paper is paywalled. Against EDI, expect about equal cost, with the exp removed from the log Phi and Mills-ratio paths.
findings.suggested_action: No change to the approved plan (v1.1.0-TODO-50): use an erfcx kernel and gate on an R::pnorm(log.p=TRUE) grid over [-40,40]. Stan PR #3406 is still unmerged as of 2026-11-19, so port xsf's Faddeeva erfcx. Optionally, compare against Zaghloul 2024 (doi 10.1007/s11075-023-01608-8) if an open copy is available.
findings.new_evidence: As of 2026-11-19, Stan PR #3406 is still open. Its latest benchmarks (2026-10-22: 1.2-1.4x, error about 2.7 ulp) superseded the PR-description table. One new lead, unverified: Zaghloul 2024, Numerical Algorithms, doi 10.1007/s11075-023-01608-8, offers a different erfcx kernel. Neither changes the approved plan; this only refreshes its sources.

finite-differences.note: Rechecked 2026-11-19. None of the three commits since 2026-11-16 touch finite-difference code. 97e466f1 adds soft_barrier helpers to _glmm_engine.h, 2faac6cf fixes spelling in a comment, and 6a3651ee unrolls score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign. numerical_hessian (_helper_functions_core.h:1178) still takes central differences of the analytic gradient (2P gradient calls, h = 1e-4·max(1,|θ|), symmetrized). The Clayton and dep-cens likelihoods still use forward differences (P+1 calls). New since the last run, none faster at P ≤ ~25 with a dense Hessian, mostly once per fit: (1) optimflex 0.1.7 (CRAN 2026-05-31, MIT) fast_hess is plain forward/central FD, nothing new. (2) nabla 0.7.2 (2026-10-28) and femtograd 0.3.1 (forward-over-reverse) are R-level AD tools, useful as test oracles only. Forward-over-reverse needs about P Hessian-vector passes, so it is no cheaper than 2P analytic-gradient calls, and it needs templated functors (the catalog already rejected this). (3) RTMB 2.0 (2026-09-17) is the AD framework; its NEWS has nothing new on Hessians. (4) pnd NEWS through 0.1.3 covers only accuracy and parallelism. (5) arXiv Oct-Nov 2026 has curvature-reuse finite-difference column refresh inside quasi-Newton methods (an optimizer change, not a derivative method). (6) Graph colouring helps only sparse Hessians; EDI's are dense, and sparseHessianFD is still archived. (7) fdHess (Koschal design) and complex step use function values, so they do not beat 2P gradient calls. Side note on accuracy, not speed: the FiniteDiff.jl docs give eps^(1/3) ≈ 6e-6 as the optimal relative central-difference step for differencing an accurate gradient. EDI's 1e-4 gives roughly 1e-8 relative truncation error, which is adequate for vcov. Retuning the step would be a minor accuracy tweak with no cost change, so it is not filed as a finding. The Adopted Louis-identity analytic Hessian (v1.0.5-TODO-2) for GLMM / ordinal GLMM remains the right fix for the one repeated use.

bordered-normal-equations.note: Rechecked on 2026-11-19 for work newer than 2026-11-16. The code changes since then (21e0679a, abd7e49d, fe905ca8) only touch Rd text, assertions, metadata and get_X() in the R Lin class; no kernel changed. The fastest exact permutation kernel is still the FWL rewrite, O(n_T p + p^2) per draw, already planned in v1.2.0-TODO-9 (ols_distr_kernel_fwl.md). New items found this run, none of which beats it: (1) Hounyo & Hwang, arXiv 2610.04217 (2026-10), is about validity, not cost, and gives no refit-free shortcut. (2) permApprox, arXiv 2602.22975, is GPD tail approximation, so it loses exactness, which catalog P4 already rejected. (3) RRPP 2.2.5 (2026-11-08) and nptest 1.2 (2026-01) add no new per-draw algorithm. (4) Fiksel (Biometrics 2024) gives a closed-form covariate-adjusted CI; it is an estimator/CI construction, not a faster kernel for this one. Batched GPU QR/Cholesky (MAGMA) does not apply to EDI's CPU build. Catalog P5 rejects stand.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Since 2026-11-16, the four commits touching this problem's files are docs, argument checks and get_X() fixes, with no change to fast_ols.cpp or any solver path. New sources this run: fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11) and estimatr 2.0.0/2.0.1 NEWS. Both keep Cholesky as the fast path, with QR as the rank-revealing fallback, which is EDI's own design (normal equations + LDLT in fast_ols_internal / fast_ols_with_var_cpp). estimatr 2.0.1 fixed the same weakness EDI's catalog already records (O10/O2, Incidental 7: Eigen LDLT::info() rarely flags rank-deficient PSD Gram matrices, so the ColPivQR fallback almost never fires). Its fix is to normalize columns and use a threshold matched to the factor's resolution before falling back to QR. That is a reference design for that robustness TODO, not a speedup, so it is not filed as a finding. Garrison/Chen/Ipsen MRCQR (arXiv 2606.18411, June 2026) is GPU-only at m=2^20, n>=16, so it does not apply at EDI's CPU sizes.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. A single lm.fit plus the HC2 post-fit is still fine at EDI sizes. Finding ols-fit#43925959437.1 (arm-wise Gram plus two small LDLT solves for Lin's per-draw randomization fit; investigate, v1.2.0-TODO-22) still stands, and Lin's fast null is unchanged (compute_fast_randomization_distr via reused worker, inference_continuous_lin.R:252). It is re-reported only to add new evidence for the equality gate: estimatr 2.0.1 NEWS documents that when a covariate is constant within one arm, lm_lin keeps the main effect but drops the interaction, and the treatment coefficient changes meaning (-1.56 to -2.00 in a published replication) while fitted values match. In the arm-wise kernel, the same case makes one arm's Gram singular, so the per-arm column drop must mirror reduce_design_matrix_preserving_treatment, or the kernel will disagree with the lm.fit path. The per-arm imputation form (Oaxaca-Blinder) is confirmed in Ding & Li, arXiv 1712.06170. The B-loop in compute_rand_bootstrap_ci_affine_coefs (lin.R:262) has the same arm structure, but it belongs to problem ols-coef-resampling and is left there. fastQR 1.2.0 (2026-11-18) adds a LAPACK-backed unpivoted QR with no speed claims, so nothing changes for the KK stacked fits (fit_combined / fit_weighted_combined).

findings.candidate: Unchanged from ols-fit#43925959437.1. With covariates centered at the w-independent full-sample means, τ̂_Lin is the difference of the per-arm intercepts from separate OLS fits of y on [1, Xc] in each arm (the imputation / Oaxaca-Blinder form). Each draw then needs two (p+1)×(p+1) Gram matrices (the second by subtracting from the fixed total) and two small LDLT solves. Added this run: the per-arm rank handling must reproduce how the interacted fit drops a column when a covariate is constant within one arm (main effect kept, interaction dropped). Otherwise the kernel returns a different treatment coefficient from the lm.fit path.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The theoretical flop ratio is about 16x per draw (8n(p+1)² vs n(p+1)²/2), as before.
findings.suggested_action: Keep this under v1.2.0-TODO-22. Add an equality fixture with a covariate constant within one arm, plus one with a duplicated covariate, both compared against lm.fit + ols_hc2_post_fit_cpp, before switching the per-draw step to arm-wise Grams.
findings.new_evidence: estimatr 2.0.1 NEWS (CRAN, version published 2026-10-10; fetched 2026-11-19) documents that in lm_lin a covariate constant within one arm drops only its interaction and changes the treatment coefficient (-1.56 to -2.00 in a replication) with identical fitted values. This is a concrete edge case the arm-wise kernel's gate must cover; the speed claim is unchanged.

brute-force-distance.note: Since 2026-11-16 the only code change here (4fc58cd0) swaps the callback result from a bare SEXP to an RObject for rchk protection, which does not change performance. For Euclidean² and L1 the output is n² (or m²), so the direct O(n²p) loop is order-optimal. This run found no 2025-26 work that changes that. The GEMM/Gram form stays rejected (catalog P1/P12; cancellation). L1 has no algebraic GEMM reformulation: the Stack Overflow and Rust SIMD references only show SIMD loops, which pair_dist_helpers already uses. New packages (dissimilarities 0.3.0, cmahalanobis 1.1.0, parallelDist 0.2.7) offer no new algorithm. The earlier R-callback finding (#43925959437.1) is deferred to 2027-05-01 and is not re-reported. New dated evidence weakens it rather than overturning the deferral: Rcpp turned unwind-protect on by default in 1.0.10 (2023-01-12) and made it unconditional in 1.1.1 (2026-01-08). The 2016 measurement of Rcpp::Function at about 7x Rf_eval predates that mechanism, which was the fix reported for Rcpp::Function overhead. The gap between Rcpp::Function and a pre-built Rf_eval is therefore probably smaller than the earlier finding assumed. Hoisting the xi/xj allocations is still a small constant-factor win.

gauss-jordan-elimination.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. It runs once per design on a p×p matrix (O(p³)), never per replicate. Replacing it with LLT is already scheduled (v1.2.0-TODO-22 / audit TODO-29, triage 'investigate'), and nothing new changes that plan. The previous finding is not re-reported.

mahalanobis-quadratic-forms.note: The only faster option is the one already scheduled: whiten once with a Cholesky factor, then run a Euclidean pair loop, giving O(np²+n²p) instead of O(n²p²) (finding #43925959437.2, 'investigate', v1.2.0-TODO-22). This run's sources confirm it again. The SciPy forum (fetched; 2024-10-02) gives the same complexity argument for cdist, with no measured benchmark. mvnfast::maha accepts a precomputed Cholesky factor. Nothing new changes that plan, so it is not re-reported. The arXiv API search (newest first) found no new exact all-pairs Mahalanobis method. Sketching (arXiv 2309.01030) is approximate, which would make it an estimator change.

findings.candidate: Also accept a compiled user distance: an RcppXPtrUtils::cppXPtr pointer routed through EDI's existing user-compiled-fn plumbing, as parallelDist does for custom distances. Keep the R-function path, but hoist the xi/xj buffers out of the loop and evaluate through a pre-built call (Rf_lang3 + Rf_eval) rather than Rcpp::Function::operator().
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this kernel. Mailing-list measurements seen in search results (not fetched; indicative only) put Rcpp::Function at several times the cost of a direct call. The XPtr path removes R interpreter overhead per pair entirely.
findings.suggested_action: Low-priority re-look: add XPtr custom-distance support and hoist the per-pair allocations. Otherwise keep the verdict 'Keep (inherent to a black-box R fn)'.

findings.candidate: LLT of (S + relative ridge × mean diag S), whiten once (Z = X L⁻ᵀ), then a direct per-pair squared-Euclidean loop on the rows of Z, not the Gram expansion: O(np² + n²p). This is the existing Adopt verdict, confirmed again.
findings.claimed_speedup: About p× on the pair loop (the audit's theoretical estimate). The Eigen benchmark at 8x8 gives LLT 0.05 ms against PartialPivLU 0.08 ms, which affects only the O(p³) part.
findings.suggested_action: No new action: this confirms v1.0.5-TODO-29 (catalog §8 TODO-1). Implement with a relative ridge and keep the direct-difference loop on Z.

list-scheduling.note: No faster acceptable method beyond what the catalog has already adopted. run_all_inference_fork_dispatch still dispatches in build order (inference_suite.R:1549, pending = seq_len(n_total); the loop at :1617-1622 takes pending[1L]). The best acceptable improvement is still LPT order (catalog §11 option row at :2064, TODO-5 at :2078; scheduled as release_v1_2_0 TODO-22). It is already decided, so it is not re-reported. New since 2026-11-16: (1) commits 5bdb9dfb and 21e0679a added per-task seeds (v1.0.6-TODO-219, run_all_inference_task_seeds and run_all_inference_with_task_seed). Each task's seed is the master seed plus a hash of its result_name, and the design permutation cache is reset per task. Results therefore no longer depend on task order or worker count, which removes the last determinism concern about reordering pending by LPT. The scheduling algorithm itself did not change. (2) Zhao & Zomaya (ICLR 2026) give smoothness bounds for makespan on identical machines with predictions: a lower bound of 2 − O(η⁻²) and an O(η²)-smooth algorithm. These are competitive-ratio refinements, not a practical rule better than LPT on estimated runtimes at EDI's tens-to-hundreds of tasks. (3) mirai 2.7.4 (2026-11-02) is still FIFO; crew 1.3.3 and future 1.82.0 add no ordering policy. (4) The R-bloggers benchmark, re-fetched, shows longest-first plus dynamic balancing at 100.8% of optimal versus 150.7% in the original order, which supports the existing LPT verdict. The caveat from the previous result still stands: LPT needs per-(class, method, type) runtime estimates capped at max_secs_per_class, and the CI manifest is per test.

inverse-transform-sampling.note: The commits since 2026-11-16 changed only .breslow_hazard (log-scale rescaling when R_k underflows, v1.0.6-TODO-51) and a comment. The inversion is still the linear which(cumhaz >= tgt) scan, and .breslow_hazard still rescans the risk set at every event time. Both are already Adopt under catalog §12 TODO-7 (reverse cumsum plus findInterval), and that is still the right fix: simIDM and VirtualPop use the same findInterval inversion of a step cumulative hazard. Nothing published since 2026-11-16 beats it. simsurv (JSS 97(3), CRAN 1.0.1, 2026-01-22) and cpsurvsim (R Journal 2022) use closed-form or root-finding inversion of parametric hazards, not a Breslow step function. mets 1.3.12 (2026-07-30) still interpolates linearly, which would change the estimator. Ordinal draws: no source benchmarks alias, inverse-CDF and Gumbel-max when each row has its own probabilities; the alias method's per-row setup cancels its gain. Clayton: the copula qrng vignette compares CDM with Marshall–Olkin, and CDM needs no gamma frailty draw.

parametric-bootstrap.note: Changed from faster_option_found: the only earlier finding (k-step bootstrap, #43925959437.1) was rejected by the owner, and the search found no new evidence against that decision. The newest k-step literature is still Andrews 2002 (Econometrica) and Davidson & MacKinnon 1999. The arXiv title listing has no new parametric-bootstrap paper after 2609.10038 (an applied CI). The commits since 2026-11-16 only add NA warnings, a minimum-B check for the LR CI and a move of the resampling flag, with no algorithmic change. The bootstrap Bartlett correction (Rocke 1989; later papers say B≈100–200 is enough) already exists in EDI as lik_ratio_bartlett_approx and is in catalog §9 (TODO-3, I4). Michael 2026 (arXiv 2606.14837) is an analytic Bartlett factor for Gaussian random-effects meta-analysis only. Sequential stopping (Besag–Clifford, Stoepker & Castro, Fischer & Ramdas) is TODO-8/TODO-156. Weighted and multiplier bootstraps are large-sample substitutes, unacceptable at small n. B=199 is exact at α=0.05 (α(B+1) is an integer). pbkrtest 0.5.5 and lme4 2.1-0 bring nothing that cuts refit cost.

random-variate-generation.note: Rechecked the CRAN Distributions task view and the zigg, dqrng and RcppZiggurat pages. zigg 0.0.2 (GPL>=2) claims 7.4x faster normals but warns of lower quality and a shorter period. dqrng 0.4.1 (AGPL-3) has had no new release. Ziggurat consumes a variable number of uniforms per normal, so it breaks set.seed stream parity. These draws are O(n) per dataset and negligible next to the refits. Nothing new for BTPE or PTRS.

findings.candidate: k-step parametric bootstrap: per replicate, take a fixed small number k of Newton steps from the original-sample estimate instead of iterating to convergence. Offered as an opt-in mode (re-reported from the previous run; still stands).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the sources. Davidson & MacKinnon (1999) say only that very few steps are needed, fewer for LR tests and with Newton than quasi-Newton. The saving is the iterations beyond k per refit, which is modest because replicates are already warm-started.
findings.suggested_action: Record the k-step bootstrap in the catalog §9 J options table as an estimator-change option. Before prototyping, measure the iteration counts the warm-started workers actually use. If they converge in 2–3 Newton steps already, drop it.

linear-scan.note: Trivial. The varying-column scan is now inline in process_subset: commit 3dabce47 removed the which_cols_vary helper and the unused extract_row_cols. It is still an O(tp) early-exit scan that reads the subset rows in place without copying them, which is the cost of reading the input, so nothing faster can exist per call. The incremental 'a column starts varying' tracking at O(p) per arrival is already planned in kk14_incremental_covariance.md TODO-1.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. I re-checked it here because the QR is repeated per arrival in 4 subsets. New since 2026-11-16: fastQR 1.2.0 (CRAN, 2026-11-18) adds LAPACK-backed unpivoted QR (qr_lapack, DGEQRF/DORGQR); its NEWS still mentions no pivoting or rank-revealing updates, so it cannot reproduce ColPivHouseholderQR's independent-column choices. arXiv 2412.05905 v3 (2026-03-06) updates the R factor only and does not mention pivoting. An arXiv title search found no 2026 paper on updating rank-revealing QR after row appends. The classic options are URV/UTV updating with Givens rotations and incremental condition estimation (Stewart; Chan RRQR updates). They do not apply to the scaled subsets: each arrival re-centres and re-scales every row, so no row-append update exists, and their pivot order would differ from ColPiv's. A pivoted Cholesky of the Gram/correlation matrix would be cheaper but squares the condition number, so rank decisions near the 1e-12 tolerance would change (an estimator change). The practical wins are already tracked: dropping the redundant second matrix_rank QR (v1.0.5-TODO-29; still present at compute_all_subject_data.cpp:159,182), and recomputing only when the varying set changes (kk14_incremental_covariance.md TODO-1/2). Side observation, not a speed issue: the i_all scaled subset appends row t-1 a second time (xt), so z-scaling counts the current subject twice; presumably this mirrors the earlier R code. Atkinson's FullPivHouseholderQR in generate_permutations.cpp is hoisted out of the draw loop, so it is not hot.

streaming-moments.note: Trivial: scale_columns is a closed-form two-pass z-score, O(tp) per call. Checked: Reichel arXiv 2605.00247 (2026-04-30) still finds Gram fastest and Welford uniquely robust to cancellation, which supports the Welford choice in kk14_incremental_covariance.md. matrixStats NEWS has no release after 1.5.0 (2025-01-07). No new speedup.

ab-timing-comparison.note: Marked trivial (developer tooling), but it sets how many repetitions each cell needs, so I researched it. The commits since 2026-11-16 (fe905ca8, abd7e49d) only added finite/any.missing checks. edi_tuning_accept_candidate (local_machine_tuning_harness.R:309) is still the unpaired rule: Δmedian ≥ 5% and > 2·IQR(candidate). The earlier finding (v1.1.0-TODO-210, investigate) still stands. One new point changes which test v1.1.0-TODO-210 should use. The catalog §12(m) option names a sign test or Hodges–Lehmann. At EDI's presets (reps 3/5/9) the exact sign and signed-rank tests reach a smallest p of 1/2^n: 0.125 at n=3, and 0.0625 two-sided at n=5. They cannot accept anything under quick, and under standard only one-sided. A paired t-interval on per-round log-ratios, or a seeded bootstrap CI, works at these n. A Julia benchmark harness (ProximalBase.jl #153, 2026-10/11) uses exactly that, with a three-way margin verdict and an A/A self-check. It also reports that 6 fixed pairs left 65 of 106 cases inconclusive, which supports adaptive extra pairs.

exhaustive-autotuning.note: Trivial (developer tooling). Checked what is new: Kernel Tuner 1.3.x (2026), the Willemsen 2026 thesis, TUNA (EuroSys'25), and Dieguez et al. (arXiv 2403.08131) on deciding between joint and orthogonal searches. All of them target large spaces. EDI has 2–3 candidates per axis, and racing and BO are already in catalog §12(m). Any saving comes from fewer repetitions per A/B, which is covered under ab-timing-comparison.

linear-search.note: The n_grid has 2–5 points, so bisection saves at most 1–2 cells. Probabilistic or noisy bisection (Horstein PBA; Rodriguez & Ludkovski's generalized PBA) pays off only with many candidate points. atime's predict() interpolates on the log-log scale to find the N for a time budget. That is not a crossover search and would not be faster here. Code changes since last time are validation-only.

findings.candidate: Same paired-difference acceptance as before (v1.1.0-TODO-210), with one refinement to the test. Use a paired t-interval on the per-round log-ratios log(a_i/b_i), or a seeded bootstrap CI. Do not use the exact sign or signed-rank test named in catalog §12(m), because with n = 3–5 pairs their smallest attainable p is 1/2^n (0.125 at n=3, 0.0625 two-sided at n=5), so they can never accept a candidate under the quick preset. Give a three-way margin verdict: faster beyond 5%, within the margin, or inconclusive (add pairs, up to a maximum). Self-check with an A/A run (candidate = baseline): the intervals should cover 0 and false accepts should be near nominal.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. In ProximalBase.jl #153, 6 fixed paired reps left 65 of 106 cases inconclusive, which shows fixed small reps are underpowered and that adaptive extra pairs are needed. The minimum-p limit is arithmetic from the exact null distribution (2^n sign patterns).
findings.suggested_action: Fold into v1.1.0-TODO-210. Pick a paired t on log-ratios (or a seeded bootstrap CI) rather than the sign test or Hodges–Lehmann from catalog §12(m). Add a margin verdict with an inconclusive state, adaptive extra pairs, and an A/A self-check on seeded synthetic timings.
findings.new_evidence: 2026-11-19: the catalog's suggested exact sign or signed-rank test cannot attain p < 0.05 at reps 3 (quick), and only one-sided at reps 5. This changes which test v1.1.0-TODO-210 should implement. Also new: ProximalBase.jl #153 (opened 2026-10-28, revised 2026-11-07/08) is a working paired log-ratio t-interval design with a margin verdict and an A/A check.

permuted-blocks.note: Unchanged since 2026-11-16. The only commit since then, 5bdb9dfb, adds roxygen documentation of the jackknife deletion unit to design_seq_one_by_one_spbr.R; no algorithm code changed. The algorithm is still optimal: one Fisher–Yates shuffle per block plus an O(1) pop per assignment, so O(n) per draw. The one standing finding is the earlier constant-factor one (investigate, v1.2.0-TODO-22): draw_ws_raw in design_seq_one_by_one_random_block_size.R:155 still calls replicate(r, random_block_size_redraw_w_cpp(...)), rebuilding a string-keyed std::map on every replicate. It is re-listed only to keep the conclusion consistent, with no change. Searches turned up nothing new. randomizr is still at 2.0.1, randomizeR at 3.0.2 (2023), and carat 2.3.0 (2026-09-08) is a design/feature package, not a faster block generator. Batched bounded-integer shuffling (doi 10.1002/spe.3369) stays rejected: small blocks gain little and it changes the stream. 2025–26 design work (merged blocks, Zhao's 2026 minimax allocation procedure) consists of alternative designs, not faster ways to draw permuted blocks.

findings.candidate: A batched random-block-size kernel modelled on generate_permutations_spbr_internal. It maps keys to dense integer ids once, keeps per-stratum std::vector state, loops over all r draws in one C++ call, and fills an n×r matrix. This is the same pattern randomizr 2.0.1 uses for block_ra.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not measured for EDI. As an analogue, randomizr 2.0.1 NEWS reports block_ra about 4–8× faster after moving to a single C++ call.
findings.suggested_action: No new action. This is already tracked as v1.2.0-TODO-22 (triage: investigate).

pocock-simon.note: No faster acceptable method found. I re-read the code after the commits since 2026-11-16 (6c4faf7e, 2faac6cf, 3395b6c3, 2c727f4c, fe905ca8, 39ee46bd). Most are doc and argument-check changes. The one algorithm-relevant change is v1.0.6-TODO-183: draw_ws_raw now replays only the t enrolled subjects instead of all n preallocated rows. That is a correctness fix and also does less work. The per-arrival C++ scoring is still O(J) for K=2: it touches only the subject's levels, which is the minimum. Each null draw has to replay the whole sequential path, O(nJ) per draw. ensure_factor_metadata is incremental after the first scan (only row t is registered), so the inventory's 'rescans all t rows, O(n^2 k)' wording is stale. The remaining R-side cost is the per-row vapply in get_subject_levels_idx inside draw_ws_raw, which is O(t·k) R calls once per draw_ws_raw call, not per replicate. That is catalog incidental #9, an implementation issue, not an algorithm one. New since the last research: carat 2.3.0 (CRAN, 2026-09-08; the page does not mention any speed or parallel change). Two arXiv papers on minimization: 2611.08378 (Nov 2026), a new design that targets shift and variance inflation, and 2610.27466, RMST inference under covariate-adaptive randomization. Both change the design or the inference, not the computation. Sequential Monte Carlo p-values (Besag–Clifford, and the anytime-valid version by Fischer–Ramdas, arXiv 2401.07365) and adaptive repetition counts (Zhang–Zhao–Luo, arXiv 2302.05977) already appear in EDI's plan files (v1.2.0 / v2.0.0, catalog). They are not new evidence. The SIGA fast-power paper (arXiv 2608.05527) stays withdrawn: it is an estimator change, and EDI runs no nested power evaluation for it to speed up.

pvalue-combination-rules.note: Trivial: Fisher chi^2_4, Stouffer, min-p and CCT are O(1)/O(k) closed forms, and nothing can be faster. Code checked since 2026-11-16: zhang_combine_exact_pvals (inference_helpers_zhang.R:20-46) and cct_combine_pvalues_full (inference_suite.R:4215-4225) are unchanged; only docs and asserts changed. Commit 5bdb9dfb added zhang_ci_inside_point_grid, a last-resort search with a 2001-point grid plus 5 optimize refinements of the combined p, run only when every candidate and optimize() are rejected. It multiplies fisher_noncentral_two_sided_pval calls by about 2000 in that rare path, but at microseconds per call that is still milliseconds. The rejected reason for the cached-logdc finding (#43925959437.1, trivial at EDI sizes) therefore still holds, and I do not re-report it. Findings #2 (tail-accurate formulas, v1.1.0-TODO-211) and #3 (DPComb / discrete adjustment, v1.2.0-TODO-206) are already being investigated, and nothing new changes them. DPComb is still 1.0.1 (2026-08-22). New comparators since last run: BL-CCT (arXiv 2603.22668), the CCT for count data study (arXiv 2504.14552) and the heavily-right / half-Cauchy line (arXiv 2501.01065, 2609.29658). All are estimator or calibration changes, not speedups. Conclusion changed from faster_option_found to none, because no speed finding is left open.

findings.candidate: Compute the central log-choose terms (log C(row1,x) + log C(row2,col1-x)) once per data set, cached alongside incid_exact_zhang_stats or computed in a per-CI-search C++ helper. Each delta_0 then needs only log_w[x] = logdc[x] + x*log_or, a log-sum-exp and the two-sided sum. This is the pattern R's own fisher.test uses: logdc is computed once by do.logdc, and dnhyper adds log(ncp)*support for each ncp.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Per evaluation it replaces about 3(S+1) lgamma calls with S+1 multiply-adds; the log-sum-exp and exp calls remain, so the expected gain is roughly 2-4x on that function. It is multiplied by the number of bisection steps in each CI search, which is the hot path for this row.
findings.suggested_action: Low-priority micro-optimisation. When touching zhang_exact_speedups.cpp, add a variant that takes precomputed central log-weights (or a vectorised p(delta_0) over the bisection), and test it for equality against the current function.

findings.candidate: Tail-accurate equivalents at the same O(1) cost: qnorm(p/2, lower.tail=FALSE), and 2*pnorm(abs(z), lower.tail=FALSE) for the combined p; -expm1(2*log1p(-p)) for min-p; and optionally the df=4 closed form p1*p2*(1 - log(p1*p2)) for Fisher. For CCT, use the ACAT form: 1/(p*pi) for p < 1e-15 and pcauchy(T, lower.tail=FALSE).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a speedup; same cost. This is a numerical robustness finding.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into v1.0.5 TODO-7 (CCT tail numerics): apply the same lower.tail/log1p rewrites to the Stouffer and min-p branches of zhang_combine_exact_pvals, with unit tests at p = 1e-20.

findings.candidate: Re-reported from the previous run, still standing. It is the Wasserstein-adjusted discrete combination of Contador & Wu (SJS 2025, DOI 10.1111/sjos.12787; arXiv 2309.07692), extended to Stouffer and the other rules in arXiv 2508.02647 (under revision at JCGS), and implemented in DPComb 1.0.1 (CRAN, MIT), which supports binomial and noncentral-hypergeometric components. Related: mid-p combination with convex-order bounds (Rubin-Delanchy, Heard & Lawson, arXiv 1505.05068), which are conservative yet more powerful. If the exact joint convolution option in catalog §11 is chosen, it can be computed in O(d log d + S log S) rather than O(d*S): sort each component's support by its log-p, take cumulative masses, and use a two-pointer sweep over the threshold log pM + log pR <= obs.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a speedup over the current O(1) combination; this is an estimator (test) change. The sources give no runtime numbers. The sort and two-pointer note is my own complexity remark on the catalog's O(d*S) exact option, not a sourced claim.
findings.suggested_action: Keep as a comparator for resolving the Investigate verdict in catalog §11. Use DPComb as a test oracle if a mid-p or adjusted variant is added. Use the two-pointer sweep if the exact convolution is adopted.

barrodale-roberts-simplex.note: Single dense fits at EDI sizes: br stays the right LP solver. quantreg 6.1 (2025-03-10) is still current and its ChangeLog has no br changes. Nothing new beats br for exact general-p QR at n ≤ low thousands. PALB (arXiv 2512.20682, Dec 2025, MIT, Rust/Python) is exact and claims to beat LP and IRLS solvers, but it covers only the unweighted median line fit. Naik–Kundu coordinate-descent LAD (2603.19336) has no exactness guarantee for the LP vertex. The deferred preprocessing-bootstrap finding (#43925959437.2, revisit 2027-05-01) is not re-reported. New finding: when the reduced design is [1, w] (no covariates), the τ-QR solution is the pair of group τ-quantiles, an O(n) selection with no LP. The BB weighted fits use weighted group quantiles, which are unique almost surely. The 97e466f1 refactor (QuantileRegrSharedPrivate) changed no algorithm. The formula rq() calls in the KK quantile components (rq(yd~1) etc.) are still the existing Adopt item (catalog TODO-6b), so they are not re-reported.

induced-smoothing.note: aftgee 1.2.1 (2024-10-07) is still current. No new O(n log n) evaluation exists for the smoothed Gehan equation. Generalized Rank Regression (arXiv 2605.23318) is a different non-convex loss, and aftPenCDA (arXiv 2606.31094) is penalized, so a different estimator. fastAFT remains an estimator change. The ISCF finding (#43925959437.1) was rejected because its host IVWC classes are unpublished. Code since: b22b4b59 adds a Bayesian-bootstrap replicate (compute_weighted_estimate_ivwc) that reruns both aftsrr fits with ISMB B=100 per BB draw, so each replicate now costs about 2×(solve + 100 O(n²p) evaluations). That raises the cost of the ISMB path but does not overturn the stated reject reason (unpublished host, SE/weight change), so it is not re-reported. Flagged here for the owner.

interior-point-lp.note: The proportion class now runs fn for both the estimate-only and the variance fits through QuantileRegrSharedPrivate (97e466f1), and its BB path still uses rq's default br. The existing Prototype covers that solver mismatch. No new IPM or first-order LP result applies at small dense n: PDLP/PDHG targets huge sparse LPs and is inexact, and HiGHS/sklearn publish no comparison against quantreg at small n. conquer 1.3.3 (2023) is unchanged and still smoothing, so it would be an estimator change. Linked to the same two-group closed-form finding as br, because for the logit(y) proportion class with no covariates the unique solution is the same group-quantile difference that fn approximates to tolerance. The deferred preprocessing-bootstrap finding is not re-reported (revisit 2027-05-01).

sandwich-estimator.note: Hendricks–Koenker nid in summary.rq is unchanged. iid, ker and nid are closed-form sandwiches. The alternatives are different estimators: rank inversion (the default for n<1000) is slower, and boot/BLB resample. The 2026 two-way cluster QR variance (arXiv 2602.16376) is a different estimator. The rank-AFT sandwich ISCF idea was rejected (see induced-smoothing). Nothing faster with the same answer was found.

findings.candidate: aftsrr(se='ISCF', B=1): the Johnson–Strawderman sandwich with closed-form V (viClo: one getSi pass building N² pairwise differences, aggregated by cluster through rowsum(id)). Same smoothed Gehan β̂ and same induced-smoothing slope A. B is unused by viClo, but aftsrr only runs the variance branch when B>0, so B must be ≥1. Optionally keep ISMB as a fallback when ISCF returns a non-finite value.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. From the aftgee source fetched this run, the variance step drops from B=100 O(n²p) estimating-function evaluations to one O(n²) closed-form pass, so variance-path fits should drop roughly by the share that the 100 resamples take of the total (the point solve is ~10–50 evaluations under BBsolve). The win grows with n because every evaluation is quadratic.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: on EDI fixtures (matched and reservoir, n 50–1000), compare ISCF vs ISMB(B=100) SE values and timings. If they agree within the A/B tolerance for coverage, switch to se='ISCF', B=1 and drop the RNG wrapper from the SE path. Catalog this as an option on the NEW-rank-AFT row.

findings.candidate: Preprocessing bootstrap (Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val & Melly 2022, Algorithm 4, extending Portnoy–Koenker 1997). Predict residual signs in each replicate from the full-sample β̂(τ), solve the reduced LP on the M ≈ m·(kn)^{1/2} uncertain observations plus two glob observations, then verify the signs and repair any that are wrong. The paper reports numerically identical estimates to the standard solver.
findings.claimed_speedup: CFM 2022 (ar5iv 1909.05782), bootstrap panel for median regression with k=20 and 50 replications: Stata bsqreg simplex 2.63 s vs preprocessing 0.42 s at n=500 (~6×), 3.14 vs 0.63 s at n=1,000 (~5×), 8.19 vs 1.89 s at n=5,000 (~4×). For a single fit at n=500, k=8, preprocessing gives no gain (fn 0.02 s vs pfn 0.04 s).
findings.suggested_action: Do not implement now. Record it in the catalog options tables (NEW-quantile-LP / NEW-quantreg) as considered: exact, cited DOI 10.1007/s00181-020-01898-0, gain unproven at EDI's small p. Re-look only if profiling after the rq.fit Adopt shows replicate QR fits dominate at n ≳ 1,000.

findings.candidate: Closed-form special case for covariate-free designs (the reduced X is [1, w]). β0 is the τ-quantile of the control y (or logit y), as an order statistic (inverse ECDF, not type-7 interpolation). β_T is the τ-quantile of the treated y minus β0. For BB replicates, use weighted group τ-quantiles, which are unique almost surely under continuous Dirichlet weights. Computed by O(n) selection in C++ or R. Fall back to the LP when the solution is non-unique (τ·n_g is an integer for either group, or ties at the cut), unless br's vertex choice is first reproduced and tested.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The cost drops from an LP solve plus R/quantreg call overhead to one O(n) selection per group. Per-draw randomization and BB loops would gain most. Unmeasured.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: add the [1, w] fast path behind a uniqueness check, and A/B it bit-for-bit against rq.fit(br) and rq(weights) on EDI fixtures (n 20–1000, τ ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.75}, odd and even group sizes, tied y). Then record it in the NEW-quantreg / NEW-quantile-LP options tables.

inverse-transform-sampling.note: norm_rand (RNG.h:129-134) has to reproduce R's 'Inversion' N(0,1) stream bit for bit, so AS 241 inversion stays. I checked for new work since 2026-11-16. Ziggurat is still the fastest normal sampler (RcppZiggurat 0.1.8 from 2025-03, zigg 0.0.2 from 2025-02, numpy and dust docs), and Box-Muller is the slowest. Both change the stream, and the zigg author recommends base R for quality. Umeda (Comput. Stat. 2024) gives new approximate inverse CDFs, which would change the answer. No hot loop calls norm_rand. Alias, Gumbel-max and binary-search inversion do not apply, because EDI does no weighted categorical sampling (catalog P2). Nothing overturns catalog P1.

lemire-bounded-integer.note: For a single draw, bounded_rand (RNG.h:324-336) is still the best known method. numpy Generator.integers cites the same Lemire 2019 paper (fetched), and I found nothing from 2026 that beats it for single draws (the only 2026 item is a blog re-derivation). The batched variant is the earlier finding #43925959437.2, deferred to v1.2.0-TODO-238 with revisit date 2027-05-01. New since then: Microsoft STL PR #6119 (open, last updated 2026-04) adds a batched std::shuffle for mt19937_64. On 2026-03-02 Lemire posted 5.2x at n=256 and 6.4x at n=1024 against std::shuffle. That was measured with a 64-bit MT-family engine, not R's 32-bit MT, and it says nothing about the RNG share of EDI's kernels, which was the reason for deferring. So I do not re-report the finding before the revisit date. I record the PR here as evidence to use at the 2027-05-01 re-assessment. Conclusion 'unclear': a faster batched option exists but is deferred, and I am not re-filing it.

mersenne-twister.note: mt_genrand, unif_rand and the RRng(uint32) LCG-scramble seeding exist to reproduce R's stream, so the catalog P1 rejections of SFMT, xoshiro, PCG and Philox for the R stream still hold. No new SFMT benchmarks: the hits are the original SFMT papers and Vigna's 2014 numbers. New evidence on quality: Schumacher, Nishimura and Matsumoto (arXiv 2512.21678, revised 2026-01-02) show MT19937 fails a run-length test, with run length 623 appearing about 40x too often. The authors call this unlikely to be a practical defect. It is a quality note, not a speed one. In code_changes.diff only a comment changed (the mti<=0 reset wording, RNG.h:112).

random-variate-generation.note: New inventory entry: .stereotype_multistart_normals (inference_ordinal_stereotype_logit.R:16-31). It runs a Lehmer/MINSTD LCG (multiplier 48271, modulus 2^31-1) and then Box-Muller, producing n_params deviates, about 5-20 values, for the 2 data-seeded starts. Commit 3395b6c3 now also calls it inside each bootstrap worker fit, through .stereotype_full_data_multistart. That still means O(n_params) interpreted iterations next to up to 9 C++ stereotype fits, so it costs microseconds against milliseconds. The double arithmetic is exact (48271*(2^31-1) < 2^53). MINSTD's lattice structure does not matter for a handful of perturbation draws, and the catalog row (line 1818) endorses this RNG-free design. Vectorizing it would gain nothing measurable. R's own r* samplers (BTPE, Ahrens-Dieter) are kept for R parity. No 2025-26 evidence of a faster acceptable sampler was found.

seed-derivation.note: Earlier finding #43925959437.1, under investigation as v1.1.0-TODO-212, still stands. The code is unchanged: the six RRng(seed_for_index(...)) call sites are binary_match_search.cpp:39, design_fixed_greedy.cpp:97/147, optimal_design_search.cpp:167/214 and rerandomization_helpers.cpp:230, and seed_for_index still truncates to 32 bits (RNG.h:307). I re-report it with new evidence that bears on the choice the TODO leaves open between Philox and xoshiro256++. (a) A Preprints.org manuscript 202609.1244 (vphilox, 15 Sep 2026; the page returned 403, so this comes from search snippets only) reports SIMD Philox4x32-10 at 0.22-0.75x the cost per byte of std::mt19937, flat across thread counts. (b) IACR ePrint 2025/2161 (revised 2026-05-10) reports practical, low-cost cryptanalytic attacks on Philox and Threefry. I could not read which round counts are broken; this matters for adversarial use, not resampling. (c) arXiv 2603.11084 (event-keyed counter-based RNG) is reconfirmed in the arXiv listing. seed_from_unif01 and draw_seed_from_r cost one uniform each (O(1)), so nothing faster is needed there.

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 55(1), doi 10.1002/spe.3369; arXiv 2408.06213). It draws k unbiased bounded integers from one word when the product of the ranges is at most 2^L. With L=32, two draws fit per word whenever the remaining length is at most 2^16, which always holds at EDI's n.
findings.claimed_speedup: The arXiv abstract says it can 'more than double the speed of unbiased random shuffling' for small to moderate arrays. Apache Commons RNG-187 estimates 'up to 2-fold for smaller arrays', and adds that slower generators gain more. Neither benchmarks MT19937 with 32-bit words, so the gain for EDI is not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add as an option row under catalog P2 and bundle it with the stream-changing RNG work under TODO-149(c). The MIT-licensed batched_random repository is a reference implementation to port and test against.

findings.candidate: Same idea as before: a counter-based or small-state child stream keyed by the 64-bit (master, index), with the within-draw position as the counter. New this run: the evidence now points to xoshiro256++ via SplitMix64, or Philox with the caveat below, as the default choice for v1.1.0-TODO-212. (1) A Sept 2026 preprint reports SIMD Philox4x32-10 at 0.22-0.75x the per-byte cost of std::mt19937, flat across threads, so Philox is no longer assumed about 10x slower than MT. (2) An ePrint revised in May 2026 reports practical attacks on Philox and Threefry. That does not matter for non-adversarial resampling, but any Philox choice should cite it and pass a BigCrush-style check on index-keyed streams. Squares (Widynski) is another counter-based option, but it needs an admissible-key derivation step.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for EDI's workload. The vphilox preprint (Preprints.org 202609.1244) claims 0.22-0.75x the mt19937 cost per byte on the bulk path; I saw this in search snippets only, because the page returned HTTP 403. The earlier sources still apply: Random123 says 'little or no overhead' per generator instance, and quuxplusone measured mt19937 seeding at about 500x the cost of xoshiro256ss.
findings.suggested_action: No new TODO. Add to v1.1.0-TODO-212's prototype step: (a) benchmark xoshiro256++ via SplitMix64 against Philox4x32-10 (Random123) as the child engine, (b) cite ePrint 2025/2161 if Philox is chosen, and (c) keep the 64-bit key fix regardless of the benchmark outcome.
findings.new_evidence: Dated after 2026-11-16 triage inputs or not seen last run. (1) vphilox preprint, Preprints.org 202609.1244, posted 2026-09-15: SIMD Philox at 0.22-0.75x the mt19937 cost per byte (search snippet; page 403). (2) IACR ePrint 2025/2161, last revised 2026-05-10: practical attacks on Philox/Threefry. (3) arXiv 2512.21678 v2, 2026-01-02: MT19937 run-length defect. Together these affect which engine TODO-212 should pick; the investigate decision itself is unchanged.

monte-carlo-randomization.note: Since 2026-11-16, commits changed the R orchestration only: a finite-draw minimum and warning, a sequential-MC resume fix (v1.0.6-TODO-166), censoring-bound shifts and custom-statistic checks. Commit 3395b6c3 also removed chained warm starts across permutations to keep results deterministic across thread counts (v1.0.6-TODO-61). Every refit now starts from the full-data MLE. That is a refit-cost question for the resampling-refit / warm-start-continuation problems, not this one. The C++ kernels are unchanged. Re-checked: Fischer–Ramdas is still at arXiv v5 / JRSS-B qkaf014; there is no newer Koning or Cheap Permutation Testing result; SciPy 1.18 permutation_test still uses (b+1)/(r+1) with near-tie tolerance. arXiv's newest permutation-test listings (to 2026-11-18) have nothing on single-test Monte Carlo speed. New this run: (1) Stoepker & Castro (arXiv 2409.18908) is an anytime-valid sequential *estimate* of the Monte Carlo p-value itself, valid at any stopping time. Its GPL-3 R implementation is the CRAN package avseqmc 1.0.2. The previous run said no R implementation of anytime-valid MC p-values existed, so finding #43925959437.1 is re-reported with this evidence. (2) permApprox (arXiv 2602.22975, Feb 2026) fits a GPD tail approximation for zero-free p-values with few permutations. It is approximate, not exact, and adds nothing at r = 501 with EDI's floor, so it is not a finding. (3) fastrerandomize (GPL-3, JAX/GPU) is rejected: it needs a Python and JAX runtime, determinism across devices is not guaranteed, and it adds nothing to EDI's CPU masked-sum kernel at EDI's sizes. (4) Batching the masked sum as a GEMM only pays with several response vectors; EDI already reuses one distribution by affine shift. (5) Rank kernels and per-replicate rematching: nothing newer found; the hoisting work is already tracked. Finding #43925959437.2 (Phipson–Smyth) is unchanged, with nothing new, and stays under v1.2.0-TODO-207.

findings.candidate: Use the Phipson–Smyth exact Monte Carlo p-value (b+1)/(r+1) per tail, two-sided 2·min(b_ge+1, b_le+1)/(r+1) capped at 1, as SciPy permutation_test and perm do. This is a robustness and validity fix, not a speedup.
findings.claimed_speedup: None (cost unchanged, O(r)). Phipson & Smyth say b/r understates the p-value by about 1/r; at r = 501 that is about 0.002, which makes the test slightly anti-conservative near α.
findings.suggested_action: Fix the catalog P4 description of the current rule. Decide, as a policy question, whether to switch to (b+1)/(r+1), or document why b/r with a floor is retained. Bundle the decision with the v1.0.6 TODO-156 stopping-rule work, since both change the reported p-value.

findings.candidate: Anytime-valid sequential Monte Carlo p-values for the standalone test. This is the earlier Fischer–Ramdas testing-by-betting finding, plus a new option: Stoepker & Castro's anytime-valid sequential *estimate* of the Monte Carlo p-value. It uses a Robbins (1970) confidence sequence with a user-set risk epsilon of overstating significance, and supports futility and other stopping criteria with min/max sample bounds. Unlike the betting p-process, it reports a p-value estimate (plus a lower confidence bound), which is closer to what EDI reports now. Draws can still come in seeded batches from the design, so the kernels are unchanged.
findings.claimed_speedup: Stoepker & Castro give no number on the arXiv abstract page; not quantified. For Fischer–Ramdas, the earlier run's reading of arXiv 2401.07365v5 §7.4 gave roughly 85–200 draws against 501 (3–6× fewer) at p ≈ 0.026, α = 0.05. Nothing was measured in EDI.
findings.suggested_action: Add Stoepker–Castro (avseqmc) next to Fischer–Ramdas binomial/mixture and Besag–Clifford in the options table of performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-156 (scheduled as v1.2.0-TODO-11). Use avseqmc as a reference oracle when prototyping the opt-in stopping rule.
findings.new_evidence: The previous run (2026-11-16) said no R or C++ implementation of anytime-valid Monte Carlo p-values was found. This run found avseqmc 1.0.2 on CRAN (GPL-3, published 2025-09-01), which implements the Stoepker & Castro anytime-valid sequential p-value estimate (arXiv 2409.18908). That is a second, estimate-reporting option for v1.2.0-TODO-11 and a GPL-3 reference implementation.

mahalanobis-quadratic-forms.note: Rechecked. The three commits since 2026-11-16 (39ee46bd, 7bf41069, e00ab78f) change design_fixed_rerandomization.R docs, abs_sum_diff scaling and the cutoff-required check. None touches the kernels. rerandomization_search_cpp already whitens once and takes squaredNorm(M(2w-1)). The R batch path already uses crossprod (GEMM) and then a p^2 form per column. compute_objective_vals_cpp's GEMM and whitened upgrade is already tracked (rerandomization_objective_vals_gemm.md). The new searches found the same generic guidance (Cholesky whitening, then Euclidean norms; arXiv 2605.27748) and mvnfast's vignette (about 2x over stats::mahalanobis from C++/OpenMP). That is a constant-factor engineering gain, not a better algorithm. No rank-one two-sample T^2 swap update applies to i.i.d. rejection draws. Within enumeration it is the O(p) Gray-code update in finding 1.

rejection-sampling.note: Earlier findings: early abandoning is deferred until 2027-05-01 (v1.2.0-TODO-239), so it is not re-reported. PSRSRR and LGR were rejected; both are still v1 only on arXiv (checked 2026-11-19), with no new evidence. The arXiv listing shows no new speed-relevant rerandomization paper since 2026-11-16. arXiv 2607.26544 is a balanced-sampling heuristic that does not keep the design law. Two new findings: (1) For small n, exact enumeration of {w : f(w) <= a} with a revolving-door Gray code and O(p) incremental d, followed by r i.i.d. uniform draws from the enumerated set. This gives exactly the same design law, and fastrerandomize ships an exact-enumeration mode for n <= ~20. The DesignFixedOptimal enumeration kernel already planned in catalog §12 could be reused. (2) The odd-n / prob_T != 0.5 path (generate_rerandomized_w_batch) runs in serial R with an O(n log n) apply(order) per candidate. Generalising rerandomization_search_cpp to any n_T would give the parallel, whitened, O(n + np) C++ path the same law. The catalog has no row for this; the v1.0.5 patch README called it an 'optional OpenMP speedup'.

selection-algorithm.note: The full order() on N scores, O(N log N), is still dominated by O(N·np) scoring. Newly checked: kit::topn (GPL-3, CRAN 0.0.21, 2026-01-23) returns order(x)[1:n] without sorting the rest, but falls back to order() for n above about 1500-2000. At EDI's r (hundreds to thousands) the gain is negligible. Floyd-Rivest (miniselect) still has only anecdotal benchmarks (about 20% over nth_element). cvcrand and fastrerandomize also use plain quantile cutoffs. Nothing overturns the catalog's 'trivial gain' verdict.

findings.candidate: Early abandoning (re-reported from 2026-11-16). Accumulate the per-component terms of f (d_j^2 or |d_j|) one row of M at a time and reject once the running sum exceeds the cutoff. The terms are nonnegative, so the decision is unchanged except for floating-point rounding exactly at the cutoff.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this problem. arXiv 2102.05221 reports a 'substantial speedup' from early abandoning in threshold search, but for elastic distances. The gain is bounded by the O(np) share of each draw, since Fisher-Yates O(n) remains.
findings.suggested_action: Add a catalog §P6 row. If it is prototyped, benchmark at n = 100-1000, p = 5-20, p_acc = 1e-2 to 1e-4.

findings.candidate: MCMC and gradient samplers: PSRSRR (arXiv 2602.07613, pair-switching MH plus an asymptotic uniformity correction) and, new this run, Langevin-Gradient Rerandomization (arXiv 2604.07524, SGLD on a continuous relaxation, explicitly non-uniform on the balanced set).
findings.claimed_speedup: PSRSRR: 10-10,000x, about 66x on STAR with n ~ 974 (arXiv 2602.07613). LGR: 'orders of magnitude' in high d, unquantified in the text (n = 500, p_a = 0.01; Figures 1-2 of arXiv 2604.07524).
findings.suggested_action: Keep the default sampler. Add arXiv 2604.07524 (doi 10.48550/arXiv.2604.07524) next to PSRSRR in catalog P6's MCMC row as 'invalid for the uniform design law'. If an alternative design is ever offered, it should be a separate, opt-in design.

findings.candidate: Small-n exact sampler. When C(n, n_T) is small (n ≤ ~20-24), walk every n_T-subset in revolving-door Gray-code order, where consecutive subsets differ by one swap (Knuth TAOCP 4A §7.2.1.3; Mütze survey §4.1). Maintain d = M·s incrementally in O(p) per step (one row of M out, one in), and record the subsets with f ≤ cutoff. This builds the acceptable set A exactly. Then draw r indices i.i.d. uniformly from A, with replacement, using the draw-indexed seeds. This is exactly the law of i.i.d. rejection sampling: uniform on A, independent draws. Dispatch when C(n, n_T)·p < (r/p_acc_est)·(n + np); p_acc can be estimated from a pilot or from the chi-square approximation. At prob_T = 0.5 the mirror halves the walk, because membership in A is symmetric. Reuse the DesignFixedOptimal enumeration kernel already proposed in catalog §12 table (a) (new TODO candidate 1: revolving door + O(p) incremental objective + OpenMP by prefix).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source. My arithmetic, not a measurement: n=20, p=5, r=1000, p_acc=1e-3 needs ~1e6 candidates × ~120 flops ≈ 1.2e8 by rejection, against C(20,10) = 1.85e5 × O(p) ≈ 1e6 by enumeration, about 100x. At larger p_acc, or n ≥ ~28, rejection wins, hence the dispatch rule. fastrerandomize offers exact enumeration (generate_randomizations_exact) and recommends Monte Carlo above about 20 units, which supports the crossover.
findings.suggested_action: Add a row to catalog §P6: 'exact enumeration of A (revolving-door Gray code, O(p) incremental), then r i.i.d. draws from A, for small C(n, n_T)'. If v1.0.5's DesignFixedOptimal enumeration kernel (catalog §12 new TODO candidate 1) is built, expose a 'collect all subsets with f ≤ a' mode and dispatch DesignFixedRerandomization's cutoff path to it. Benchmark at n = 12-24, p = 2-10, p_acc = 1e-1 to 1e-4.

findings.candidate: Generalize rerandomization_search_cpp to any n_T. Use d = M·s with s_i = 1/n_T for treated and -1/n_C for control, M = L^{-1}X' (whitened once), so f = ||d||^2 (for abs_sum_diff, standardize and use the L1 norm). The kernel already provides O(n) Fisher-Yates (shuffle_vec, as in complete_randomization_imbalanced_cpp), per-draw-index seeding, and block-ordered merging, so thread-invariant determinism carries over. Route every cutoff path through this one kernel.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this path. The sort-of-uniforms step costs O(n log n) per candidate against O(n) for Fisher-Yates (Wikipedia, Fisher-Yates shuffle, 'sorting' variant), plus R per-column apply overhead and no parallelism. FastRerandomize (arXiv 2501.07642v3) reports pure-R rerandomization baselines far slower than compiled or batched code (e.g. 112 s base R vs 5 s at n = d = 100). Those numbers are GPU-vs-R, not CPU, so they only indicate scale.
findings.suggested_action: Add a catalog §P6 / §12 row for 'native any-n_T rerandomization_search_cpp'. Prototype it and benchmark generate_rerandomized_w_batch against the C++ kernel at n = 51-501 (odd), p = 5-20, prob_T ∈ {0.3, 0.5}, p_acc = 1e-2 to 1e-3.
