barrodale-roberts-simplex.note: The earlier finding (#43925959437.1, deferred to 2027-05-01) still stands and is not re-reported, because the revisit date has not arrived and there is no new evidence. Code check: the 2026-11-19 commits only move the quantile private methods into QuantileRegrSharedPrivate (v1.0.6-TODO-193). The algorithm is unchanged: rq.fit(br) for estimate-only fits, and formula rq() for weighted bootstrap fits. quantreg is still 6.1 (2025-03-10); its ChangeLog shows no new br, preprocessing or warm-start work. Chernozhukov–Fernández-Val–Melly (arXiv 1909.05782): preprocessing is exact, but its gains show only at large n. The one-step estimator is an estimator change. PALB (arXiv 2512.20682) still covers only the τ=0.5 line fit.

bayesian-bootstrap.note: fwb 1.0.0 NEWS (fetched): its speed-ups are in weight generation, exact percentile CIs and keeping the lm/glm fast-refit path. It also adds per-replicate RNG streams, which EDI already has. None of this makes an exact refit faster. The Lopes–Polson–Sokolov generative/weighted BB work (arXiv 2512.20051) and GMS/GBS (arXiv 2006.00767) amortise the refits with a neural generator, which changes the estimator. BOB tunes the weights, which changes the target. The cond-logit BB/PB change since the last run is documentation and control-flow only.

lbfgs.note: The code changed. Commit 2026-11-18 (v1.0.6-TODO-163) gave compute_weibull_rand_bootstrap_parallel_cpp internal column standardisation, but replicates still start at params0.setZero() (fast_weibull_regression.cpp:898) and run L-BFGS (maxit 100, tol 1e-8) with no Newton polish. The observed fit (fit_weibull_aft_with_column_scaling) now gets a smart start plus up to 5 Newton polish steps on the standardised scale. That fit's own comment says L-BFGS alone stops about 1e-3 away in the coefficients. So replicates are now both slower to converge and solved less precisely than the observed statistic. New finding: reuse the helper (smart start or warm start, then Newton polish) in the bootstrap kernel. This extends catalog §5 TODO-3 (Prototype). Mestdagh et al. 2015 (doi:10.1038/srep16970) back the use of better start values in bootstrap refits.

newton-raphson.note: The aggregated-Newton finding #43925959437.2 was rejected because the kernel has no caller. It is not re-reported: there is no new evidence and compute_coxph_rand_bootstrap_cpp is still uncalled. FastSurvival 2.0.0 (2026-11-16, MIT) is unchanged. New: coxstream 0.1.0 (CRAN 2026-06-20, MIT) is a streaming Newton-Raphson Cox that matches coxph with Efron ties. It targets out-of-memory n, so it brings no speed gain at EDI's sizes, though it could serve as an extra oracle. The adjacent-category parallel Newton change (2026-11-17) reuses exp() values; it is a benchmarked micro-optimisation that keeps the algorithm.

parallel-refit-loop.note: The FRB finding #43925959437.3 was rejected because it changes the estimator. It is not re-reported. Checked: FRB 2.0-1 is unchanged, and the HPC task view lists only R-level frameworks (future, mirai, foreach, RcppParallel) and parallel RNG packages (dqrng, sitmo), none faster than in-C++ OpenMP with per-draw seeds. The robust kernel commits (fused allocation-free weight update; MAD rescale each iteration for M) keep the algorithm. The cold start is still the Prototype (TODO-8). The stereotype L-BFGS loop is still dead code. Eigen issue 3201 (per-call GEMM packing malloc) applies only above a 128 KiB buffer, so not at EDI's p.

warm-start-continuation.note: Sequential null anchoring is unchanged. The only changes to inference_all_abstract_rand.R are control-flow and warning edits, including a simplified sequential-MC early stop. New: Xu (arXiv 2512.14024, doi:10.48550/arXiv.2512.14024) inverts randomisation tests exactly by writing the statistic as a rational function of the parameter. EDI already does this for additive-shift linear estimators (the cached affine randomisation distribution, compute_rand_bootstrap_ci_affine_coefs). It does not apply to the nonlinear refits that use null anchoring. The k-step bootstrap (Andrews 2002) still changes the statistic.

worker-reuse.note: Permuting w changes the design, so the single-QR multi-response trick (R-help, Ripley/Bates) does not apply. The permuted score test (arXiv 2501.03530) avoids refits, but only by changing the statistic. Commits since the last run touch the OLS/Lin/quantile/PPO worker loops only for refactoring, documentation and parity. The recorded C++ batch-kernel Prototypes stand.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, still stands.) The intercept-only refit is the sample τ-quantile, computable with one std::nth_element (O(m)), with all draws batched in C++ using per-draw-index seeds. For p>0 refits, Portnoy–Koenker preprocessing seeded by the observed fit (Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val & Melly) is exact, but its gains appear only at large n.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for the closed form. It removes the model.frame and simplex overhead; the catalog's own estimate for the formula overhead alone is 3–10×. The preprocessing headline (÷100) is at n=50,000, p=20, not at EDI's sizes.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into the existing Adopt (v1.0.5-TODO-19 / catalog TODO-6b). Special-case p==0 to nth_element after a tie-rule identity test, and otherwise keep rq.fit.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, updated.) Collapse each draw to per-distinct-event-time arm counts and run Newton at O(K) per iteration. FastSurvival 2.0.0's coxph_fast now does exact Newton-Raphson with coxph's start, convergence rule and Efron/Breslow ties, so it can serve as a reference implementation.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this kernel. FastSurvival 2.0.0 NEWS makes no speed claim for the Newton version. The gain is O(n) to O(K) per iteration, which is small unless ties are heavy.
findings.suggested_action: Note this in small_kernel_hoists_batch.md Item C, and act only if compute_coxph_rand_bootstrap_cpp gains a caller. Use FastSurvival (MIT) as a test oracle.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, still stands.) Fast robust bootstrap (Salibián-Barrera & Zamar 2002; CRAN FRB): one weighted LS solve per replicate using the full-sample robustness weights, plus a linear correction.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified; roughly K× fewer weighted solves than K-iteration IRLS, in theory.
findings.suggested_action: Record FRB in the catalog options table as an estimator-change option. Revisit only if a true MM estimator is adopted; ROBU (arXiv 2606.26611) would then also be relevant for its initialisation.

findings.candidate: In the bootstrap kernel, build each replicate's start from weibull_aft_start_or_legacy on the standardised X_b (O(np²), deterministic per draw). Then run the same short L-BFGS and the same Newton polish, for example by calling fit_weibull_aft_with_column_scaling with a lower maxit. Alternatively, run the in-file damped Newton directly from that start, since the analytic Hessian already exists. Replicates would then converge to the same gradient tolerance as the observed statistic.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this kernel. The catalog's own estimate is L-BFGS ~15–40 iterations versus Newton ~4–8 (2–4× fewer passes at p ≤ 10). Mestdagh et al. (2015) report large gains from better start values in bootstrap refits of ML models; their ~10× figure includes an approximate bypass mode, so it is not directly comparable.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into catalog §5 TODO-3. Make compute_weibull_rand_bootstrap_parallel_cpp reuse fit_weibull_aft_with_column_scaling (smart start + Newton polish) instead of zero-start L-BFGS. Benchmark at EDI's BRT sizes for both iteration count and NA-draw rate, and check that replicate β_T at the observed data matches the observed fit to within 1e-8.

A new search for weighted / Bayesian-bootstrap U computation turned up only generic O(n log n) merge-sort weighted-sum methods (e.g. arXiv 1810.11332), which are slower than O(n+K) here.

closed-form.note: Trivial: compute_jt_statistic2_from_counts is O(K) and the fast_ridit_analysis_result contrast is O(n); both are at the cost of reading the input. No code change since the last run.

delong-structural-components.note: Speed: EDI's O(n log K)+O(n) placements are at or below the Sun-Xu O(N log N) used by pROC 1.19.1 (2026-08-27); no new faster algorithm turned up. Earlier finding ridit-mann-whitney#43925959437.1 (Brunner-Konietschke unbiased variance) has decision investigate (v1.2.0-TODO-208) and is not re-reported. One new reference for that TODO: CRAN wmwAUC 1.0.0 (2026-07-31, MIT; Grendar, arXiv 2511.20308 v3, 2026-07-21) offers tie-valid Exact Unbiased and Bias-Corrected variance corrections for the empirical AUC. It could serve as a cross-check in the TODO-208 simulation. It is an accuracy reference, not a speedup, so no new finding is filed. Other recent arXiv work (2609.19986 Brunner-Munzel reinterpretation; 2611.11456 censored semi-supervised MW; 2504.01796 Birnbaum-Klose-based test; 2602.16040 covariate-adjusted Wilcoxon) has no computational gain at EDI's setting.

ridit-scoring.note: Scoring is O(n log K) by binary search and the per-replicate rebuild is O(n log n). The O(n+K) level-slot version is already tracked (ridit_kernel_level_slots.md TODO-1..3). ridit_distr_parallel.cpp:91/:93 still compare reference strings per element (already tracked). New searches found no faster ridit scoring method. New on CRAN is pridit (2026-05), which does PCA of ridit scores, not two-sample work. DescTools 0.99.60 has no new release since 2025-03.

findings.candidate: The Brunner & Konietschke (2025) unbiased rank-based estimator of the Mann-Whitney variance. It is built from the same placements, is valid with ties, is non-negative for n_i >= 2, and is L2-consistent.
findings.claimed_speedup: None. It costs the same O(n) after the placements EDI already computes. The gain is accuracy: the authors show that existing estimators, including DeLong's, are biased at small samples (not quantified here).
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: add the unbiased Brunner-Konietschke variance as an option (or as the small-n default) beside the DeLong SE. Compare the type-I error and CI coverage of both at small n_T/n_C with heavy ties, in the TODO-106 simulation.

bisection.note: Checked: the commits since 2026-11-16 (2c727f4c, fe905ca8, 39ee46bd, 0ccb39d2) change only docs and asserts. miettinen_nurminen_speedups.cpp still has the 60-step inner bisection (line 60) and the ≤50-step outer bisection (line 160). The one faster acceptable option known is the closed-form cubic plus Brent (finding risk-difference-ci#43925959437.1). It was deferred to 2027-05-01 as v1.2.0-TODO-241, so it is not re-reported here, and this run found nothing that overturns the deferral. Nothing else beats it. TOMS 748 (Boost, BSL-1.0) and the SciML 2026 bracketing benchmark, where ModAB beats Brent and ITP on generic test functions, are only marginal over Brent for a smooth monotone z(δ) at microsecond cost. sasLM 1.0.1 RDmn uses uniroot, which confirms Brent-class inversion is the norm. No new paper or package found faster.

closed-form.note: Trivial: the RD point estimate and the unpooled Wald SE (with the N/(N−1) factor) are an O(n) single pass over the counts. Commit 39ee46bd only edited the roxygen text in inference_incid_wald.R.

miettinen-nurminen-score.note: Beyond the deferred finding risk-difference-ci#43925959437.1 (closed-form cubic constrained MLE plus Brent; revisit 2027-05-01, v1.2.0-TODO-241), which is not re-reported because nothing new overturns it, nothing faster turned up. Package checks: lrstat is still 0.3.4 (2026-09-15), ratesci 1.1.1 (2026-10-07; NEWS has no RD root-finding change, only the non-iterative Brown-Li Jeffreys RD, which is a different estimator), cicalc 0.2.2, and gsDesign 3.11.0 (testBinomial/ciBinomial invert the MN test). sasLM 1.0.1 (2026-07-14) RDmn uses uniroot and matches ratesci to 8 digits, so it is a new test reference but no speedup. Two papers are estimator changes, not speedups: Mathematics 2026 14(1):45 (z-standard/profile score intervals via polyroot) and arXiv 2609.10865 (Elliptically Optimal). The code changes since the last run are assert and doc edits only.

newcombe-hybrid-score.note: The independent CI is O(1) from two Wilson limits. The p-value is a Brent inversion over α in about 10–15 evaluations. No closed-form inverse and no package with a Newcombe p-value was found: ratesci's MOVER has no test, and its 1.1.x NEWS adds paired MOVER only. The paired φ-correction accuracy finding (#43925959437.2) was rejected because newcombe_paired_ci_cpp has no caller. The only change since is a new roxygen block in fe905ca8 (still 'phi ... taken as 0 when a margin is empty'), which does not overturn the rejection, so the finding is not re-reported. The previous run marked this method faster_option_found only because of that accuracy finding; with the finding rejected, the conclusion is now no_faster_acceptable_found.

wilson-score-interval.note: Trivial closed form, O(1). Like scipy, statsmodels uses an exact quantile (norm.isf). EDI's use of fast_qnorm is the accuracy item v1.0.5 audit TODO-7, already tracked.

findings.candidate: Closed-form Farrington–Manning/MN cubic for p̃_C in trigonometric form, plus Brent on z(δ) ∓ z_{1−α/2} for each bound. Both are already implemented in C++ in CRAN lrstat 0.3.4: remlRiskDiff clamps the acos argument, handles the repeated root, and uses the pooled estimate at δ≈0; mnRiskDiffCIcpp calls brent(f, -1, est, 1e-6). cicalc 0.2.2 (R) and ratesci 1.1.1 (R) use the same cubic.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The catalog's theoretical estimate is ~30–60× fewer flops for the inner solve, and Brent cuts the outer loop from ~50 to roughly 8–15 evaluations. Absolute cost is already microseconds.
findings.suggested_action: When implementing v1.0.5 audit TODO-3 and the brent_ci_inversion.md scope extension to mn_ci_internal, port lrstat's remlRiskDiff (src/miettinen_nurminen.cpp) and its Brent outer root. Test against lrstat::mnRiskDiffCI and remlRiskDiff over an (x_t, n_t, x_c, n_c, δ) grid that includes the boundary cases. Low priority.

findings.candidate: Newcombe (1998b) method 10 with the corrected φ. When AD−BC > 0, the numerator becomes max(AD−BC−N/2, 0). This is ratesci's MOVER-NW ('MOVER_newc') and statsmodels' 'newcombe'.
findings.claimed_speedup: none: this is an estimator/accuracy correction, not a speedup (O(1) either way)
findings.suggested_action: Resolve the Investigate verdict: apply the N/2 correction to the positive φ numerator, and add a test against ratesci::moverpairci (Wilson base, Newcombe correction) or statsmodels confint_proportions_paired(method='newcombe').

irls.note: Changed since 2026-11-16. Commit e00ab78f (2026-11-17, v1.0.6-TODO-50) made the Huber 'M' path re-estimate the MAD scale at the top of every IRLS iteration. It now stops on MASS::rlm's relative-residual-change test, and the default maxit went from the old 10–25 cap to 100. The commit comment says up to 26 iterations were needed on a 20-subject reservoir with outliers. Commit c397cbc5 fused the weight update with no algorithmic change. Two consequences. (a) The deferred Newton finding (robust-m-regression#43925959437.1, revisit 2027-05-01) is not re-reported. Madsen–Nielsen / Chen–Pınar finite termination assumes a fixed scale, and the M path no longer has one, so the new code weakens rather than strengthens that lead. (b) Two new leads that keep the estimator are reported. The first is a safeguarded extrapolation (SQUAREM, JSS 2020 doi 10.18637/jss.v092.i07; damped Anderson, arXiv 1803.06673) of the joint (β, MAD) fixed-point map, which now converges linearly over many iterations. The second is the Huber–Dutter 'H-algorithm' / deweighting MM step (Heng, Zhou & Lange, arXiv 2501.02475 v2, May 2026). It reuses the Cholesky/R factor of XᵀX that the OLS start already computes, so each iteration costs O(np + p²) instead of O(np²). Also checked: robustbase NEWS (0.99-7, 2026-02-04, no IRLS change); pyinit 1.1.5 (2026-01-08); statsmodels 0.15.0 (2026-08-27: RLMDetSMM, M-scale, no IRLS change); FAMM (arXiv 2606.27638), which is an approximation, i.e. an estimator change, not proposed; Ollila–Mian block MM, which targets Huber's Proposal-2 criterion, a different estimator; FRB, already rejected in resampling-refit-loop.

sandwich-estimator.note: Commit e00ab78f added Huber's κ small-sample factor (as in summary.rlm). It is still a closed form, O(n + p³), on the cached OLS R factor, so nothing can be faster. Searches found no 2025–2026 M-estimator-specific correction. The accuracy concerns (Koller–Stahel, mean ψ′→0) are unchanged and are not speed issues.

selection-algorithm.note: Changed by commit e00ab78f: the MAD median now runs once per IRLS iteration on the M path (up to maxit = 100), not once per fit. The mad_scale lambda also allocates a new std::vector each call and fully sorts when n<512. At p≈2–3 an O(n log n) sort can be comparable to the O(np²) weighted crossprod per iteration, so hoisting the buffer and using nth_element at smaller n are plausible constant-factor wins. No source benchmarks selection at n≤1000: the miniselect post benchmarks 2^16 and 10^7 elements; robscale claims fused single-buffer MAD without figures. Catalog O9 judged one call per fit; the per-iteration frequency is new. Not filed as a finding without a source at EDI's sizes; recommend a profile on the M path.

findings.candidate: Finite-termination Newton for the Huber M-estimator (Madsen & Nielsen 1990; Chen & Pınar 1998). It is an active-set Newton on the piecewise-quadratic Huber objective: once the inlier set is correct, one step lands exactly on the minimizer. Each step costs O(np²), the same as IRLS.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Chen & Pınar's abstract claims only 'improving the efficiency' and proves finite termination with no assumptions on the problem. A separate source reports Huber IRLS converging in 4–5 iterations, so the iteration saving at EDI's sizes may be small. The main gain is exact convergence under capped maxit.
findings.suggested_action: Revisit catalog O8's 'Newton instead of IRLS' row for the Huber path only. Prototype Madsen–Nielsen/Chen–Pınar Newton and A/B its iteration counts and estimate differences against IRLS at n≈50–1000, p≲10, especially in KK randomization draws where maxit is capped.

findings.candidate: A deterministic S-step start for the true-MM prototype: Peña–Yohai candidates (RobStatTM::lmrobdetMM, pyinit) or DetS-style robust-Mahalanobis subsets (statsmodels RLMDetS/RLMDetSMM), then a bisquare M-step at the S-scale. Both remove the need for an RNG-seed contract.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The catalog's DetS row estimates ~5–20× current per fit, against ~50–200× for FAST-S. None of the sources fetched gives timings at EDI's sizes.
findings.suggested_action: Fill catalog O8's DetS '[cite needed]' with Peña & Yohai 1999 (pyinit/RobStatTM) and statsmodels RLMDetS. In the TODO-4 MM prototype, A/B a deterministic start against FAST-S on time per fit and on breakdown under leverage contamination at n≈50–1000, p≲10.

findings.candidate: Wrap the joint (β, MAD) IRLS map in a safeguarded extrapolation: SQUAREM (Varadhan–Roland; Du & Varadhan 2020, JSS) or damped Anderson acceleration with restarts (Henderson & Varadhan). Fall back to the plain step whenever the residual-change merit does not decrease. The fixed point, and so the estimator within acc, is unchanged.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for IRLS. The SQUAREM JSS paper and the Henderson–Varadhan abstract claim large reductions in map evaluations for linearly convergent EM/MM schemes, and the catalog's own row cites 2–10× fewer iterations as literature-typical. Toth & Kelley (via search) show Anderson acceleration helps only linearly convergent iterations, which this joint-scale iteration is.
findings.suggested_action: Under the v1.2.0 robust-regression perf lane (v1.2.0-TODO-3), log iteration counts for the M path in KK randomization draws. If the median is well above ~10, prototype a SQUAREM-style step on (β, σ) and A/B iterations, time and |Δβ| against plain IRLS and MASS::rlm.

findings.candidate: Huber–Dutter 'H-algorithm' / deweighting MM step. Huber ρ″ ≤ 1 (and bisquare ψ′ ≤ 1), so the quadratic majorizer with unit curvature gives β ← β + (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ σ̂ψ(r/σ̂). That is OLS on pseudo-responses, reusing the R factor from the OLS start. Each iteration then costs O(np + p²) instead of O(np² + p³). Heng, Zhou & Lange (arXiv 2501.02475 v2, revised 2026-05-16) present this as the way to reuse the Gram matrix and its Cholesky across iterations.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified at EDI's sizes. Heng–Zhou–Lange claim per-iteration savings from Gram/Cholesky reuse but report no IRLS-vs-deweighting numbers on the abstract page. An aggregator summary of Dutter (1977), not verified, says the H-algorithm was 'generally slightly faster' than W (IRLS) in the linear case. The per-iteration flop saving is about a factor p, but the H-step converges linearly, possibly in more iterations.
findings.suggested_action: Add an 'H-algorithm (modified residuals, fixed (XᵀX)⁻¹)' row to catalog O8. If v1.2.0-TODO-3 profiling targets the per-iteration cost, prototype it for method = 'M' only and A/B iterations and time against the current W-algorithm at n≈50–1000, p≈2–10.

sandwich-estimator.note: I found no faster acceptable method that is new since 2026-11-16. The faster option from the last run (finding sandwich-variance#43925959437.1: the p×p Bell–McCaffrey df plus the k×k CR2 meat reduction from estimatr 2.0) still stands, but it was deferred until 2027-05-01. The deferral's condition still holds: cluster_robust_cr2_variance has the same two callers (inference_continuous_ols.R:399, inference_continuous_lin.R:392), and neither is inside a resampling loop. Commits since the last run: 3395b6c3 only changes the CR2 non-estimability floor to a relative noise floor and leaves the Umat / crossprod(Umat) df path unchanged. 97e466f1 refactors gcomp_logistic_cluster_post_fit_cpp into a shared template with a meat_fn lambda; the algorithm is the same, O(np²+p³), with one hash-map score-sum pass. The other commits touch documentation and warnings only. I checked each entry again. HC0 (R helpers, OLS LPM) is a closed form. HC2 already uses exact leverages in O(np²), which is minimal. The cluster GLM meat is one score-sum pass plus G rank-1 updates. Lin–Wei uses prefix sums; the monotone-pointer idea was rejected and nothing new turned up. New this run: (a) the Niccodemi et al. (2020) k×k CR2 formula, implemented in the CR2 package's CR2eff. This is the same idea as deferred finding .1, and its author's own 2025-10-03 benchmark shows it slower than clubSandwich on a 160-cluster dataset, so it gives no new evidence for un-deferring. (b) estimatr 2.0.1 NEWS has no new speed entry. (c) sandwich 3.1-3, clubSandwich 0.7.0 (2026-05-04) and fixest 0.14.2 have no vcov speed changes. (d) coxdev 0.4.0 offers the same O(n)-per-column score residuals as EDI. (e) I found no 2026 arXiv, JSS or R Journal paper with a faster HC/CR algorithm.

findings.candidate: The p×p (r×r) formulation, as now shipped in estimatr ≥2.0.0 C++ (lm_robust_helper.cpp). Bell–McCaffrey df: trace(P) and ‖P‖²_F come from a few p×p Gram products of per-cluster p-vectors, P = S − U − Uᵀ + D, without forming the G×G or n×G objects. Meat: clusters with n_g > k are reduced to a k×k eigenproblem via a thin QR of [U_c, X_c], giving A^{-1/2}X = X + Q(B^{-1/2} − I)QᵀX. Equivalently, use dfadjust vignette Lemma 2 (generalized inverse), which handles singular I−H_gg. Same CR2 estimator and the same df.
findings.claimed_speedup: estimatr 2.0.0 NEWS: about 2× end-to-end on a 1,000-observation, 100-cluster model from the df change alone (a 500×500 cluster matrix replaced by five 3×3 matrices). MacKinnon–Nielsen–Webb (arXiv 2301.04527): the n_g×n_g route is fastest only for cluster size ≤4. Neither number was measured in EDI.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype. Port the estimatr r×r Satterthwaite df (MIT, attribute) and the large-cluster k×k reduction into C++ (or vectorised R). Drop Umat. A/B test against the current function and clubSandwich::coef_test(vcov='CR2', test='Satterthwaite'), including a singular I−H_gg case. Priority rises if the CR2 SE is used inside studentized bootstrap / randomization loops.

findings.candidate: Monotone pointer over the sorted event times, or survival's single backward pass (coxscore2.c), O(n+K) with identical results.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. It removes a log K factor from a non-dominant term.
findings.suggested_action: Optional: do it together with the I-6 fix in compute_robust_vcov; no standalone change.

bernoulli-coin-flips.note: Trivial: one draw per subject, and the C++ kernels are O(n) per draw. Commits 3395b6c3 and 6ae5d609 changed the iBCRD redraw. It now passes n_T/n, so the redraws use the trial's treated count, and keeps the first t rows. Both are correctness fixes; the cost is still O(nr). randomizr 2.0.1 (2026-08-27) adds C++ only to block_ra and the new balanced_ra, with nothing faster for simple or complete assignment. dqrng 0.4.1 is unchanged (AGPL-3).

efron-biased-coin.note: generate_permutations_efron_cpp keeps running counts, O(n) per draw, which is the floor. Commit 3395b6c3 now draws t rows, not n: a correctness change with no cost impact. New since 2026-11-16: arXiv 2611.08378 (Nov 2026; minimization with bounded marginal imbalances) and arXiv 2607.17176 (Jul 2026; doubly adaptive BCD for multiple arms) are new designs, not faster samplers. Sengupta et al., Biometrika 2026 (doi 10.1093/biomet/asag032), covers IPW/AIPW inference under the Efron and Wei designs, which is an estimator topic. The Hollander-Peña / Markaryan-Rosenberger exact routes buy exactness, not speed, and are already tracked. carat 2.3.0 is unchanged.

sequential-replay.note: Since the last run, commit 3dabce47 (v1.0.6-TODO-42) makes the generic draw_ws_raw (design_seq_one_by_one_abstract.R:303-330) restore private$w with on.exit. Commit 3395b6c3 (v1.0.6-TODO-183) advances and restores private$t. This fixes the side effect half of the earlier finding. The speed half still stands: the urn still has no C++ kernel, and assign_wt recounts sum(w==1) over the full w at each step, so the replay costs O(r n^2) R ops. A running-count C++ kernel is O(rn). The new inventory row for KK21-stepwise exact replay (condition_on_ws_for_rand_tests = FALSE) refits weights per step per draw. That cost belongs to the KK21 weight-fit problem, and no faster exact replay exists because the rule depends on the path. No paper or package found offers a vectorized or batched replay faster than a compiled Markov-chain kernel.

urn-design.note: The rule is O(1) per arrival given counts; the per-real-arrival O(t) recount is not hot. Wei's UD is Friedman-type and not exchangeable, so the sequence law has no beta-binomial shortcut. Count-distribution results (Kuba-Mahmoud-Panholzer, Chen-Kuba generalized Friedman urns) give the law of n_T, not the sequence, so they cannot replace sequential simulation. Rivals: MESS::rud 0.6.0 simulates one sequence per call, and its GPL-2 license is not GPL-3 compatible. RARfreq 0.1.5, grouprar and randomizeR 3.0.2 are pure R. None is faster. The speed gap is in the replay (see sequential-replay).

findings.candidate: Add a dedicated C++ urn draw kernel, generate_permutations_urn_cpp. It keeps running counts (nT, nC) with p = (α+β nC)/(2α+β(nT+nC)) and is seeded per draw index from edi_rng::draw_seed_from_r() like generate_permutations_efron_cpp: O(rn) compiled, with the same distribution. It does not touch the R6 state, so the on.exit restores become unnecessary for the urn.
findings.claimed_speedup: O(r n^2) interpreted to O(r n) compiled; complexity argument from catalog §12 (k)/(l), not measured
findings.suggested_action: Keep v1.2.0-TODO-22 (C++ urn kernel). v1.0.6-TODO-42's side-effect part appears done (on.exit restore in commit 3dabce47); close that part once it is tested.
findings.new_evidence: 2026-11-19 commits 3dabce47/3395b6c3 fixed the private$w/private$t side effect (v1.0.6-TODO-42, -183), so the finding narrows to the C++ kernel alone; the speed gap is unchanged.

sequential-monte-carlo-stopping.note: The earlier finding (Fischer & Ramdas betting tests, JRSS-B 87(4):1200, 2025, doi:10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf014; owner decision 'investigate', v1.2.0-TODO-34) still stands. I re-checked it this run and nothing published since 2026-11-16 beats it: no new arXiv versions of 2401.07365 (v5, Dec 2024), 2404.15586 (v4, Aug 2025) or Stoepker & Castro 2409.18908 (v1 only, unpublished). Package checks: simctest 2.6.1 (2024-11-04), MChtest 1.0-4 (2026-08-31), rfvimptest 0.1.4 (2025-05-08); MCHT is still 404 on CRAN. The commits since the last run (3dabce47, 5bdb9dfb) change only how non-finite draws are handled. A prefix below max(mc_min_draws, max(10, 10%)) finite draws now skips its look instead of returning NA, and na.rm = FALSE returns NA on the first non-finite prefix. The per-look 99% Clopper-Pearson band, the batch size max(25, 2√r) and the α threshold are unchanged, so the previous draw-count comparison (current band ≥210 draws, 225 after batching, to reject; betting 39–80) still applies. One related item: Koning & van Meer, 'Anytime Validity is Free' (arXiv 2501.03982 v5, Dec 2025), shows how to induce an anytime-valid sequential test that matches any fixed-N test at N. It does not treat Monte Carlo tests, so its saving there is not quantified. It could address the keeps_estimator concern in v1.2.0-TODO-34: the decision at full r would agree with the fixed r=501 test. Glazer & Stark (arXiv 2405.05238) reuse one Monte Carlo sample across every null in CI inversion. EDI already does this through common random numbers and cached prefixes, so it is not a new finding.

findings.candidate: Anytime-valid sequential Monte Carlo test by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSS-B 2025): the binomial strategy, or the binomial mixture with c<α. Stop to reject when wealth ≥ 1/α and for futility when wealth < α. Keep the batching and fall back to fixed r. Optional refinement for keeping the fixed-r answer: induce the sequential test from the fixed-r test (Koning & van Meer, arXiv 2501.03982), so that it agrees with the r=501 decision at r.
findings.claimed_speedup: Unchanged from the previous finding; these are closed-form minimum draws, not benchmarks. To reject at α=0.05 the binomial strategy needs 44 / 53 / 80 draws with 0 / 1 / 2 losses and the mixture with c=0.04 needs 39 (the paper's figure). The current band needs ≥210, i.e. 225 after batching. The paper's Section 7.4 reports a mean of 85 and a median of 53 permutations, against 200 for Besag-Clifford (h=10). The end-to-end saving per CI search is not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: No new action. Keep this under v1.2.0-TODO-34. When prototyping, also consider the Koning–van Meer induced-test construction, so that the decision at r matches the fixed r=501 test.
findings.new_evidence: Nothing overturns or supersedes the 'investigate' decision. One addition, dated 2025-12-21: Koning & van Meer's arXiv 2501.03982 v5 shows anytime-valid tests can be induced to match a fixed-N test at N. This bears on the finding's keeps_estimator=unknown. I re-checked the code commits since the last run (3dabce47, 5bdb9dfb): the stopping rule is unchanged, so the draw-count comparison still holds.

crude-monte-carlo.note: The previous finding (Boos-Zhang 1/B extrapolation, simulation-study-engine#43925959437.1) is deferred until 2027-05-01. This run found no new evidence (no new simhelpers release past 0.3.2, no 2026 Boos-Zhang work), so it is not re-reported. The precision-targeted Nrep is already catalog §12 option (n). Wu & Kawai arXiv 2510.22688 is still at v3 (2026-06-20), and SimDesign 2.25-2.28 adds no MCSE-based stopping. Control variates and common random numbers, the general variance-reduction family, have no benchmark for statistical method comparisons. result_key_store.cpp is unchanged: an FNV-1a uint64 unordered_set, O(1) per key. Commit 97e466f1 only refactored the inference-call error handling into call_inference(); no speed change.

findings.candidate: Boos & Zhang (2000) linear extrapolation in 1/B. Inside each replicate, compute the CI and p-value on several subsamples of the B resample statistics already drawn (e.g. b = 39…B). Then regress the coverage or rejection indicator on 1/b across replicates and report the intercept as the B=∞ coverage or power, with a cluster-robust MCSE. Implemented in simhelpers::extrapolate_coverage / extrapolate_rejection (0.3.0+, exclude_above added in 0.3.2, 2026-11-12).
findings.claimed_speedup: Boos & Zhang's abstract says linear extrapolation corrects the finite-B bias and so reduces computation time in Monte Carlo power studies. In Pustejovsky's worked example (R=2500), 399 bootstrap draws per replicate plus extrapolation gave coverage 0.946 (MCSE 0.004), against 0.9516 from brute force with B=2399: about 6× fewer resamples. CI computations rose about 8×, so it only pays when draws, which in EDI are refits, cost far more than computing a CI. Not quantified for EDI.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: add an opt-in 'extrapolated' summary for bootstrap and randomization cells. Record the p-values and CIs at nested sub-B values inside each replicate, and validate against a brute-force large-B run on a few cells. Use simhelpers::extrapolate_* (GPL-3) as the reference implementation.

ordinal-binary-expansion.note: The commit since 2026-11-16 (39ee46bd) is documentation only. It corrects the adjacent-category row-count wording and the return field name (num_iter); the algorithm is unchanged. The expansions emit at most 2 (AC) or min(y+1,K-1) (CR) rows per subject, so their O(nK) cost equals the output size. Rival versions re-checked on CRAN: VGAM 1.1-14 (2025-12-04), ordinalNet 2.14 (2026-02-13), rms 8.2-1 (2026-11-01) and GLMcat 1.0.0 (2025-09-04). None has a release after 2026-11-16, and none brings a new algorithm. Grouping person-period rows into binomial counts helps only with discrete covariates, which do not occur at EDI's sizes. Structure-exploiting fits that never build X_aug are already catalog §2 (3) / TODO-3, so they are not re-reported. For the AC stacked composite likelihood, the open question is still SE validity (conditional ACLR with a sandwich variance, PMC3085191; Mukherjee et al. 2007), not speed.

analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form score, observed Hessian and expected_hessian, O(n K d^2). Checked for new work since 2026-11-16. The 2026 sources found (arXiv 2606.04356, a structural-estimation comparison) again say AD is no faster than hand-coded derivatives. The mnlogit Hessian-structure gain (JSS v75 i03, DOI 10.18637/jss.v075.i03, fetched) is the same constant-factor idea the catalog already marks Keep ('sparsity = incidental'). The commits since then (centering and scaling the design) do not change the derivative code.

log-sum-exp.note: Trivial: max-shifted log-sum-exp, O(K) per observation with small K, at the lower bound; nothing faster that is as accurate.

multistart.note: Since the last research, v1.0.6-TODO-172 (commit 3395b6c3) also runs the deterministic multistart (up to 9 nonconcave fits) in every parametric-bootstrap worker fit, so the multistart cost now covers all resampling refits. New sources since 2026-11-16: arXiv 2602.13450 (Nehzati & Cussen; v2 June 2026) gives Bayesian inference on how often random restarts reach the same optimum. It is random-restart based and gives no stopping rule, so it does not apply to EDI's RNG-free starts. Not previously considered (catalog §5 and multistart_nonconcave_likelihoods.md have no entry): variable projection, i.e. profiling out (alpha, beta) for fixed loadings gamma. Given gamma, the stereotype likelihood is a concave multinomial logit in (alpha, beta), and EDI already supports fixing gamma (fixed_idx; adjacent-category start at inference_ordinal_stereotype_logit.R:196). For K=3 the outer problem is 1-D, so a deterministic grid plus polish finds the global optimum and could replace the multistart. See the finding: speed not quantified, low confidence.

newton-raphson.note: Newton then L-BFGS fallback. Rival software checked again: clustord 2.0.1 (2026-03-03), VGAM 1.1-14 NEWS (no rrvglm solver change; rrvglm is alternating-only since 1.1-10), gnm 1.1-5 (2023, unchanged), ordinalgmifs 1.0.9 (stagewise, high-dimensional only) and the CRAN Optimization task view (trust, RcppTrust, marqLevAlg, already in the taxonomy). None is faster than C++ analytic-Hessian Newton/L-BFGS at EDI's sizes. LM/trust-region remains tracked as catalog TODO-6 (Prototype). The variable-projection idea is reported under multistart because its main benefit is global reliability, not per-iteration speed.

profile-likelihood.note: Variance fallback only: 3 warm-started damped-Newton profile refits plus a second finite difference. The new searches found no newer single-curvature method; modified-profile corrections are an estimator change, not a speedup. Not a hot path.

reparameterization.note: Cumulative-softmax ordered phi. The 2026 arXiv papers found (2609.26113 cumulative softmax, 2608.10406 and 2609.33515 softplus increments) use equivalent-cost monotone maps, and none shows better conditioning. The new design centering/scaling (v1.0.6-TODO-172) is a separate, exact conditioning fix that leaves gamma unchanged.

findings.candidate: Variable projection (profile over the loadings): for fixed gamma (hence fixed phi), logit_j = alpha_j + phi_j x'beta is linear in (alpha, beta), so the inner fit is a strictly concave multinomial logit with a unique MLE that Newton finds from any start. The fit is then a (K-2)-dimensional outer problem in gamma alone. For K=3 (one free score) a deterministic 1-D grid over gamma with warm-started concave inner Newton fits, then a Brent/Newton polish on the best cell, gives the global ordered-score MLE up to grid resolution, with no random starts. For K>=4 the same reduction shrinks the nonconcave search to K-2 dimensions, so starts can be placed in gamma space only. EDI already fits with gamma held fixed (fixed_idx; the adjacent-category stage at inference_ordinal_stereotype_logit.R:196), so the inner solver exists.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Plausibly comparable or lower cost at K=3: about 10-20 warm-started concave Newton fits of 2-4 iterations each, against up to 9 cold nonconcave fits that often fall back to long L-BFGS runs. The main gain is reliability (a deterministic global optimum at K=3), not wall-clock.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype for K=3 only: a 1-D grid over gamma (e.g. 15-25 points in the logit-phi scale, plus phi in {0,1}) using fast_stereotype_logit_cpp with fixed_idx = gamma_idx, warm-started along the grid, then a free polish from the best point. A/B it against .stereotype_full_data_multistart on the reference fixtures and simulated nulls for NLL attained, beta_T and wall-clock, before considering it for resampling loops.

m-out-of-n-subsampling.note: Since 2026-11-16 the code changes (72ea20ba, 5bdb9dfb, dd255899, 97e466f1, fe905ca8) are robustness refactors only: a shared resampling_centered_pivot_for_inference, the ratio usable-fraction gate (v1.0.6-TODO-230), deadline checks, re-throwing control conditions, and assertion tightening. The cost stays B·fit(m) or B·fit(b). Checked for anything new: Ohlendorff et al. 'Cheap subsampling' has a new version, v4 (arXiv 2501.10289, 2026-10-01). Lam & Wang's cheap bootstrap for SGD appeared in JMLR 27 (2026). The previous result's list still holds: scalable subsampling (Biometrika 2024), adaptive BLB (2608.16892), and the Ma–Leng–Wang optimal subsampling bootstrap for massive n. moonboot 2.0.1 (2025-12-08) and dqrng 0.4.1 add no new sampling algorithm. Nothing computes the same √m- or FPC-scaled subsampling distribution with fewer refits. Cheap bootstrap / cheap subsampling is the same idea as earlier finding #43925959437.1 (triage: investigate, v1.4.0-TODO-20). It is not re-reported: the v4 preprint is supporting material for that TODO, not a change to it. Partial Fisher–Yates for the draw primitive remains catalog TODO-2. I mark this no_faster_acceptable_found because the only faster candidate changes the estimator and is already on the roadmap.

minimum-volatility.note: Commit 97e466f1 only makes control conditions (timeouts) abort the grid. The grid is unchanged: 9 points, n^0.5 to n^0.9, B = 251. Checked: the Jach–McElroy–Politis KS criterion (as applied in arXiv 2309.04926) uses the same grid of subsampling distributions with a different statistic, so it costs the same. moonboot's m selectors (R Journal RJ-2025-031: Bickel–Sakov, Götze–Račkauskas, Sherman–Carlstein double bootstrap) are similar or higher in cost. Ma–Leng–Wang hyperparameter selection under a compute budget targets BLB or subsampled double bootstrap at massive n. blocklength (HHJ, Politis–White, Lahiri plug-ins) targets time-series block length. No 2025–2026 work on minimum volatility itself turned up. The catalog already lists fixed m = n^0.7 as the cheap, non-adaptive alternative.

analytic-derivatives.note: The likelihoods and gradients stay closed form at O(np), and no faster way to compute them was found. What is new is commit 5bdb9dfb (v1.0.6-TODO-132, 2026-11-19). It switched the IVWC frailty and Clayton fits in compute_treatment_estimate_during_randomization_inference and shared() to estimate_only = FALSE, so every resampling replicate now computes the FD observed information: central differences, 2(p+2) gradient evaluations, in fast_weibull_frailty.cpp:236/402, and forward differences, p+3 evaluations, for Clayton. The catalog's NEW-fd-hessian 'Keep' reason ('once per fit, not per iteration') assumed the Hessian stayed out of the resampling loop, and that no longer holds. There are two improvements: (1) difference only the free coordinates when fixed_idx pins the variance components (bit-identical SE); (2) a closed-form GH observed information (Pan & Thompson 2003; Charvat 2023 for LAGHQ). See the finding.

boundary-reduced-refit.note: dep_cens_fit_retry runs only after the multistart fails: one cold refit plus at most one refit with atanh(rho) pinned at the +/-3 clamp, O(2 iters n p) on a rare path. The literature on correlation near the boundary (Terza-style reparameterization for censored bivariate normal) and the glmmTMB guidance on dropping degenerate components both amount to the same reduced refit. A true bound-constrained L-BFGS-B is the only alternative, is already listed in catalog NEW-nonconcave-dependence-mle, and gives no speed gain. Nothing faster.

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: Both earlier findings (#43925959437.1 cluster-total collapse, #43925959437.2 LAGHQ) stand and are triaged 'investigate' (v1.2.0-TODO-22, v1.2.0-TODO-11). I re-checked Charvat 2023 (doi 10.1080/00031305.2022.2110939) and mexhaz on CRAN (2.6, 2024-06-28, unchanged), and searched again for non-adaptive GH frailty work with closed-form derivatives; nothing newer. GLMMadaptive 0.9-9 was published 2026-11-17, but its NEWS gives no entry for it. No new evidence changes the triaged findings, so they are not re-reported. The new Hessian finding uses this kernel's posterior moments.

lbfgs.note: LBFGS++ latest is v0.4.0, which adds final_approx_hessian accessors and makes no speed claim. MultiFrailty 0.1.0 (2026-08-07) uses maxLik NR/BFGS with numDeriv, and CopulaCenR 1.2.4 is unchanged. Neither is faster than C++ L-BFGS with an analytic gradient. The warm-start and initial-Hessian literature found nothing new for resampling refits.

multistart.note: The commits since 2026-11-16 do not change the start ladders. Searches found only general multistart guidance (clustered starts, Knitro and estimagic), nothing showing fewer local solves at 3-4 starts and small p for copula or dependent-censoring likelihoods. The 2026 GMM preprint (arXiv 2604.04032) is an estimator change. Keep.

findings.candidate: Cluster-total (sufficient-statistic) collapse. log T = Xβ + u + σε·ε with extreme-value ε is a PH model with frailty exp(-u/σε), so for cluster g at node k the conditional log-lik is const_g + Σ_i δ_i base_wi + D_g δ_k − H_g e^{δ_k}, with D_g=Σδ_i and H_g=Σ_i exp(base_wi), both computed once per evaluation in O(n). Each (g,k) term is then O(1). The gradient needs only per-cluster posterior moments E_g[e^δ], E_g[δ e^δ] and E_g[δ], giving per-observation scalars s_i = (exp(base_wi)·E_g[e^δ] − δ_i)/σε and one Xᵀs GEMV. Total O(np + GK), and the n×K r/w matrices disappear. This is the reduction Charvat (2023) uses to write the cluster integrand for a normal-intercept shared frailty. It is an algebraic identity, so the estimator is unchanged.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. My operation count: node work drops from O(nK) to O(GK), about 2× at EDI's pairs, and the gradient drops from O(nKp) to O(np), about K=20× on that term. This subsumes catalog §5 TODO-4 (O(nK+np)). Theoretical, not measured.
findings.suggested_action: Widen catalog §5 TODO-4 to the full cluster-total collapse (O(np+GK)), not just the GEMV hoist. Benchmark it against the current kernel at n=50–500 pairs, p=2–10, and check that log-lik and gradient agree to 1e-10 relative.

findings.candidate: Lambert-based adaptive GH (LAGHQ, Charvat, The American Statistician 77(1):41–50, 2023). For a shared frailty model with a normal random intercept, the cluster mode is closed form: b̂_g = D_gτ² − W0(H_gτ² e^{D_gτ²}), using the collapsed statistics above. The curvature is H_g e^{b̂}+1/τ², and the paper gives closed-form gradient and Hessian of the approximate likelihood. This removes both objections the catalog recorded against AGQ for this kernel (no nested optimization, and an exact gradient without implicit differentiation). Fewer nodes (e.g. 5–9) then suffice. Charvat's GPL(>=2) package mexhaz imports lamW and is the likely reference implementation. Boost.Math lambert_w0 (BH, BSL-1.0) supplies W0 in C++.
findings.claimed_speedup: The source gives no timings; it claims maximisation is 'convenient and efficient'. Theoretical: one W0 per cluster instead of 3–5 Newton steps, and K≈5–9 instead of 20 nodes, so roughly 2–4× per evaluation on top of the collapse. Not measured.
findings.suggested_action: Add Charvat 2023 LAGHQ to v1.0.5 TODO-153 (performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md) as the AGQ route for fast_weibull_frailty.cpp, and name the file in its scope. Prototype it after the collapse finding, check mexhaz for the formulas, then A/B against K=50 non-adaptive GH for σu up to e^1.5.

findings.candidate: (1) Exact and cheap: in the FD Hessian, difference only the free coordinates (fixed_spec.free_idx). Central-difference column i depends only on perturbing parameter i, and the symmetrized free block uses only free rows and columns, so the inverted block and the SE are bit-identical. The frailty replicate cost drops from 2(p+2) to 2p gradient evaluations, and Clayton from p+3 to p+1. (2) Larger: a closed-form observed information for the GH frailty likelihood. It is the posterior-weighted complete-data Hessian minus the posterior score covariance (Louis identity), per Pan & Thompson 2003, who give the closed-form score and observed information for GH-approximated GLMMs. With the cluster-total collapse of finding #43925959437.1, this is O(np^2 + GK) and costs about one gradient pass. If LAGHQ (#43925959437.2) is adopted, Charvat 2023 gives the closed-form Hessian directly. Same estimator and same beta; SEs, and hence the IVW pooled estimate, change only at FD-error level (more accurate).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Theoretical: at p=2, option (1) cuts the frailty Hessian from 8 to 4 gradient evaluations and Clayton from 5 to 3. Option (2) cuts the frailty Hessian to about 1-2 gradient-equivalents. Against a warm-started L-BFGS replicate of an estimated 20-40 evaluations, that is roughly 10-25% of per-replicate time for the frailty IVWC classes (my estimate, unmeasured).
findings.suggested_action: Reopen catalog NEW-fd-hessian (its Keep reason no longer holds after v1.0.6-TODO-132). First restrict FD to free_idx in WeibullFrailtyNormalLikelihood::hessian, ClaytonWeibullLikelihood::hessian and DepCensTransformLikelihood::hessian, and test that the SE is bit-identical. Then fold an analytic GH information into v1.2.0-TODO-22 alongside the cluster-total collapse, and benchmark per-replicate time for the frailty IVWC randomization test at n=50-500 pairs.
findings.new_evidence: Catalog NEW-fd-hessian chose Keep because the Hessian 'runs once per fit, not per iteration'. Commit 5bdb9dfb (2026-11-19, v1.0.6-TODO-132) and 72ea20ba (2026-11-20) made every IVWC resampling and randomization replicate a full fit with vcov (estimate_only = FALSE), so the FD Hessian is now inside the resampling loop.

analytic-derivatives.note: WeibullAFTLikelihood / WeibullAFTLikelihoodGeneral are unchanged in substance since 2026-11-16. The only commits were a comment spelling fix and 6a3651ee, which unrolls two off-diagonal columns at a time in score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign; results are bit-identical, with lower add latency. Closed-form O(np) NLL/gradient plus an O(np^2) crossprod Hessian is already the floor. This run found no TMB/RTMB or dfr.dist evidence that AD beats hand-coded closed forms: the dfr.dist vignette favours an analytic score plus an AD Hessian over full AD, and EDI already has both derivatives analytic.

lbfgs.note: New since 2026-11-16 (commit 3dabce47, v1.0.6-TODO-163): fit_weibull_aft_with_column_scaling standardizes badly scaled columns, runs the default L-BFGS, then adds up to 5 full Newton polish steps with the analytic Hessian and LLT. The code comment says L-BFGS stops on its relative function-decrease rule 'while coefficients are still ~1e-3 off'. So on standardized data EDI now pays for an L-BFGS run (catalog: 15-40 iterations) plus Newton steps. The standardization also removes the ill-conditioning that was the main risk of Newton-first. This is new evidence for the catalog's existing Prototype (v1.0.5 TODO-3, Newton default); see the finding. LBFGSpp: no release after v0.4.0.

multistart.note: Re-checked at 3915dfb2: robust_survreg_with_surv_object still sets init = rep(0, p+1) (helper_robust_regression.R:153) and jitters with unscaled rnorm (:201). The only change is a maxiter comment. The earlier finding weibull-aft-mle#43925959437.1 is already triaged investigate (v1.1.0-TODO-213) and nothing changes it, so it is not re-filed. survreg's documented init(x, weights) start (checked again this run) still supports it. arXiv 2102.07356 (noniterative auxiliary estimating equations) offers only a GMM start, not the MLE, and adds nothing beyond the moment start already proposed.

Rfast2 censweib.reg (Newton-Raphson, C++, GPL >= 2) is another implementation, not a faster algorithm. New code: weibull_fit_standardized_retry (R, 2557834b) now overlaps the C++ internal standardization. It runs only after a failed fit, so it is not a hot path, but the two could be merged.

sandwich-estimator.note: The rowsum-of-scores plus crossprod pair-cluster meat is O(np^2) and minimal; the code is unchanged. This run's search found only CR2/jackknife variants (MacKinnon-Nielsen-Webb arXiv 2301.04527, linear models), which would be estimator changes. The survival 3.8-0 robust-variance fix with case weights matters only for validating the survreg fallback with weights.

findings.candidate: Make the first attempt with init omitted (NULL) so survreg uses the distribution's documented init(x, weights) mean/variance start. Before any jitter, add scale-aware deterministic starts: intercept = mean log-time and log-scale from the residual SD (the weibull_smart_cold_start pattern applied to lognormal/loglogistic). Keep the seeded jitter only as a last resort, scaled by SE or |start|. Re-reported from 2026-11-16; the code is unchanged.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The expected gain is fewer failed survreg calls per fit: a zero intercept is far from log(time) at typical time scales.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into multistart_nonconcave_likelihoods.md as the concrete 'deterministic data-driven starts' prototype: init=NULL first, then a moment start, then scaled jitter. A/B the failure rate and the attempts per fit.

findings.candidate: For the unclustered case, call survival::survreg.fit(x = cbind(1, X), y = Surv(...), weights, offset = 0, init = warm, controlvals = survreg.control(), dist = survreg.distributions$weibull, ...) on the prebuilt matrix, falling back to the formula path on error. This is the same Newton–Raphson, likelihood and start, and mirrors the existing coxph.fit interim path. The end state remains the native weighted C++ kernel (bayesian_bootstrap_performance.md item 2).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified; no source benchmarks survreg.fit against survreg. The gain is removing the per-draw formula and model-frame overhead, multiplied by B.
findings.suggested_action: Add as an interim sub-item beside the coxph.fit interim in bayesian_bootstrap_performance.md item 2, guarded by a fallback. Benchmark per-draw time first; prefer going straight to the native C++ weighted kernel if that is near.

findings.candidate: On the standardized scale, run the existing damped Newton (newton_then_lbfgs) from the smart cold start and drop the L-BFGS phase plus separate polish; keep L-BFGS only as Newton's existing fallback. The standardization now removes the conditioning problem that was the main risk of Newton-first. Apply the same in the BRT kernel, with the smart or observed-MLE start that the catalog already lists. This is new code-level evidence for the catalog's Prototype v1.0.5 TODO-3, not a new idea.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source. The catalog's own estimate is L-BFGS 15-40 iterations versus Newton 4-8. The current path adds up to 5 Newton steps on top of L-BFGS. arXiv 2310.01589 reports, in another model, that Newton iterations from an L-BFGS endpoint are usually needed only once, which supports Newton converging quickly near the optimum. Expected gain is modest (perhaps 1.2-2x per fit at p <= 10), multiplied in bootstrap and randomization loops.
findings.suggested_action: Attach to the existing v1.0.5 TODO-3 prototype. Benchmark the standardized-scale newton_then_lbfgs path against lbfgs+polish (iterations, wall time, failure rate) on survival::colon and the simulation DGPs, including compute_weibull_rand_bootstrap_parallel_cpp with a smart start.

analytic-derivatives.note: Unchanged. Re-searched AD vs hand-coded derivatives (RTMB/LaMa vignettes; a 2026 arXiv structural-estimation paper, 2606.04356, finds AD can be slower than manual derivatives). Nothing beats EDI's closed-form O(n·k) score and O(n·k²) observed information with distinct-y special-function tables. The ZAP/ZOIB expected_hessian functions are still dead code.

closed-form.note: Trivial: the closed-form ZIP θ→∞ limit (softplus/log-add-exp) is a single O(n k) pass; nothing faster.

finite-differences.note: Unchanged. The ZipLimitLikelihood FD Hessian is fallback-only and costs O(nk²), the same order as an analytic Hessian. A search on complex-step/AD replacements found nothing ZIP-specific and no speed gain, only accuracy notes (AD-based ZIP Hessians in deep-inference, an econometrics AD-vs-FD study).

laplace-approximation-tmb.note: Updated from the code diff. Commits 3395b6c3 and 3dabce47 (2026-11-19) changed both weighted glmmTMB replicate calls to glmmTMBControl(parallel = 1L), for determinism (v1.0.6-TODO-62/64). That covers the 'parallel=1' half of finding #43925959437.1. Both calls (inference_count_hurdle.R:537-546, inference_count_zero_augmented_poisson_abstract.R:1179-1189) still pass no se argument, so sdreport still runs on estimate-only replicates. glmmTMB on CRAN is still 1.1.15.2 (2026-09-29, AGPL-3); its refman now documents a per-fit use_rtmb switch (RTMB backend), with no speed claim. RTMB 2.0 (2026-09-17) NEWS has no DataEval or thread-safety change. Finding .2 (weighted C++ kernels, fastglm oracle) is unchanged and under investigate (v1.2.0-TODO-23), so it is not re-reported.

lbfgs.note: Unchanged. New comparator found: fasthurdle (GitHub mkanai/fasthurdle, v1.2.0, 2026) uses C++ BFGS via roptim with an analytic Hessian for scores. It claims 2.2–6.6× over pscl::hurdle at n=1e3–1e5, the same class as EDI's C++ L-BFGS with analytic gradients, so it is not faster than EDI. fastglm is still 0.1.4 (2026-11-11 republication, GPL-2|GPL-3), with SQUAREM-EM at about 4× over pscl, already judged no faster. The r-help guidance (BFGS default; EM more robust but slower) is consistent with EDI's design.

likelihood-factorization.note: Unchanged. pscl/countreg hurdle docs still describe two separate optim fits, and fasthurdle and fastglm_hurdle also fit the parts independently. Nothing is faster for an exactly separable likelihood.

newton-raphson.note: Unchanged. The search on damped/trust-region Newton vs alternating IRLS+Brent θ for the hurdle-NB found only fastglm's alternating scheme, which is no faster than EDI's block-separable Newton with count-only null refits. No newer method was found.

truncated-series-summation.note: TruncatedNegBinCount::expected_hessian is still dead code. The earlier finding #43925959437.3 was rejected because it is dead code (v1.0.6-TODO-43). There is no new evidence: the trigamma-free method (arXiv 2306.04798) and a Jeffreys-prior ZT-NB information derivation (arXiv 2401.03649) do not touch a live path, so there is no speedup to claim.

findings.candidate: Weighted direct C++ fits (catalog §10 TODO-3). fastglm 0.1.4 already ships weighted C++ fitters: fastglm_hurdle (logistic plus truncated Poisson/NB, IRLS with Brent θ) and fastglm_zi (SQUAREM-EM, IRLS M-steps). Use them as a reference and test oracle for adding weights to EDI's own fast_hurdle_negbin / fast_zinb / fast_zero_augmented_poisson kernels, or as an interim back-end.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the fastglm CRAN benchmarks vignette (package author's machine), at p=2: ZIP n=1000 median 2.47 ms, ZINB n=1e4 78.6 ms, hurdle-NB n=1e4 32.1 ms. There is no direct comparison with glmmTMB. In the R Journal glmmTMB paper (NB GLMM), mgcv took 0.03× and gamlss 0.24× of glmmTMB's time. The speedup over glmmTMB at EDI sizes is therefore not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: In catalog §10 TODO-3, record fastglm_hurdle/fastglm_zi (weights=) as the reference for weighted kernels. Prototype weights in EDI's C++ kernels and benchmark against glmmTMB per replicate at n=50–2000.

findings.candidate: A scalar tail-probability series with an adaptive cutoff and a rank-1 update per observation, or a trigamma-free evaluation of the trigamma expectations (Yu, Dousti Mousavi & Yang).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The arXiv abstract says 'highly efficient and much more accurate than previous methods'. Analytically, each term drops from O(p²) plus allocations to O(1).
findings.suggested_action: Delete the dead expected_hessian, or rewrite it with a tail-series or trigamma-free method if it is ever needed.

findings.candidate: Pass se = !estimate_only to glmmTMB() at both weighted call sites. Optionally also pass conv_check = 'skip' on estimate-only replicates. The parallel = 1L half of the earlier candidate is already done.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The glmmTMB refman documents se only as 'whether to return standard errors', and says eigval_check 'may be very slow' with many fixed effects.
findings.suggested_action: Under v1.1.0-TODO-214: parallel = 1L has landed, so only se = !estimate_only remains. Add it at inference_count_hurdle.R:537 and inference_count_zero_augmented_poisson_abstract.R:1182, then time a B=200 run.
